.I wanted to clarify this question as to why “inability of the ventricles to accept blood” is the best answer vs the other regarding MI and fibrous distensible tissue.  
First of all MI, while absolutely can lead to heart failure, it is not always a guarantee. That is not necessarily why that is the right answer, rather the key word “distensible” meaning stretched would be the key word. Distensible fibrous tissue would be systolic heart failure, meaning over stretch while diastolic heart failure would be non-distensible fibrous tissue.

2251 PT 2201 SEC1100 CARDIOPULMONARY PT 1
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

Course Description 
In this course students will focus on examining the pathophysiology and management of individuals with cardiovascular and pulmonary disease with emphasis on the physiologic systems that support to the performance of aerobic exercise and human movement. Specific attention will be given to the implications of cardiovascular and pulmonary disease on physical therapy practice, and how to consider these implications when applying the principles of exercise prescription to healthy individuals and people with co-morbid chronic diseases. This course will also include an overview EKG rhythm interpretation, cardiovascular and pulmonary diagnostic testing, lab value analysis, case analyses of cardiovascular and pulmonary assessment data, and instruction in vital sign assessment.

Course Outcomes 
On completion of this course, students will be able to:

CO1: Explain to clients the structure and function of the neuromuscular system and discuss expected changes during exercise.  
CO2: Describe to clients the structure and function of the cardiovascular system and demonstrate expected changes during exercise.  
CO3: Educate clients about the structure and function of the pulmonary system and illustrate expected changes during exercise.  
CO4: Compare and contrast the relative energy yield for different macronutrients and discuss how different sources of energy (i.e., ATP, phosphocreatine, blood glucose, glycogen, triglycerides and protein) are used during exercise.  
CO5: Contrast the systemic adaptations that occur in the organ systems in response to increased and decreased use. 
CO6: Describe the different components (frequency, intensity, time, and type) of exercise prescription for aerobic fitness and resistance exercises and apply the ACSM guidelines to a healthy population.  
CO7: Perform the basic components of a cardiopulmonary examination by applying proper techniques to obtain accurate physiological measures for heart rate, blood pressure, shortness of breath, rate of perceived exertion, and pulse oximetry.  
CO8: Analyze changes in vital signs with position changes, physical activity, and exercise and determine if a normal or abnormal response has occurred.  
CO9: Describe the electrical conduction system of the heart, analyze an EKG strip to determine heart rate and rhythm, and contrast the physiology behind normal and abnormal EKG’s.  
CO10: Identify major atrial and ventricular EKG arrhythmias from EKG strip presentations and describe appropriate clinical response as it relates to physical therapy interventions.  
CO11: Identify emergency rescue procedures as they pertain to physical therapy practice in patients who experience airway obstruction and choking, bleeding, syncope, chest pain, shortness of breath, as demonstrated either by symptomatology or by abnormal rhythms on EKG.  
CO12: Identify and interpret the results of cardiovascular and pulmonary diagnostic tests including objective information derived from laboratory, diagnostic, and procedure data.   
CO13: Identify a physical therapy plan on care based on degree of abnormality of laboratory values and provide rationale for postponing physical therapy intervention when a patient has critical lab values.  
CO14: Describe and demonstrate how to prescribe and modify exercise for an individual with cardiopulmonary disease including the frequency, intensity, duration and progression of the program.   
CO15: Identify and discuss the benefits of exercise and physical activity for individuals with and without cardiopulmonary diseases.  
CO16: Identify individuals that may be at increased risk of a coronary event, respiratory event, or heart failure and demonstrate how these findings would impact clinical monitoring and physical therapy interventions.  
CO17: Demonstrate competency in clinical decision making through identification of exercise contraindications and termination points in individuals with cardiopulmonary disease.    
CO18: Identify the role of the physical therapist and other members of the health care team with patients that demonstrate cardiopulmonary impairments.  
CO19: Apply principles of exercise physiology to construct exercise prescriptions for different populations of people with chronic diseases AND co-morbid cardiopulmonary conditions.

Expectations for Participation
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

The following guidelines outline the participation expectations of students in the University of Pittsburgh's Physical Therapy program.  The Expectations for Participation guidelines aim to support a community and classroom culture where all students feel safe to participate.

.Online Student Conduct
    Appropriate online student conduct is a University priority. You are required to observe the same University standards of courtesy and interpersonal respect that govern face-to-face classroom behavior, including appropriate tone and language when engaged in all forms of communication with students and instructors. This includes synchronous and asynchronous course elements, such as emails, discussion forums, group work, assessments, and live sessions. Be respectful. Be inclusive. 

    Remember: All comments and discussions should be respectful of the instructor and fellow students; disagreements are fine, but personal attacks are not.

    Please visit Student Affair's Office of Student Conduct website to review the Student Code of Conduct. 

.Course Communication
    You should log into Canvas several times per week to work through learning modules. Course announcements will be used to post timely changes from the instructor. You are expected to check your official University of Pittsburgh email (pitt.edu) on a frequent and consistent basis to remain informed of University communications, as some may be time sensitive. Your official University email address should be used for all course communications. The most effective way to reach your instructor is through their University of Pittsburgh email or office telephone number. Instructor contact information can be found on the course overview page. Emails should be titled with the course number for clarity.

 
Live Session Attendance
    Synchronous live sessions will be held weekly through Zoom. Login details will be provided into the Canvas Zoom tab. Sessions may be recorded at the discretion of the faculty. You will be expected to complete the assigned asynchronous content prior to the synchronous sessions. The duration of time for the asynchronous sessions will be 1.5 to 2.5 hours per module. Attendance at live sessions is a course requirement. If you are unable to attend a weekly live session, please contact your faculty at least one day prior to your absence to make arrangements. Multiple absences may negatively impact your overall course grade. Although technical and connectivity issues may occur, you must make every effort to engage in live sessions through the software. Active participation involves asking questions and contributing to the discussion.

    Synchronous live session netiquette:
        Log unto the course from a distraction-free, quiet environment.
        Please do not use profanity or inappropriate language
        Consider using a headset with an external mic for best hearing and speaking capabilities.
        Dress professionally
        Be visible with a camera (without others or pets in frame)
        Remain visible throughout the session
        Be fully engaged with faculty and peers.
            If you would like to participate in the discussion or answer a question, use the “Raise Hand” feature. Then unmute
            yourself after you are called on by your faculty.  Remember to mute your microphone when you aren’t speaking.
            If you would like to use the chat feature, remember that it is public, and a record of the chat may be kept
            and archived.
            Important: The chat feature should be used only for class-related discussions—comments, sharing of resources, etc. Keep remarks on-topic and courteous. Remember that this is still our classroom.
 

.Discussion Board Participation 
    Discussion boards may be used in the course to reinforce course concepts and stimulate student engagement with their faculty and peers. If your course is using discussion forums (Canvas discussion forums, Yellowdig, etc.), please note that participation in asynchronous discussions is a course requirement.   Discussions are graded based on a rubric to evaluate student understanding of course content. Posts should demonstrate connections to module materials, including readings, lectures, interactives, and peer/instructor contributions. 

    Discussion Board Netiquette:
        Respect the opinions of others.
        Stay on topic.
        Be explanatory and justify your opinions with credible sources.
        Be clear and precise in your writing.  
        Avoid jargon and fully write out the text for acronyms the first time they are used in a comment or reply.

    Exam/Quiz Policies 
    Post-Exam and Quiz Communication 
    •  After an exam students should not contact the faculty or adjuncts for 48 hours and quizzes for 24 
    hours. This will allow students time to reflect and make discoveries in order to ask questions, as well 
    as allow faculty time to review the exam and make any adjustments needed. 
    •  Post-exam reflections will be required in order to meet with faculty regarding the exams. They 
    should be completed prior to the meeting. Reflections must be complete and thorough in order to 
    meet with faculty to discuss the exam.  
    •  Quizzes that are not completed on time will be assigned a grade of zero. 
    •  Exams must be started and completed within the testing window unless something is worked out 
    with the instructor, otherwise it may be deemed academic dishonesty if the exam begins any time 
    after the scheduled start time.

('Written Exam Policy.pdf')
    University of Pittsburgh 
    Department of Physical Therapy 
    
    Written Examination Policy                 
    Page 1 of 5 
    
    Effective Date: August 6, 2024          
    Responsible Party: Policy Committee and Department Leadership.  
    Scope: This policy applies to all students, faculty, and administrators involved in the 
    examination process.    
    
    1.  Purpose  
    The purpose of this policy is to establish guidelines for written examinations administered in 
    the Doctor of Physical Therapy (DPT) program. Periodic assessment of content knowledge 
    and clinical application via written examination is essential for teaching, learning, and 
    evaluation purposes. This policy reflects the academic standards outlined in the Commission 
    on Accreditation in Physical Therapy Education (CAPTE) Standards & Required Elements and 
    the Physical Therapy Code of Ethics, ensuring integrity, fairness, and professionalism in the 
    assessment process of rigorous physical therapy education. This policy also encourages 
    students to strive for academic excellence and mastery of the material, ensuring adequate 
    preparation to meet the demands of professional practice.  
    2.  Policy  
    This written examination policy is applicable to all major written examinations throughout 
    the DPT program.  This document establishes the rules and procedures regarding 
    examination retake/remediation, scheduling, and student conduct for major written 
    examinations. 
    3.  Definitions  
    Major examination: Any written examination or quiz administered to a student in a 
    proctored environment.  
    4.  Major Written Examination Retake/Remediation 
    There is no opportunity for retake or formal remediation of written examinations. 
        4.1      Course instructors may present different opportunities for students to demonstrate 
    understanding of course content.                      
    Physical Therapy Department Policy                                                                                          Written Examination Policy 
    
    Page 2 of 5 
    
    5.  Examination Scheduling 
    5.1.  The course instructor will provide the date and time of each written examination in 
    the course syllabus.  
    5.2.  All major written examinations will occur during the assigned class time OR during 
    non-class time that allows for full cohort participation. 
    Examinations scheduled during non-class time should remain between 10:00 AM – 
    6:00 PM Eastern US time. 
    Exceptions to the examination schedule may be made for students with an approved 
    excused absence.  In this case, an alternative examination schedule will be arranged 
    by the course instructor and the student. Exceptions to the examination schedule 
    will not be made for an unexcused or an unapproved absence. 
    5.3.  Within a given course, all major examinations must be administered to all students 
    at the same time, and in a proctored environment (In-person/Proctorio/Zoom).  
    The length of time provided to complete an examination should not exceed the 
    scheduled class time.  
    5.3.1.  All students are expected to begin the major examinations at the designated 
    start time scheduled by the course instructor. 
    5.3.2.  Students are expected to refer to the course syllabus and/or Canvas 
    materials to confirm the examination start time. 
    5.3.3.  Failure to begin the examination within 15 minutes of the designated start 
    time may result in a zero-grade for the examination. 
    5.4.  Alternative testing arrangements recommended by the Office of Disability Resources 
    and Services (DRS) at the University of Pittsburgh will be accommodated by the 
    course instructor. 
    6.  Testing Environment 
    6.1.  Room expectations: Desk/table surfaces and the surrounding floor are free from 
    any clutter that could be perceived as course material. 
    6.2.  Any wall hangings, posters, or dry erase boards with course material MUST be 
    covered or removed during the examination. 
    6.3.  Skeletons or other course related models MUST be removed from the room. 
    Physical Therapy Department Policy                                                                                          Written Examination Policy 
    
    Page 3 of 5 
    
    6.4.  For online testing, all students are expected to keep their laptop computers 
    updated for use with the required proctoring software and associated browsers for 
    all examinations and online work. 
    6.4.1.  Students are required to use a camera for all online proctored examinations 
    as an added measure of security; cameras must be positioned such that the 
    student’s face is fully in frame and identifiable throughout the examination. 
    6.4.2.  It is required that an appropriate and private examination space is used for 
    all online examinations. 
    Inappropriate examination spaces would include coffee shops or other 
    public spaces, automobiles, and family occupied spaces within the home 
    that would cause distraction and interruption with examination. 
    6.4.3.  A secure and stable wireless internet connection is required for all online 
    examinations. 
    Logging into an examination from a public Wi-Fi network is not preferred as 
    this may often result in test takers being removed from Proctorio.  
    
    7.  Student Conduct Expectations 
    Beyond the course instructor, students should neither seek nor accept any assistance during 
    the examination. It is imperative that students do not appear, to any degree, to seek or accept 
    any such assistance (as monitored by the instructor or proctoring software). The student must 
    recognize the necessity of strict adherence to all examination rules and the standards of 
    academic integrity to avoid any unauthorized testing practices, and to avoid even the 
    appearance of unauthorized practices. 
    It is required that students adhere to the following: 
    7.1.  The Program, School, and University Academic Integrity Code 
    7.2.  The program’s Academic Integrity attestation 
    7.3.  Smartwatches, cellphones, iPads, additional lap-tops, textbooks, class notes, “scrap 
    paper”, and/or peer-to-peer communication should not be accessed during an 
    examination unless explicitly approved or required by the instructor. 
    7.3.1.  Access to the designated whiteboard and calculator tools will be permitted 
    for online examinations. 
    Physical Therapy Department Policy                                                                                          Written Examination Policy 
    
    Page 4 of 5 
    
    7.4.  Headphones and air pods are not permitted during examinations; however, 
    students can use traditional “ear plugs” for noise reduction purposes.  Headwear 
    should allow for clear observation of the head, ears and face. 
    7.4.1. Exceptions will be granted for individuals requiring medical devices (i.e. 
    hearing aids) as well as for individuals who wear headwear as part of their 
    religious/ethnic practice. 
    7.5.  To ensure adherence to conduct expectations, it is recommended that students be 
    familiar with “red flag” activities as identified by the proctoring software used 
    during written examinations. For example, eye movements that frequently and 
    consistently move away from the test/computer screen, talking, or the use of non-
    approved course materials to complete the examination will produce a conduct 
    warning to be reviewed by the course instructor. 
    7.5.1.  Students should exhibit professional behavior during examinations. 
    7.5.2.  Refrain from inappropriate language, getting up and moving around, leaving 
    the room and re-entering, etc. 
    7.5.3.  Any student found to be out of compliance with any of the aforementioned 
    requirements will be charged with violation of written examination policy 
    and the department’s academic integrity policy. 
    8.  Posting/Review of Examination Questions 
    8.1.  Upon completion of a major examination, the questions and associated answers 
    will not be made “automatically” available for students to review.  To maintain 
    examination integrity, instructors will develop an appropriate review plan that 
    addresses areas of concern as reflected by the cohort’s examination performance.  
    Review plans will include a process for reviewing individual student inquiries in a 
    manner that maintains examination integrity while also providing valuable 
    “learning” feedback to the student. 
    Course instructors may consider individual review of major examination 
    performance under the instructor’s direct supervision or under the supervision of a 
    teaching assistant, versus large-group review to reduce risk of examination integrity 
    issues. 
    9.  Consequences of Policy Violation 
    9.1.  Failure to adhere to the examination policy may result in a letter-grade reduction or 
    a zero-grade for the respective major examination and will result in a formal 
    notification of a conduct violation (see Conduct Policy). See Graduate, SHRS, and 
    Physical Therapy Department Policy                                                                                          Written Examination Policy 
    
    Page 5 of 5 
    
    DPT Student Handbooks for additional information related to  academic policies and 
    professional conduct.  
    
    10. Forms  
    There are no forms related to the policy.

('Practical Exam Policy.pdf')
    University of Pittsburgh 
    Department of Physical Therapy 
    
    Practical Examination Policy                 
    Page 1 of 4 
    
    Effective Date: August 6, 2024          
    Responsible Party: Policy Committee and Department Leadership.  
    Scope: This policy applies to all students, faculty members, and administrators engaged in the 
    practical examination process.    
    
    1.  Purpose  
    The purpose of this policy is to establish guidelines for practical examinations 
    administered in the Doctor of Physical Therapy (DPT) program. The use of practical 
    examinations as part of student assessment is critical in determining the student’s level 
    of competency with psychomotor skills, clinical reasoning, and decision making. This 
    policy reflects the academic standards outlined in the Commission on Accreditation in 
    Physical Therapy Education (CAPTE) Standards & Required Elements and the Physical 
    Therapy Code of Ethics, ensuring integrity, fairness, and professionalism in the 
    assessment process of rigorous physical therapy education. This policy also encourages 
    students to strive for academic excellence and mastery of the material, ensuring 
    adequate preparation to meet the demands of professional practice.  
    2.  Policy  
    This practical examination policy is applicable to all skill-based practical examinations 
    throughout the DPT program. This document establishes the rules and procedures 
    regarding scheduling, student conduct, retake/remediation, and performance 
    expectations for practical examinations. This policy provides comprehensive guidelines 
    for the examination process; however, it does not encompass every possible scenario. 
    The program reserves the right to address situations that may arise on a case-by-case 
    basis, ensuring fairness, consistency, and adherence to the program’s academic 
    standards. 
    3.  Definitions  
    Not Applicable 
    Physical Therapy Department Policy                                                                                        Practical Examination Policy 
    
    Page 2 of 4 
    
    4.  Practical Examination Scheduling 
    4.1  Course instructors will provide the date and time of each practical examination in 
    the course syllabus.  
    4.2  The practical examinations will occur during assigned class periods. 
    4.3  Exceptions to the exam schedule may be made for students with an approved 
    excused absence.  In this case, an alternative examination schedule will be arranged 
    by the course instructor and the student. If scheduling exceptions need to be made 
    for an approved excused absence, this will be scheduled with the course 
    coordinator and the student. Exceptions to the exam schedule will not be made for 
    unexcused or an unapproved absence.  
    5.  Student Conduct Expectations 
    Adherence to the academic and examination code of conduct is required:  
    5.1.  It is expected that students will adhere to the Program, School, and University 
    Academic Integrity Code. 
    5.2.  Students are expected to recall and adhere to the Academic Integrity attestation.  
    6.  Practical Examination Retake/Remediation 
    6.1.  Students who do not pass the first practical examination will be permitted one 
    opportunity to retake the practical examination.  
    6.2.  Students who miss a practical examination for an unexcused absence (See 
    Attendance Policy) will not be provided an opportunity to reschedule the practical 
    examination. For additional information refer to item 7.3 in this document. 
    6.3.  Re-take Options: Upon the recognition of the need for a student to retake a 
    practical examination, the following re-take options will be considered with 
    reference to the underlying circumstances associated with the specific student 
    performance.  
    6.3.1.  Option 1: The “re-take” practical will be scheduled as an in-person session 
    the same day as the original practical examination. 
    -  This can be considered at the discretion of the faculty. 
    6.3.2.  Option 2: The “re-take” practical will be scheduled for a later date and time.  
    Physical Therapy Department Policy                                                                                        Practical Examination Policy 
    
    Page 3 of 4 
    
    6.4.  Based on the student’s performance, faculty will develop an individualized 
    remediation plan and re-take schedule commensurate with the degree of 
    remediation required. The remediation plan and re-take of the practical 
    examination may be arranged 1) as an in-person (instructor/adjunct) OR virtual 
    (instructor) session and 2) within OR outside the semester the course is offered – at 
    the discretion of the instructor The table below outlines various scenarios that may 
    occur:

    7.  Passing Expectations for Practical Examinations  
    7.1.  All practical examinations offered in the DPT program require a passing score of 
    ≥70%.  A student is required to pass all the practical examinations in order to pass 
    the overall course.

    Practical Examination Policy

    7.2.  The highest score that can be achieved for a retake of a practical examination 
    (despite level of performance) is 70%. 
    7.3.  Failure to pass a retake practical examination OR having an unexcused absence for 
    a scheduled practical will result in a failing grade for course.  
    7.4.  In the case where a student has been unable to successfully pass a required course, 
    a faculty meeting will be held to discuss the student’s case and make 
    recommendations regarding their future status in the program.

//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
Help and General Questions Forum
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

Welcome to the Help and General Questions Forum! This forum is designed to provide you with a space to ask questions, seek clarifications, and receive general support related to the course. Whether you need assistance with course content, assignments, or any other course-related inquiries, this forum is here to help. 

 

Discussion Guidelines:
Be Respectful: Treat all forum participants with respect and professionalism. Avoid using derogatory or offensive language.

Constructive Communication: Engage in constructive and meaningful discussions. Provide helpful and relevant information when responding to fellow students' questions.

Stay on Topic: Keep your questions and responses focused on course-related matters. If you have unrelated concerns, please use the appropriate channels or forums.

 

Posting Instructions:
To post a question or concern, follow these steps:

Click on the "Reply" button to post your question(s) or concern(s).

For the first  line of the reply, please provide descriptive text.  For example, Unable to access lecture in Module 3. 

Next, clearly state your question or concern. Include any relevant details, such as the course module or topic, assignment number, or supporting materials that may help others understand your query better. For example, I am not able to access and view the lecture on page 3.3.  I am receiving an error message stating that I do not have permission to view (Insert screenshot).

 

Response Timeframe:
Our faculty and teaching assistants strive to provide prompt assistance within 24-48 hours (excluding weekends and holidays). Please note that response times may vary depending on the volume of inquiries.

 

Preferred Question Format:
To help us address your questions effectively, please consider the following:

Structure your questions in a clear and concise manner.

Include relevant course details, such as module or topic references, assignment titles, or specific examples.

If applicable, attach any supporting materials or screenshots that may aid in understanding your question.

Do NOT post exam, quiz, or assignment answers.
 

Search the Forum:
Before posting a new question, we encourage you to search the forum to see if your query has already been answered. This helps avoid duplicate questions and allows you to find existing solutions quickly.

 

Etiquette and Respectful Communication:
Maintain a respectful and professional tone in all forum interactions. Remember that this is a collaborative learning space, and everyone's contributions are valued. Avoid engaging in personal attacks or offensive language.

 

Instructor Participation:
While the Help and General Questions Forum primarily fosters student-to-student interaction, our faculty, co-faculty, and teaching assistants will monitor and engage in discussions. They will provide guidance, clarification, and additional support as needed.

 

Additional Support Channels:
If you require additional assistance, you can also reach out to the faculty during office hours or via email. Refer to the course syllabus for further details on available support resources.

We look forward to your active participation in the Help and General Questions Forum! Remember, this is a community where we learn together and support each other's academic journey.

.Blood Flow through the Heart:
    Review the following image to better understand how blood flows through the heart and into systemic circulation via the aorta. You should be able to name all the different structures here, as well as the direction of flow within and through each of these structures.

    ('Blood Flow through the Heart.png')
        (Γ)
            Blood Flow through the Heart:

            - Superior vena cava
            - Aorta
            - Pulmonary artery
            - Pulmonary veins
            - Right atrium
            - Pulmonary valve
            - Aortic valve
            - Tricuspid valve
            - Left ventricle
            - Right ventricle
            - Inferior vena cava

            ---

            ### Detailed Explanation:

            The heart is a vital organ responsible for pumping blood throughout the body. Here's a step-by-step explanation of the blood flow through the heart:

            1. Deoxygenated Blood Entry: Blood from the body enters the heart through the superior vena cava and inferior vena cava into the right atrium.
            2. Right Atrium to Right Ventricle: The blood then flows through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle.
            3. Pulmonary Circulation: From the right ventricle, blood is pumped through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary artery and then to the lungs. In the lungs, blood receives oxygen and releases carbon dioxide.
            4. Oxygenated Blood Return: Oxygenated blood returns to the heart through the pulmonary veins into the left atrium.
            5. Left Atrium to Left Ventricle: Blood flows from the left atrium through the mitral valve into the left ventricle.
            6. Systemic Circulation: Finally, the left ventricle pumps the oxygenated blood through the aortic valve into the aorta, which distributes it to the rest of the body.

            This cycle repeats continuously, ensuring that oxygen-rich blood reaches all parts of the body and deoxygenated blood is sent to the lungs for reoxygenation.

.Mechanics of Breathing
     In the image below you should be able to understand and explain the mechanics of breathing, including terms such as, muscles of inspiration, elastic recoil on expiration, atmospheric pressure vs intrapleural pressure, and gas exchange.

    ('Mechanics of Breathing.png')
        (Γ)
            Mechanics of Breathing

            - Breathing in:
            - Chest expands
            - Ribs elevate
            - Diaphragm contracts

            - Breathing out:
            - Chest contracts
            - Ribs lower
            - Diaphragm relaxes

            ---

            ### Detailed Explanation:

            Breathing, or respiration, involves the movement of air into and out of the lungs. This process can be divided into two main phases: inspiration (breathing in) and expiration (breathing out).

            1. Inspiration (Breathing In):
            - Chest Expansion: During inspiration, the chest cavity expands. This is achieved by the contraction of the intercostal muscles, which lift the ribs upwards and outwards.
            - Diaphragm Contraction: The diaphragm, a dome-shaped muscle located below the lungs, contracts and flattens. This increases the volume of the thoracic cavity.
            - Pressure Changes: As the thoracic cavity expands, the pressure inside the lungs (intrapulmonary pressure) decreases below atmospheric pressure, causing air to flow into the lungs.

            2. Expiration (Breathing Out):
            - Chest Contraction: During expiration, the chest cavity contracts. The intercostal muscles relax, allowing the ribs to move downwards and inwards.
            - Diaphragm Relaxation: The diaphragm relaxes and returns to its dome shape, decreasing the volume of the thoracic cavity.
            - Pressure Changes: As the thoracic cavity decreases in volume, the pressure inside the lungs increases above atmospheric pressure, causing air to flow out of the lungs.

            ### Additional Concepts:

            - Muscles of Inspiration: These include the diaphragm and the external intercostal muscles.
            - Elastic Recoil on Expiration: The lungs have elastic properties that allow them to return to their original shape after being stretched during inspiration.
            - Atmospheric Pressure vs Intrapleural Pressure: Atmospheric pressure is the pressure exerted by the weight of the air in the atmosphere. Intrapleural pressure is the pressure within the pleural cavity, which is always slightly negative relative to atmospheric pressure.
            - Gas Exchange: This occurs in the alveoli of the lungs, where oxygen from the inhaled air diffuses into the blood, and carbon dioxide from the blood diffuses into the alveoli to be exhaled.

.Pulmonary System
     The pulmonary system is the lungs, their airways, and their vascular network.

    ('Pulmonary System.png')
        (Γ)
            Pulmonary System

            - Trachea
            - Superior lobe
            - Bronchus
            - Lobar bronchus
            - Segmental (tertiary) bronchus
            - Cardiac notch
            - Inferior lobe
            - Left lung

            ---

            ### Detailed Explanation:

            The pulmonary system, also known as the respiratory system, is responsible for the exchange of gases (oxygen and carbon dioxide) between the body and the environment. Here's a step-by-step explanation of the key components and their functions:

            1. Trachea: The trachea, or windpipe, is a tube that connects the larynx (voice box) to the bronchi of the lungs. It allows air to pass through to the lungs.

            2. Bronchus: The trachea divides into two main bronchi (left and right), each leading to one lung. The bronchi further divide into smaller branches called lobar bronchi.

            3. Lobar Bronchus: Each lobar bronchus supplies air to a specific lobe of the lung. The right lung has three lobes (superior, middle, and inferior), while the left lung has two lobes (superior and inferior).

            4. Segmental (Tertiary) Bronchus: The lobar bronchi further divide into segmental bronchi, which supply air to specific segments within each lobe.

            5. Cardiac Notch: The cardiac notch is an indentation on the left lung that accommodates the heart.

            6. Lobes of the Lungs: The right lung has three lobes (superior, middle, and inferior), while the left lung has two lobes (superior and inferior). Each lobe is further divided into segments, each supplied by a segmental bronchus.

            ### Additional Concepts:

            - Alveoli: The smallest air sacs in the lungs where gas exchange occurs. Oxygen from the inhaled air diffuses into the blood, and carbon dioxide from the blood diffuses into the alveoli to be exhaled.
            - Vascular Network: The lungs have a rich network of blood vessels that facilitate the exchange of gases. The pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs, and the pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart.

.Structure
    The upper respiratory tract is the nose, pharynx, and larynx. Pictured is the lower respiratory tract. The section in green is the conduction zone and moves air in and out of the lung. The blue zone is the respiration zone where actual gas exchange occurs.

    ('Structure.png')
        (Γ)
            Structure

            - Trachea
            - Primary bronchus
            - Bronchus
            - Bronchi
            - Bronchioles
            - Respiratory bronchioles
            - Alveolar ducts
            - Alveolar sacs

            ---

            ### Detailed Explanation:

            The respiratory system is divided into two main parts: the upper respiratory tract and the lower respiratory tract. The image focuses on the lower respiratory tract, which includes the structures involved in the conduction and exchange of gases.

            1. Conduction Zone (Green):
            - Trachea: The trachea, or windpipe, is a tube that connects the larynx to the bronchi. It allows air to pass through to the lungs.
            - Primary Bronchus: The trachea divides into two primary bronchi (left and right), each leading to one lung.
            - Bronchus: The primary bronchi further divide into secondary (lobar) bronchi and then into tertiary (segmental) bronchi.
            - Bronchioles: The bronchi continue to divide into smaller branches called bronchioles. These are the smallest airways in the conduction zone.

            2. Respiratory Zone (Blue):
            - Respiratory Bronchioles: These are the smallest bronchioles that lead to the alveolar ducts. They are part of the respiratory zone where gas exchange begins.
            - Alveolar Ducts: These ducts connect the respiratory bronchioles to the alveolar sacs.
            - Alveolar Sacs: These are clusters of alveoli, which are the tiny air sacs where gas exchange occurs.

            ### Additional Concepts:

            - Gas Exchange: This occurs in the alveoli, where oxygen from the inhaled air diffuses into the blood, and carbon dioxide from the blood diffuses into the alveoli to be exhaled.
            - Conduction Zone: This zone is responsible for moving air in and out of the lungs but does not participate in gas exchange.
            - Respiratory Zone: This zone is where actual gas exchange occurs between the air and the blood.

.Alveoli
    This is where gas exchange occurs at the lung. The oxygen enters the lung tissue and carbon dioxide is removed from the lung and back to the air to be exhaled.

    ('Alveoli.png')
        (Γ)
            Alveoli

            - Bronchiole
            - Pulmonary artery
            - Pulmonary vein
            - Capillary network
            - Alveoli

            ---

            ### Detailed Explanation:

            The alveoli are tiny air sacs in the lungs where the exchange of gases takes place. Here's a step-by-step explanation of the key components and their functions:

            1. Bronchiole: The bronchioles are the smallest airways in the lungs that lead to the alveolar ducts. They are part of the conducting zone and help move air into the alveoli.

            2. Pulmonary Artery: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle of the heart to the lungs. This blood is rich in carbon dioxide and low in oxygen.

            3. Pulmonary Vein: The pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood from the lungs back to the left atrium of the heart. This blood is rich in oxygen and low in carbon dioxide.

            4. Capillary Network: The capillary network surrounds the alveoli and is where the exchange of gases occurs. Oxygen from the inhaled air diffuses into the blood in the capillaries, and carbon dioxide from the blood diffuses into the alveoli to be exhaled.

            5. Alveoli: The alveoli are tiny, balloon-like structures at the end of the respiratory tree. They are the primary site of gas exchange in the lungs. Each alveolus is surrounded by a network of capillaries where oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged.

            ### Gas Exchange Process:

            - Inhalation: When you inhale, air travels through the bronchioles and reaches the alveoli. Oxygen from the air diffuses through the walls of the alveoli and into the capillaries.
            - Oxygen Transport: The oxygen binds to hemoglobin in red blood cells and is transported to the rest of the body.
            - Carbon Dioxide Removal: Carbon dioxide, a waste product of cellular respiration, diffuses from the blood in the capillaries into the alveoli.
            - Exhalation: When you exhale, the carbon dioxide is expelled from the alveoli and out of the body.

            This continuous process ensures that your body receives the oxygen it needs and removes carbon dioxide efficiently.

.Lung volumes
    Below is the tracing of lung volume found in a normal pulmonary function test and definition of each volume measured.

    ('Lung volumes.png')
        (Γ)
            Lung Volumes

            - Inspiratory Reserve Volume (IRV)
            - Inspiratory Capacity (IC)
            - Vital Capacity (VC)
            - Tidal Volume (TV)
            - Total Lung Capacity (TLC)
            - Expiratory Reserve Volume (ERV)
            - Functional Residual Capacity (FRC)
            - Residual Volume (RV)

            ---

            ### Detailed Explanation:

            The graph represents various lung volumes and capacities measured during a pulmonary function test. Here's a detailed explanation of each term:

            1. Tidal Volume (TV): The amount of air inhaled or exhaled during normal breathing. It represents the regular, rhythmic breathing cycle.

            2. Inspiratory Reserve Volume (IRV): The additional volume of air that can be inhaled after a normal inhalation. It measures the lung's capacity to take in extra air beyond the tidal volume.

            3. Expiratory Reserve Volume (ERV): The additional volume of air that can be exhaled after a normal exhalation. It measures the lung's capacity to expel extra air beyond the tidal volume.

            4. Residual Volume (RV): The volume of air remaining in the lungs after maximal exhalation. This air cannot be expelled and ensures that the lungs do not collapse.

            5. Inspiratory Capacity (IC): The sum of Tidal Volume and Inspiratory Reserve Volume. It represents the maximum amount of air that can be inhaled after a normal exhalation.

            6. Functional Residual Capacity (FRC): The sum of Expiratory Reserve Volume and Residual Volume. It represents the volume of air remaining in the lungs at the end of a normal exhalation.

            7. Vital Capacity (VC): The sum of Tidal Volume, Inspiratory Reserve Volume, and Expiratory Reserve Volume. It represents the maximum amount of air that can be moved in and out of the lungs during a given time period.

            8. Total Lung Capacity (TLC): The sum of Vital Capacity and Residual Volume. It represents the total amount of air contained in the lungs at the end of maximal inspiration.

            ### Additional Definitions:

            -ERV: Expiratory reserve volume; maximal volume that can be expired from a resting expiration.
            -FRC: Functional residual capacity; volume of gas in lungs at resting expiratory level.
            -IC: Inspiratory capacity; maximal volume that can be inspired from resting expiratory level.
            -IRV: Inspiratory reserve volume; maximal volume that can be inspired from end-tidal inspiratory level.
            -TLC: Total lung capacity; volume of gas in lungs at end of maximal inspiration.
            -VC: Vital capacity; maximal volume that can be expired after maximal inspiration.
            -MVV: Maximal voluntary ventilation; the amount of air that can be moved in and out of the lungs during a given time period.
            -RV: Residual volume; the volume of air contained in the lungs after a maximal expiration.
            -TV: Tidal Volume; amount of air that moves in or out of the lungs with each respiratory cycle.

            These measurements are crucial for assessing lung function and diagnosing respiratory conditions.

.Vital Signs
    ('Vital Signs.png')
        (Γ)
            Vital Signs

            The below charts show normal vital signs for adults and what are abnormal vital signs.

            1. Heart Rate
            - Normal: 60-100 beats per minute
            - Abnormal:
                - < 60 bradycardia
                - > 100 tachycardia

            2. Respiratory Rate
            - Normal: 12-18 breaths per minute
            - Abnormal:
                - < 10 bradypnea
                - > 20 tachypnea

            3. Blood Oxygen
            - Normal: 95-100%
            - Abnormal:
                - < 90% hypoxia

            ---

            ### Detailed Explanation:

            Heart Rate:
            - Normal: A heart rate of 60-100 beats per minute is considered normal for adults. This range indicates a healthy heart function.
            - Abnormal:
            - Bradycardia: A heart rate of less than 60 beats per minute. This can indicate an issue with the heart's electrical system or be a result of certain medications or conditions.
            - Tachycardia: A heart rate of more than 100 beats per minute. This can be caused by stress, anxiety, fever, or heart conditions.

            Respiratory Rate:
            - Normal: A respiratory rate of 12-18 breaths per minute is considered normal for adults. This range indicates healthy lung function.
            - Abnormal:
            - Bradypnea: A respiratory rate of less than 10 breaths per minute. This can be caused by respiratory depression, head injury, or certain medications.
            - Tachypnea: A respiratory rate of more than 20 breaths per minute. This can be caused by fever, anxiety, lung disease, or heart conditions.

            Blood Oxygen:
            - Normal: A blood oxygen level of 95-100% is considered normal for adults. This range indicates that the blood is carrying a sufficient amount of oxygen.
            - Abnormal:
            - Hypoxia: A blood oxygen level of less than 90%. This can indicate a problem with lung function, heart function, or circulation.

            These vital signs are crucial for assessing overall health and identifying potential medical conditions.

.Blood Pressure Stages 
    ('Blood Pressure Stages .png')
        (Γ)
            Blood Pressure Stages

            1. Blood Pressure Category: Normal
            - Systolic (upper #) mm Hg: less than 120
            - Diastolic (lower #) mm Hg: less than 80

            2. Blood Pressure Category: Elevated
            - Systolic (upper #) mm Hg: 120-129
            - Diastolic (lower #) mm Hg: less than 80

            3. Blood Pressure Category: High Blood Pressure (Hypertension Stage 1)
            - Systolic (upper #) mm Hg: 130-139
            - Diastolic (lower #) mm Hg: or 80-89

            4. Blood Pressure Category: High Blood Pressure (Hypertension Stage 2)
            - Systolic (upper #) mm Hg: 140 or higher
            - Diastolic (lower #) mm Hg: or 90 or higher

            5. Blood Pressure Category: Hypertensive Crisis (Seek Emergency Care)
            - Systolic (upper #) mm Hg: higher than 180
            - Diastolic (lower #) mm Hg: and/or higher than 120

.Terms to know 
    Terms related to measures of cardiovascular functi on  
        -BP: blood pressure; BP = CO x TPR or BP = (SV x HR) TPR; reported as SBP/DBP 
        -DBP: diastolic blood pressure - measures the pressure in your arteries when your heart rests between beats or when the heart is filling with de -oxygenated blood to move through the heart.  
        -SBP: systolic blood pressure - measures the pressure in your arteries when your heart beats or when blood is released into systemic circulati on from the left ventricle.  
        -CO or Q: cardiac output; CO=Heart RateStroke Volume; measured in mL/min or the total amount of blood the heart pumps in a minute 
        -ECG: Electrocardiogram; recording of electrical signals of the heart. The ECG reading will contain waves and intervals that match the electrical conducti on through the heart as depicted above.  
        -HR: heart rate; measured as the number of beats in a minute. 
        -SV: stroke volume; measured in mL and is the total amount of blood pumped from the left  ventricle during each heartbeat. 
        -TPR: total peripheral resistance or the level of resistance in the vascular/arterial system; measured as the amount of force exerted on the arteries in circulati ng blood. 
        
    Terms related to measures of pulmonary functi on  
        FVC: forced vital capacity; maximal volume that can be expired after maximal inspiration   
        FEV1: forced expiratory volume in 1 sec; maximal volume that is expired in the first sec   
        FEV1/FVC: ratio of the FEV1 to FVC; low values can indicate COPD  
        PFT: Pulmonary Functi on Test; include measurement of lung volumes, FVC, maximum voluntary venti lation  
        RR: respiratory rate; number of breaths per minute 
        TV: tidal volume; volume of air inspired by lungs in each breath   
        VE: Minute venti lati on; Amount of air inspired by lungs in one minute  
        
    Terms related to measures of exercise prescripti on  
        -FITTE Principle: Mnemonic for elements of exercise prescripti on; F (requency), I(ntensity), T(ime), T(ype), E(njoyment)  
        -HRmax: maximum heart rate during exercise, in beats per minute  
        -HRreserve: diff erence between maximum heart rate and resti ng heart rate  MET: Metabolic Equivalent; standard unit for quantif ying intensity of aerobic exercise relati ve to the resti ng metabolic rate; equal to 3.5 mL of oxygen intake per kg body mass per minute   
        -RPE: Rati ng of Perceived Exerti on; scale for measuring an individual’s perceived work eff ort during exercise  
        -VO2: volume of oxygen inspired in Liters per minute  
        -VO2max: maximum capacity of volume of oxygen inspired during aerobic exercise, in liters per minute  
        -VO2reserve: diff erence between maximum oxygen intake and resti ng oxygen intake   
        
    Terms related to cardiovascular dysfuncti on  
        CAD: coronary artery disease OR blockage in the coronary arteries 
        CHF: Congesti ve Heart Failure  
        CKD: Chronic Kidney Disease  
        DVT: Deep vein thrombosis  
        HF: Heart Failure 
        HTN: hypertension or high blood pressure 
        Hypotension: low blood pressure 
        MI: myocardial infarcti on or heart att ack  
        PAD: peripheral arterial disease 
        PVD: peripheral venous disease 
        
    Terms related to pulmonary dysfuncti on  
        -COPD: Chronic Obstructi ve Pulmonary Disorder 
        -Obstructive : a group of pulmonary diseases characterized by presence of airfl ow obstructi on that is att ributable to either chronic bronchiti s or emphysema  with diffi culty with expiration  (getti ng air out  of the lungs) 
        -PE: Pulmonary Embolism; a blood clot that is in the lungs 
        -Restrictive : a group of pulmonary diseases in which there is reduced lung compliance and diffi culty  with lung expansion and inspirati on  (getti ng air in to the lungs)  
        
    Terms related to oxygenati on status  and blood gases 
        -Acidemia: conditi on that causes an increase in hydrogen ions in the blood, resulti ng in a decrease in pH. It can also be defi ned as abnormally high blood acidity, which can be caused by an increase in acidic substances or a decrease in alkaline substances. This means that the serum pH is lower than normal, with arterial pH less than 7.35 
        -Alkalemia: also known as alkalosis, occurs when the concentrati on  of hydrogen ions in the blood decreases, resulti ng in an increase in pH. This means that the serum pH is higher than normal, with arterial pH greater than 7.45 
        -Hypoxia: low level of oxygen in the ti ssues of the body  
        -Hypoxemia: low levels of oxygen in the blood 
        -Hyperoxemia: parti al pressure  of oxygen (PaO2) in arterial blood gas analysis is higher than 100 mmHg 
        -Hypercarbia/Hypercapnia:  high level of carbon dioxide in the blood, above the normal range of 35–45 mmHg 
        -Hypocarbia/Hypocapnia:  low level of carbon dioxide in the blood, below the normal range of 35–45 mmHg 
        -Hyperventi lation : rapid or deep breathing in the presence of low oxygen, causes CO2 levels to drop 
        -Hypoventi lation :  shallow or slow breathing, CO2 levels rise 
        -PaO2: Pressure of oxygen in the arterial blood 
        -SaO2: Saturati on of oxygen on hemoglobin measured from arterial blood 
        -SpO2: Saturati on of oxygen on hemoglobin measured with a pulse oximeter 
        
    Terms related to lab values 
        ABG: Arterial Blood Gases 
        CBC: Complete Blood Cell Count  
        HCT: Hematocrit; % of red blood cells in plasma 
        Hb: Hemoglobin; the primary molecule for transportati on of oxygen in the blood  
        Plt: Platelets  
        RBC: Red Blood Cell 
        WBC: White Blood Cell

Roles of Individuals on Interprofessional Team

Module Introduction
Now we’re going to delve into how a physical therapist fits into the healthcare team that provides services to patients at risk for or diagnosed with cardiopulmonary disease and impairments.
When considering a healthcare team, it is important to realize that many different types of providers provide interventions for patients with cardiopulmonary conditions. Medical providers, such as, doctors, nurses, respiratory therapists, nutritionist/dietitian, and exercise physiologists, to name a few, are a part of this very important team. The physical therapist is also a critical member of this team, and it is important to know the role of each care provider, as it will play a role in communication and services provided to this patient population. 
Participate in the following learning activity;
Instructions: Identify the member of the interprofessional team who is most likely to provide the following service. In some cases, more than one provider may provide the service.
Providers to choose from:
Medical Doctor (MD)
Nurse (RN)
Physical Therapist (PT)
Respiratory Therapist (RT)
Exercise Physiologist (EP)

Physical Therapist (PT)

As you can see, the IP team works closely to meet the needs of the cardiopulmonary patient.  Even so, it is important to understand the scope of the practice of each individual on the team. You will note our profession offers many interventions that are within the PT scope of practice in addition to exercise, including some of those that are less known such as airway clearance, breathing strategies, suctioning, oxygen titration, and various others that you will become familiar with as you move through the cardiopulmonary series. PTs also work with other providers such exercise physiologists who may be involved in exercise prescription and cardiac rehabilitation services, but have separate goals of treatment. Understanding the patient’s full medical picture, such as, lab values, medical status and components of the patient’s diagnosis and making clinical decisions that could affect exercise capabilities and/or require PT intervention is very important part of PT practice. This is also an area that is required for a PT to communicate efficiently with the health care team, as if a patient has an order for PT from the medical doctor, but there is a concerning lab value that may make then unsafe to exercise, the PT must have the ability to communicate that concern.

Myocardial infarction (MI)
This is the technical term for a heart attack. The word myocardial refers to the heart muscle or 'myocardium'. Infarction refers to a blockage in blood supply.
.Cystic Fibrosis
“The infant that tastes of salt will surely die. This observa-
tion  from  ancient  European  folklore  is  probably  the  first
recognition of cystic fibrosis (CF), a disease that is character-
ized by abnormal salt transport, and in early times, death in
infancy.” 4
Today, CF is recognized as a multisystem disorder affecting
both children, and increasingly young adults. 5  In 2007, 45%
of the individuals in the CF Patient Registry were adults (18
years and older). 6  Cystic fibrosis affects every organ system
that has epithelial surfaces, 7  with the most prominent symp-
toms in clinical presentation relating to pulmonary and pan-
creatic  involvement.  The  pulmonary  system  is  affected  by
chronic  airway  obstruction  and  inflammation,  thick  tena -
cious mucus, and recurrent bacterial infections. In addition,
the  pancreas  develops  exocrine  pancreatic  insufficiency,
which  affects  both  gastrointestinal  function  (fat  maldiges-
tion) and the growth and development of individuals with
CF. 8   Other  organs  affected  include  the  upper  airway  (sinus
infections),  male  reproductive  tract  (obstructive  azoosper-
mia), and sweat glands (elevated sweat chloride levels).

2.0. Module Introduction
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

Module Introduction 
Welcome to Module 2! In this module you will learn about the basic anatomy of the Electrocardiogram (ECG) as it relates to the electrophysiological mechanisms within the heart over a full cardiac cycle. You will be learning how to recognize irregular ECG rhythms and relate that to patient presentation and appropriate clinical response. This module will detail each component of the ECG, arrhythmic ECG readings and the clinical application and response when there are arrhythmias present; including those that are considered lift threatening.  

Learning Objectives
By the end of this week, you will be able to: 

Identify the basic anatomy of the ECG related to the electrophysiological principles the heart, and name each component of the ECG, including waves, intervals and segments as they appear on a normal ECG strip. 
Calculate the heart rate on the ECG strip, and determine if the heart rate is normal, tachycardic, or bradycardic. 
Determine and name arrhythmias and determine how a patient symptomology to abnormal ECG rhythms. 
Apply ECG reading to clinical practice and identify appropriate clinical response to abnormal ECG readings during rest and exercise.

    Introduction to Electrocardiography

    .Electrocardiography
    • Understanding an electrocardiogram (ECG) requires the following:
    • Basic understanding of the electrophysiology and anatomy of the 
    heart/conduction system
    • Knowledge of both normal and abnormal ECG waveforms
    • Practice in systematic review of 12-lead/single lead ECG rhythm 
    strips
    • PT should be able to determine if tracing is benign or life-threatening


    .Why are ECGs performed?
    Diagnosis or evaluation of symptoms

    Monitor the heart’s electrical activity

    Determine effectiveness or side effects of medication

    Exercise ECG

    24 Hour Holter monitor 


    .Basic Electrophysiological Principles
    • Unique properties of cardiac muscle 
    1. Automaticity
    • Discharge an electrical stimulus
    2. Rhythmicity
    • Regularity with which pacing 
    occurs
    3. Conductivity
    • Can spread impulses
    • SA node has normal rate of 60 to 100 
    bpm
    • AV node has firing rate of 40 to 60 bpm
    • His-Purkinje portions have a firing rate 
    of 30 to 40 bpm 


    .Basic Electrophysiological Principles
    • The conduction system
    • Composed of myocytes arranged in a pathway that spreads 
    electrical activity throughout the four chambers
    1. Electrical pulse initiated in the SA node in atria
    2. Travels to left atrium via Bachmann bundle
    3. Travels to AV node, atrial kick
    4. Travels to His bundle and bundle branches
    5. Travels to Purkinje fibers in the ventricles


    .Basic Electrophysiological Principles
    • The autonomic nervous system
    • Sympathetic division 
    • Discharges norepinephrine
    • Acts on SA node, AV node, ventricles
    • Stimulates adrenal gland to secrete catecholamines
    • Increases HR, conduction velocity, contractility, irritability
    • Parasympathetic division
    • Discharge acetylcholine
    • Vagus nerve is main component in control of the heart
    • General inhibitor on rate and conduction velocity


    .Automaticity Foci
    • Other “potential pacemakers” will 
    take over if the SA node fails to 
    pace
    • Other foci are called “ectopic” foci 
    and each has inherent rate
    • Locations
    • Atria (atrial automaticity foci)
    • AV junction (junctional 
    automaticity foci)
    • Ventricles (ventricular 
    automaticity foci)


    .Basic Electrophysiological Principles
    • Electrical stimulation makes the cell 
    membrane more permeable to the flow of 
    ions
    • Depolarization
    • electrical stimulation of specialized cells that cause 
    contraction
    • Repolarization
    • Myocytes return to their resting negative charge (Polarized)


    .Basic Electrophysiological Principles

    At rest K+ inside, 
    Na+ outside the 
    cell
    (-) inside/ (+) 
    outside cell
    ↓
    Electrical impulse 
    makes membrane 
    more permeable 
    to Na+
    ↓
    Na+ in & K+ out
    (-) to (+) charge 
    inside the cell
    ↓
    Depolarization & 
    Contraction


    .How does this look on an ECG?
    • Average of all the action potential of the heart
    • Cycle of depolarization and repolarization
    • Y-axis = Amplitude/Height of waves (voltage) is measured in millivolts 
    (mV)
    • 1mV = 10 mm (high)
    • X-axis = Time (seconds)


    .Anatomy of the ECG
    • Represent the conduction 
    system with points of 
    repolarization & 
    depolarization
    • Waves
    • Segments 
    • Intervals 


    .P-Wave
    • Atrial depolarization & 
    contracting to force last bit of 
    blood into the ventricles
    • Accounts for 15-20% stroke 
    volume
    • SA node impulse in R atrium & 
    spread to left atrium via 
    Bachmann bundle 


    .P-R Interval
    • Spread of depolarization 
    reaches AV node
    • AV node delays conduction 
    from atria 1/10 of a second 
    • Represents “atrial kick” for 
    final ejection of blood 
    before ventricular 
    contraction
    • Accts for ~30% of CO over 
    cardiac cycle


    .QRS Complex
    • Ventricular depolarization as 
    impulse reaches the 
    Purkinje fibers
    • Atrial Repolarization hidden 
    within QRS complex
    • Q is first negative deflection
    • R is first positive deflection
    • S is first negative deflection 
    after R wave


    .S-T segment

    • End of the S wave and ends at the 
    beginning of the T wave
    • J point
    • The point at which the thin line of 
    the QRS tracing turns into a thick 
    line.
    • Bbeginning of the ST segment
    • Often used as the landmark when 
    the ST segment is abnormal
    • With the T-wave is a sensitive indicator
    of oxygen supply & demand and reflects 
    the status of the ventricular myocardial 
    tissue


    .T-wave
    • Ventricular repolarization
    • End of systole
    • Indicator of oxygen 
    demand/supply status of 
    ventricular myocardium


    .ECG Intervals
    • P-R interval is 0.12 and 0.20 
    second. 
    • QRS complex is 0.06 to 0.10 
    second. 
    • Q-T interval is 0.32 to 0.40 
    second. 


    .Putting it Together


    .12 Lead ECG
    • 6 limb leads, 6 chest leads 
    assessment:
    • Heart rate 
    • Heart rhythm
    • Hypertrophy
    • Infarction 
    • Single lead assessment:
    • Heart rate 
    • Heart rhythm
    • Arrythmias 


    .What the leads can tell us . . . 
        Table 3.2 Coronary Anatomy and Location of Infarction

        1. Right Coronary Artery
        - Location of Infarct: Inferior
        - ECG Changes: II, III, aVF
        - Common Complications: Risk of atrioventricular block and arrhythmias; 50% have right ventricular infarct

        2. Left Main
        - Location of Infarct: Anterior and lateral
        - ECG Changes: V1-V6; I, aVL
        - Common Complications: Pump dysfunction or failure

        3. Left Anterior Descending (LAD)
        - Location of Infarct: Anterior
        - ECG Changes: V1-V4
        - Common Complications: Pump dysfunction or failure

        4. Circumflex
        - Location of Infarct: Lateral
        - ECG Changes: V5, V6; I, aVL
        - Common Complications: None specific


    .Determining Heart Rate 
    Counting small boxes 
    • # of small boxes between the R waves and divide this number into 1500.
    • This method is used for regular rhythms.


    .Determining Heart Rate 
    • 6-second tracing 
    • identifying 6 seconds on the 
    electrocardiogram paper 
    • counting the number of QRS 
    complexes in the 6-second 
    strip
    • number of QRS complexes in 
    6 seconds multiplied by 10 
    gives the heart rate for 1 
    minute. 


    .Regular or Irregular Rhythm?
    • How can you tell if the rhythm is 
    regular?
    • Use “R to R interval”
    • used to assess regularity
    • Artifact can occur due to 
    muscle tremors / movement, 
    loose electrodes, electrical 
    interference

        Systematic Approach for Assessment of ECG
            Evaluate the P-Wave (p wave)
            Evaluate the P-R interval (PR)
            Evaluate the QRS complex and interval
            Evaluate the T-Wave (t wave)
            Evaluate the R to R (RR, R-R) interval
            Evaluate the heart rate using 6 second strip approach (QRSs x 10 → Normal b/w 60-100)
            Observe the patient and evaluate any symptoms
        Sinus Node Rhythms
            Γ Normal Rhythm (60-100)
                Normal Sinus Rhythm (NSR) (Sinus = the Pacemaker)
                Sinus Bradycardia
                Sinus Tachycardia
                    Supraventricular Tachycardia (SVT)
            Γ Abnormal Rhythm
                Sinus Arrhythmia
                Sinus Pause or Block
        Atrial Arrhythmias
            Premature Atrial Complex Γ('08 Rate and Rhythm _ Premature Atrial Contraction (PAC).mp4')
                Non-compensatory pause
                Complete compensatory pause
                ---------------------------------
                Atrial Tachycardia
            Paroxysmal Atrial Tachycardia (PAT) or Paroxysmal Supraventricular Tachycardia (PSVT)
            Atrial Flutter
            Atrial Fibrillation
    ('02 2.1_ECG Abnormalities and Clinical Application Part 2.pdf')
        Heart Blocks
            First Degree AV Block
            Second Degree AV Block, Type I (Wenckebach or Mobitz I)
            Second Degree AV Block, Type II (Mobitz II)
            Third Degree AV Block
        Ventricular Arrhythmias
            Premature Ventricular Contractions (PVC)
                Bigeminy—when every other beat is PVC
                Trigeminy—when every third beat is PVC
                Unifocal—all PVCs appear identical in configuration
                Multifocal—more than one PVC is present and no two appear similar in configuration
                Paired—two PVCs are together
                VTACH—triplet  or ventricular tachycardia
            Normal Sinus Rhythm with One Premature Ventricular Contraction
            Sinus Rhythm with Multifocal Premature Ventricular Complexes
            Sinus Rhythm with an Episode of Unifocal Trigeminy of Premature Ventricular Complexes
            R-wave on T-wave PVC Progressing to Ventricular Fibrillation
            Triplet PVC (3-beat VTACH)
            Ventricular Tachycardia (V-Tach) or Torsade de Pointes
            Sustained V-Tach
            Ventricular Fibrillation

    • Evaluate the T wave
    • Evaluate the R to R interval
    • Evaluate the heart rate using 6 second strip approach
    • Observe the patient and evaluate any symptoms


    .Clinical Decision Making and ECG
    Understand the clinical significance of the following:
    • Rapid atrial arrhythmias
    • atrial fibrillation and flutter
    • controlled vs. uncontrolled ventricular response
    • Premature ventricular complexes (PVC)
    • Rapid ventricular arrhythmias
    • ventricular tachycardia
    • Heart blocks--second and third degree 
    • ST segment depression and elevation


    .Sinus Node Rhythms 

    .Normal Sinus Rhythm (NSR) ('')
    Impulse begins in SA node with conduction through normal 
    pathway of depolarization


    .Sinus Bradycardia ('')
    Impulse begins in SA node with conduction through normal 
    pathway of depolarization, BUT at a slower rate <60 bpm

    Clinical Implications for Tachycardia and 
    Bradycardia
    Tachycardia
    • Normal exercise response
    • Found when the demands for O2 are 
    increased (HF, infection, anemia, 
    exercise)
    • Increased heart rate increases 
    cardiac workload (more blood and 
    oxygen required), can stress a 
    weakened heart and result in 
    decrease CO
    • Monitor response to activity

    Bradycardia

    • New onset
    • If the person is symptomatic
    • If symptomatic, it will likely be treated 
    with medications or a pacemaker


    .Sinus Pause or Block
    SA node fails to initiate an impulse for one or two cycles
    (Γ)
        Encara que es diu Sinus, es el QRS complexe el que no apareix
        RATE
            N/A
        RHYTHM
            Ésta tindria el ritme regular si no fora per la pausa


    Supraventricular Tachycardia (SVT)
    Tachycardia in which the origin of the electrical signal is either the atria 
    or the AV node

    .Atrial Arrhythmias 


    .Important Concepts Moving Forward
    1. Ectopic foci
    • Area of the heart that is discharging an impulse other then the SA node
    • Rapid atrial or ventricular depolarization outside of normal synchronous 
    electrical activity
    • In the atria leads to atrial depolarization
    • In the ventricle leads to ventricular depolarization
    2. Ventricular response
    • Response to atrial depolarization as impulse travels from atria through AV 
    node and into the ventricles
    • Can be normal, fast or slow based on response to normal SA node 
    depolarization vs atrial ectopic foci depolarization


    .Premature Atrial Complex
    Ectopic foci in the atria that initiates an impulse before the next impulse is initiated by the SA node
    (Γ)
        P-Wave
            -Busca el/els P-Wave que són diferent dels demés (P-Waves diferents en definitiva)
            -Pot haver fusió de P-Waves amb T-Waves (b/c of the Prematurity)
            -(See '08 Rate and Rhythm _ Premature Atrial Contraction (PAC).mp4' 12:05sec (Bigeminy) i 15:17sec (Trigeminy) about "Trigeminy—when every third beat is PVC")
        R-R intervals
            Ademés entre els R-R intervals que post vore regulars, el prematur ve antes estropejant la continuitat
        ----------------------------------------------------
        Non-compensatory pause Γ(See '08 Rate and Rhythm _ Premature Atrial Contraction (PAC).mp4' 07:41sec i 17:06sec)
        Complete compensatory pause
        ----------------------------------------------------

            N/A
        RHYTHM
            Ésta te el ritme iregular


    .Atrial Tachycardia Γ('Atrial Tachycardia ECG.mp4') (No gens clar ¿?)
    Three or more premature atrial complexes in a row & associated with a rapid 
    ventricular response, this rate will override SA node depolarization capabilities
    (Γ)
        Pus considerdar esta com a una variació de l'anterior (Premature Atrial Complex)
        Lead II: regular, rapid and narrow QRS pattern
        HR: 170-230 b/m (until 150 is Sinus Tachycardia but beyond that is Atrial Tachycardia)
        At rest HR over 150 b/m
        ----------------------------------------------------
        RATE
            N/A
        RHYTHM
            N/A


    .Paroxysmal Atrial Tachycardia (PAT) or Paroxysmal Supraventricular Tachycardia (PSVT)
    Sudden onset of atrial tachycardia or repetitive firing from an atrial 
    focus, episodic burst


    .Atrial Flutter
    Rapid succession of atrial depolarization caused by a single ectopic foci 
    in the atria that depolarizes at a rate of 250 to 350/min


    .Atrial Fibrillation 
    Erratic quivering or twitching of the atrial muscle caused by MULTIPLE 
    ectopic foci that emit constant electrical impulses


    .Clinical Implications for Atrial Fibrillation and Atrial Flutter
    • Controlled vs. Uncontrolled 
    • If ventricular response rate (HR) is over 100, cardiac 
    output may be diminished, considered “uncontrolled”
    • Physiological monitoring should occur during exercise. 
    • Activity should be engaged cautiously with rates over 100. 
    At high rates (>150 bpm), activity is postponed

    ECG Arrythmias and Clinical 
    Application

    .Heart Blocks


    .First Degree AV Block 
    Impulse is initiated at SA node, but delayed on way to AV node
    (Γ)
        Observa que hi ha un P-Wave, però després hi ha una pausa llarga que és el "P-Q Segment". Això es perque el AV Node, reté la conducció de l'impuls


    .Second Degree AV Block, Type I (Wenckebach or Mobitz I)
        Γ('First vs Second Degree Heart Block - EKG Rhythm Interpretation.mp4')
        Γ('Mobitz Type I vs Type II Second Degree Heart Block.mp4')
    Transient disturbance occurring high in the AV junction & prevents some 
    of the impulses through the AV node
    (Γ)
        -P-Wave + pausa i QRS complexe, P-Wave + pausa més llarga i QRS complexe, P-Wave + pausa més més llarga i QRS complexe, P-Wave + pausa i no QRS complexe
            Després de un P-Wave, no hi ha QRS complexe, sino una pausa llarga, i després ve un altre P-Wave


    .Second Degree AV Block, Type II (Mobitz II)
        Γ('First vs Second Degree Heart Block - EKG Rhythm Interpretation.mp4')
        Γ('Mobitz Type I vs Type II Second Degree Heart Block.mp4')
    Non-conduction of impulse to the ventricles without change in the P-R 
    interval, block is usually below bundle of His
    (Γ)
        -Lo mateix que antes "Second Degree AV Block, Type I (Wenckebach or Mobitz I)", pero "P-Wave + pausa" es constant hasta que es pert el "QRS complexe"



    .Third Degree AV Block Γ('First vs Third Degree Heart Block.mp4')
    All impulses that are initiated above the ventricle are not conducted
    (Γ)
        -P-Waves són regulars, però no hi ha correspondència amb els QRS complèxes; hi ha una descoordinació total perque no hi ha correspondència entre els dos. 


    .Clinical Implications of a 3rd Degree AV Block
    • Symptoms- Patient may 
    have chest pain, dizziness, 
    SOB
    • Medical emergency!
    • Pacemaker Placement 
    Required


    .Ventricular Arrhythmias 


    .Premature Ventricular Contractions (PVC)
    • Ectopic foci originates an impulse from somewhere in the ventricles 
    • Ventricular ectopic depolarization occurs early in the cycle before the SA 
    node actually fires 
    • Wide bizarre QRS complex without a p-wave
    • Characteristics of PVCs:
    • Bigeminy—when every other beat is PVC
    • Trigeminy—when every third beat is PVC
        Γ('08 Rate and Rhythm _ Premature Atrial Contraction (PAC).mp4')
    • Unifocal—all PVCs appear identical in configuration
    • Multifocal—more than one PVC is present and no two appear similar in 
    configuration
    • Paired—two PVCs are together
    • VTACH—triplet or ventricular tachycardia


    .Normal Sinus Rhythm with One Premature Ventricular Contraction


    .Sinus Rhythm with Multifocal Premature Ventricular Complexes


    .Sinus Rhythm with an Episode of Unifocal Trigeminy of Premature Ventricular Complexes


    .R-wave on T-wave PVC Progressing to Ventricular Fibrillation


    .Triplet PVC (3-beat VTACH)


    .Clinical Implication of PVCs
    • Palpation: 
    • Skipped beat in regular rhythm followed by stronger beat
    • With increased frequency of PVC’s, filling time of ventricles decreases, decreased cardiac output
    • Shortness of breath, dizziness may occur
    • PVCs are usually the precursors of more serious ventricular dysrhythmias (ventricular tachycardia 
    and ventricular fib)
    • The following conditions involving PVCs require prompt and vigorous treatment. Proceed with 
    caution.
    • PVCs occurring at a rate exceeding six per minute 
    • Occur as two or more consecutively 
    • PVCs fall on the peak or down slope of the T wave (period of vulnerability) 
    • Are of varying configurations, indicating a multiplicity of foci


    .Ventricular Tachycardia (V-Tach) or Torsade de Pointes
    A series of 3 or more PVCs in a row; due to rapid firing by a single 
    ventricular focus with increased automaticity


    .Sustained V-Tach


    .Ventricular Fibrillation 
    Erratic quivering of the ventricular muscle resulting in no CO

    Isolated PVCs may be benign and the patient may be asymptomatic.
    15:23

    15:29
    filling time of the ventricles decreases,
    15:33

    17:23

This lecture will cover what can be discovered on a 12 lead ECG, and we will briefly cover findings of cardiac ischemia, infarction, and injury.
