    > > > 

    Findings on a 12-lead ECG

    .Findings on a 12 Lead ECG
        Ischemia
        • Reduced blood flow 
        to myocardium due to 
        occlusion of coronary 
        arteries from 
        vasospasm, 
        atherosclerotic 
        occlusion, thrombus 
        • t wave inversion or 
        ST segment 
        depression

        Injury
        • Arterial occlusion 
        with ischemia
        • Elevation of ST 
        segment above 
        baseline indicates 
        acute injury

        Infarction
        • Cell death resulting 
        from complete 
        occlusion of coronary 
        artery
        • Pathological Q wave


    .Findings on a 12 Lead ECG 
    • ST segment depression at rest in presence of chest pain
    • subendocardial infarction; may indicate a pending transmural infarction
    • ST segment depression in absence of ischemia or angina may be 
    due to ``digitalis toxicity
    • Presence of significant Q wave is also diagnostic of infarction
    • Leads that demonstrate presence of T wave inversion, ST segment 
    changes, or Q waves identify location of ischemia, injury, or 
    infarction


    .What does it appear as on ECG?
        ('2022-10-03 10_40_51-StrokesPlus.png')
            Ischemia
                T wave changes
                    Inverted T wave
                    Tall, peaked T wave
                    Depressed ST segment
            Injury
                ST segment changes
                    Elevated ST segment
            Infarction
                Q wave changes

    .S-T Segment on ECG (reminder)
    • The ST segment on the 
    electrocardiogram tracing begins at 
    the end of the S wave and ends at 
    the beginning of the T wave. 
    • J point
    • Denotes the junction of the QRS 
    complex and the ST segment on 
    the electrocardiogram 
    • Often used as the landmark to 
    determine is there is significant 
    ST segment elevation or 
    depression 


    .Measuring S-T Segment Elevation/Depression ('')


    .Acute Myocardial Infarction on 12 Lead

    Note the ST elevation in 
    leads II, III, aVF
    Acute inferior myocardial 
    infarction


    .Inverted T Wave on EKG ('')
    • Electrocardiogram tracing 
    showing an inverted T wave, 
    often indicating ischemia 
    (arrows). 


    .Locations of Insult
    • Ischemia, Infarction, or Injury and Locations
    • Significant Q waves in leads V1, V2, V3, V4 indicates infarction in 
    anterior portion of left ventricle
    • V1 and V2 only —“septal” infarctions
    • Significant Q waves in leads II, III, and aVF indicates inferior infarction
    • Q waves in leads I and aVL indicates lateral infarction
    • Posterior infarcts are most difficult to detect 
    • May see ST segment depression (not elevation) in the septal and anterior 
    precordial leads (V1-V4)

2.5. ECG Self-Assessment
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////// (!!Q)

Llegenda
    Correct! → la inmediatament inferior es la resposta correcta

Question 1
0 / 
Which of the following components of the ECG impulse represents the ventricular depolarization? 
  P wave 
  P-R segment 
Correct!
  QRS complex 
  ST segment 
The QRS complex is the electrical stimulus of ventricular depolarization and is normally followed closely by ventricular contraction 

 
Question 2
0 / 
A single-lead tracing or rhythm strip can be used to determine all of the following EXCEPT: 
  Heart rate 
  Heart rhythm 
  Presence of arrhythmia 
Correct!
  Presence of ischemia 
The single-lead tracing or rhythm strip can be used only to determine heart rate, rhythm, or the presence of arrhythmia. If hypertrophy, ischemia, or infarction is susp ected, then a 12-lead ECG should be obtained. 

 
Question 3
0 / 
When a therapist is assessing the cardiac cycle for rhythm and rate disturbances, which of the following assessment approaches is used to evaluate the P-R interval? 
Correct!
  Is the duration between 0.12 and 0.20 second? 
  Is the duration between 0.06 and 0.10 second? 
  Is it regular? 
  Does one occur before every QRS? 
When evaluating the P-R interval, the therapist determines whether it has a normal duration of 0.12 to 0.20 second. 

 
Question 4
0 / 
A premature ventricular complex that occurs every third beat on an ECG is named: 
  Bigeminy 
Correct!
  Trigeminy 
  Unifocal 
  Paired 
When analyzing PVCs occurring on a patient’s ECG it is important to note when and how frequent they occur. When you see one happening every 3rd beat or QRS, QRS, PVC, then you would name that a trigeminy. A Bigeminy is when every other beat is PVC, a Unifocal is when all PVCs appear identical in configuration, and a Paired is when two PVCs are together 

 
Question 5
0 / 
The development of mural thrombi secondary to the coagulation of blood in the heart chamber subsequently leading to a potential stroke occurs in which of the following heart arrhythmias?  
  Atrial flutter 
Correct!
  Atrial fibrillation 
  Atrial tachycardia 
  Sinus pause or block 
Atrial fibrillation has the potential for developing mural thrombi because of the coagulation of blood with fibrillating atria. Mural thrombi may lead to emboli. 

 
Question 6
0 / 
A 68-year-old male collapses in his yard while mowing. The EMTs immediately obtain an ECG strip that reveals grossly irregular up and down fluctuations of the baseline in an irregular zigzag pattern. Which of the following arrhythmias is potentially occurring? 
  Ventricular tachycardia 
Correct!
  Ventricular fibrillation 
  Atrial flutter 
  Atrial fibrillation 
An ECG of a ventricular fibrillation results in a picture of grossly irregular up and down fluctuations of the baseline in an irregular zigzag pattern. 

 
Question 7
0 / 
Which of the following changes on an ECG BEST indicate a period of ischemia? 
  ST-segment elevation 
Correct!
  ST-segment depression 
  Enlarged QRS complex 
  Presence of a significant Q wave 
Ischemia is classically demonstrated on the 12-lead ECG with T wave inversion or ST-segment depression.

2.8. Module 2 Quiz

(See ANKI: 'T01_CP_inCan_M02_Quiz')
    Question 1
    The ability of cardiac muscle cells to spread impulses to adjoining cells very quickly BEST describes which of the following properties? 
    
    Automaticity
    Rhythmicity
    Conductivity
    Electricity
    
    Conductivity
    The property of conductivity is one of three properties of cardiac muscle cells and describes the ability of the cardiac muscle cells to spread impulses to adjoining cells very quickly.
    Heart muscle possesses the following properties: Automaticity – pacemaker ability. Conductivity – each cell has ability to conduct impulses to the next cell. Contractility – ability to contract (make each cell shorter or longer).
    
    
    Question 2
    Increased sympathetic activity through the release of norepinephrine and epinephrine from the adrenal gland results in which of the following changes in the heart? 
    
    Reduces conduction velocity throughout the atrioventricular node.
    Decreases the irritability of the heart.
    Increases the contractility of the heart muscle
    Depresses the automaticity of the heart.
    
    Increases the contractility of the heart muscle
    Increased sympathetic activity through the release of norepinephrine and epinephrine increases the heart rate, increases conduction velocity throughout the AV node, increases the contractility of the heart muscle, and increases the irritability of the heart.
    
    Question 3
    Which of the following components of the ECG impulse represents the atrial kick or the delayed conduction of the electrical impulse by the AV node one-tenth of a second? 
    
    P-wave
    P-R segment
    QRS complex
    S-T segment
    
    P-R segment
    The P-R segment is considered the isoelectric line or the atrial kick. The AV node delays conduction of the electrical impulse from the atria allowing for the mechanical contraction of the atria to eject blood into the ventricles.
    
    Question 4
    The rhythm strip reveals the following findings: all P waves are upright and normal in appearance and occur before every QRS complex, the P-R interval is between 0.12 and 0.20 second, the QRS complexes are identical, the QRS complex is between 0.04 and 0.10 second, the R-R interval is regular, and the HR is between 60 and 100 bpm. These findings BEST describe which of the following? 

    
    Sinus Bradycardia
    Sinus Tachycardia
    Normal Sinus Rhythm
    Atrial Arrhythmia
    
    Normal Sinus Rhythm
    All the findings describe a normal rhythm strip.
    
    Question 5
    The rhythm strip reveals the following findings: all P waves are upright, normal in appearance, and exist before every QRS complex, the P-R interval is between 0.12 and 0.20 second, the QRS complexes are identical and are between 0.04 and 0.10 second, the R-R interval is regular, and the HR is >100 bpm. These findings BEST describe which of the following? 
    
    Sinus Bradycardia
    Sinus Tachycardia 
    Normal Sinus Rhythm
    Atrial Arrhythmia
    
    Sinus Tachycardia
    All of the findings are normal except the heart rate was >100 bpm indicating sinus tachycardia
    
    Question 6
    The rhythm strip reveals the following findings: P waves are absent, leaving a flat or wavy baseline, the QRS complexes are between 0.04 and 0.10 second, the R-R interval is characteristically defined as irregularly irregular, and the rate varies, but is called “ventricular response.” These findings BEST describe which of the following? 
    
    Atrial Flutter 
    Atrial Fibrillation
    Supraventricular Tachycardia
    Atrial Tachycardia
    
    Atrial Fibrillation ↓

    Question 7
    Which of the following heart blocks is characterized by no communication between the atria and the ventricles, thus resulting in no coordination between the firing of the atria and the firing of the ventricles, creating a complete independence of the two systems? 
    
    First-degree AV block
    Second-degree AV block, type I
    Second-degree AV block, type II
    Third-degree AV block

    Third-degree AV block
    In third-degree (complete) AV block, all impulses that are initiated above the ventricle are not conducted to the ventricle. In complete heart block, the atria fire at their own inherent rate and a separate pacemaker in the ventricles initiates all impulses.
    
    Question 8
    Which of the following changes on an ECG BEST indicates the presence of acute infarction? 

    ST-segment elevation
    ST-segment depression
    Enlarged QRS complex
    Absence of P wave
    
    ST-segment elevation
    In the presence of acute infarction, the ST-segment elevates and then later returns to the level of the baseline (within 24 to 48 hours). 
    
    Question 9 ↓
    Repolarization of the ventricular is BEST described as which of the following? 

    T wave
    QRS Complex
    P wave
    S-T Segment
    
    T wave
    Repolarization is complete with the ending of the T wave. The T wave represents the ventricular repolarization. No mechanical contraction is occurring, so the T wave is indicating an electrical phenomenon that records the return of potassium inward and sodium outward changing the polarization of the cell.
    
    Question 10
    Which of the following BEST defines atrial tachycardia? 
    
    R-R intervals are irregular
    Heart rate is >200 bpm
    Three or more premature atrial complexes in a row
    P-R intervals are irregular with a duration of 0.25 second

    Three or more premature atrial complexes in a row
    The definition of atrial tachycardia is three or more premature atrial complexes in a row.
    .Atrial Fibrillation = The rhythm strip reveals the following findings: P waves are absent, leaving a flat or wavy baseline, the QRS complexes are between 0.04 and 0.10 second, the R-R interval is characteristically defined as irregularly irregular, and the rate varies, but is called “ventricular response.”

//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
3.0. Module Introduction
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

In this module we will cover pathophysiology, presenting signs and symptoms, and exercise recommendations for several cardiovascular conditions. Conditions that will be covered: ischemic cardiovascular conditions, such as hypertension and acute coronary syndromes, and cover cardiac muscle dysfunction leading to heart failure. These diagnoses covered will give you insight on the common cardiovascular conditions you may encounter as a physical therapist in any setting, as well as provide you with information on how these conditions can impact your physical therapy plan of care. You will also begin to review the lab manual and vitals videos as a part of this module, as vitals are a key component in assessing patients with cardiovascular disease, and this will also prepare you for the upcoming vitals lab.

Learning Objectives
By the end of this week, you will be able to: 

Describe the pathophysiology and process of hypertension, coronary artery disease, and heart failure. 
Discuss hallmark signs and symptoms related to the covered cardiovascular diagnoses. 
 Identify risk factors associated with cardiovascular disease. 
Explain medical management for each cardiovascular disease and related prognostic factors. 
Assess PT findings related to each condition that would impact exercise prescription, explain how the condition should be monitored, and recommend interventions to optimize outcomes.

3.1. Background Readings and Materials
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

Before participating in the activities for this module, please carefully read the following materials:

Required 
Hillegass, E. (2016). Essentials of cardiopulmonary physical therapy (4th ed.). Elsevier Saunders: St. Louis, MO. ISBN-10: 0323430546;
Chapter 3 & 4 

Cardiopulmonary Lab manual See ('PT 2026_Mod3_Cardiopulmonary 1 Lab Manual-1.pdf') ← Γ(This is a section here in the document too)

Hillegass et al. (2022). Role of Physical in the Management of Individuals at Risk for or Diagnosed with Venous Thromboembolism: Evidenced-Based Clinical Practice Guidelines Download Role of Physical in the Management of Individuals at Risk for or Diagnosed with Venous Thromboembolism: Evidenced-Based Clinical Practice Guidelines2022 ('2022 DVT Guidelines.pdf') 2022. Physical Therapy Journal 102(8) 143-66. doi: 10.2522/ptj.20150264. 
This reading is an important reading for any physical therapist working in any setting. This is a clinical practice guideline to assist a PT in managing patient’s with DVTs, and gives valuable insight into screening and treatment for patients with suspected or diagnosed DVT. This will allow for improved ability to decrease incidence, and reduce complications associated with DVT.

Shoemaker et al. (2020). Physical Therapist Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Individuals with Heart Failure ('Physical Therapist Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management.pdf'). Physical Therapy Journal. 100, 14-43 
This article will give you insight in the clinical decision-making process when managing patients with heart failure of varying degrees. After this reading you will have more ability to make appropriate clinical decisions after patient examination via a structured process.  

Green, Daniel J. “Exercise Training as Vascular Medicine: Direct Impacts on the Vasculature in Humans ('06 Exercise Training as Vascular Medicine_Direct Impacts on the Vasculature in Humans.pdf'). Exercise and sport sciences reviews 37.4 (2009): 196–202. Web. 
This article will allow you to see and better understand how exercise directly impacts the vasculature in human beings. This reading directly correlates to what is discussed as how we as PT’s can prescribe exercise at a level to make long terms vascular changes in patients with high blood pressure or other cardiovascular risk factors. It will allow you to see that exercise alone can create arterial remodeling via endothelial dependent vasodilation as is a direct response to exercise.  These changes in turn lower total peripheral resistance levels, hence lowering blood pressure.

Recommended
Allen, J. (2010). The utility of troponin measurement to detect myocardial infarction: Review of the current findings ('07 300710-VHRM-5306-the-utility-of-troponin-measurement-to-detect-myocardial-inf.pdf'). Vascular Health and Risk Management 6, 691–699.  
This reading describes the use of troponin measurements and the role of troponin values in evaluation and management of acute myocardial infarction. The article will give you further understanding of how troponin release relates to MI severity, and this will allow you to relate troponin measurement trends with MI staging, prognosis and management.

    3 

    .Radial Heart Rate: 
    1. Heart rate is the number of times one’s heart beats per minute. Each heartbeat is an indicator of a 
    single cardiac cycle occurring. Heart rate can be measured by palpating various arteries in the body. 
    2. The examiner should initiate taking the radial pulse by locating the patient’s radial artery. The radial 
    artery is found on the lateral portion of the anterior wrist or thumb side.  
    3. To palpate the pulse the examiner should place their middle and index finger over the radial artery, then 
    feel for how many beats or pulses can be felt over one minute. The examiner should not use their 
    thumb for palpation, as this will cause for misreading the patient’s pulse rate. 
    4. For a new patient the examiner should compare right to left side and ensure the rate is taken over 60 
    seconds. Other options do include taking the pulse over 15 seconds then multiplying by 4 or 30 seconds 
    then multiplying by 2, but this method should only be used during exercise or with a patient that has no 
    underlying cardiac condition. 
    5. Examiners should note rate, rhythm, and force. Rate measures are defined as: Normal: 60-100 bpm, 
    Tachycardia > 100 bpm, and Bradycardia < 60 bpm. Pulse amplitude can be defined as: increased or 
    bounding, normal, weak, or absent.  
    6. The radial heart rate is the most accessible and commonly measured site during exercise, so it is 
    important to note heart rate responses that are normal or abnormal when assessing this heart rate site. 
    Normal exercise HR responses could include Increase in HR with increasing work intensities, 
    Stabilization of HR (steady state) during each workload and/or HR should stabilize during recovery but 
    may not return to baseline levels within 5-min. While an abnormal exercise HR response could include 
    HR fails to rise with increase in workload, Noticeable change in heart rhythm, and/or Onset of angina or 
    angina-like symptoms 

    4 

    .Brachial Heart Rate: 
    1. The examiner should initiate taking the brachial pulse by locating the patient’s brachial artery. The 
    brachial artery is found medial to the biceps muscle insertion in the antecubital fossa.  
    2. To palpate the pulse the examiner should place their middle and index finger over the brachial artery, 
    then feel for how many beats or pulses can be felt over one minute. The examiner should not use their 
    thumb for palpation, as this will cause for misreading the patient’s pulse rate. 
    3. For a new patient the examiner should compare right to left side and ensure the rate is taken over 60 
    seconds. Other options do include taking the pulse over 15 seconds then multiplying by 4 or 30 seconds 
    then multiplying by 2, but this method should only be used during exercise or with a patient that has no 
    underlying cardiac condition. 
    4. Examiners should note rate, rhythm, and force. Rate measures are defined as: Normal: 60-100 bpm, 
    Tachycardia > 100 bpm, and Bradycardia < 60 bpm. Pulse amplitude can be defined as: increased or 
    bounding, normal, weak, or absent.  
    5. The brachial pulse is commonly utilized as a site for blood pressure assessment, but also may be utilized 
    if the radial pulse is weak or unable to be located distally.  

    5 

    6 

    .Manual Blood Pressure: 
    Blood pressure is a method to determine the amount of force blood exerts on the arterial walls 
    during systole and diastole. The more pressure exerted on the arterial walls the more work the 
    heart must do to pump blood into systemic circulation, leading to risk of certain cardiovascular 
    conditions. 
   

    .Manual Blood pressure device:     
    1. Prior to taking a blood pressure assessment the examiner should have all tools required, including, a 
    stethoscope and the blood pressure cuff.  
    2. We first should review the components of the blood pressure cuff. Here you will see the device contains 
    an inflatable rubber cuff or bladder, a mercury guided scale or sphygmomanometer, a tube to the 
    sphygmomanometer, and an air bulb with a controllable valve. Each of these components has a 
    specialized function that will be reviewed in the following steps. 
    3. It is important to note that the examiner must ensure they have the proper cuff size for the patient, or 
    the BP reading will not be accurate. The cuff length should be 75 – 100% of the patient’s measured arm 
    circumference.  Be sure to check this before completing the following steps. You may also utilize the 
    index on the inside of the cuff to measure for appropriate cuff size, which when wrapped around the 
    arm the while index line at the cuff edge should fall between the range’s lines.  
    • 7-9 inches (17.78 cm to 22.86 cm) = adult small cuff 
    • 9-13 inches (Range: 22.86 cm to 33.02 cm) = standard adult cuff 
    • 13-17 inches (Range: 33.02 cm to 43.18 cm) large adult cuff 

    7 

    .Steps for measurement of Manual BP: 
    1. Have the patient sitting in a chair with back support for 3-5 minutes prior to initiating the blood pressure 
    reading. 
    2. Prior to placing the cuff over the arm, the examiner should initiate by palpating and locating the 
    patient’s brachial artery to know where it is located for later stethoscope placement, which is found in 
    the antecubital fossa.  
    3. Once the artery can be felt the cuff should be placed with the bladder length of the cuff is over the 
    arterial pulsation site on the arm. This is usually marked on the cuff by an arrow. The cuff should be 
    pulled tightly and secured. Once secured, to ensure a proper fit the examiner can place 2 fingers 
    underneath the cuff edges, which should fit very snugly underneath.  
    4. Once the cuff is placed the examiner should then confirm the patient’s arm is supported at the level of 
    the right atrium or the midpoint of the sternum, either by a stable surface or by the examiner.  
    5. Next, palpate the radial artery at the wrist, then inflate the cuff using the air bulb with the valve closed. 
    At this time, you should feel the disappearance of the pulse. Be sure to be looking at the 
    sphygmomanometer while you inflate, as when the pulse is no longer palpated you should increase the 
    cuff pressure a minimum of 30 mmHg above that point.  
    6. Now place the stethoscope over the brachial artery site as you begin to deflate the cuff at a rate of 2-
    3mmHg/s while listening to the sounds via your stethoscope.  

    8 

    7. The first audible sharp tapping sound or Korotkoff sound I is the SBP, and the final loss of all sounds or 
    Korotkoff V is the DBP and should be recorded nearest the even number. As the cuff is deflated it is 
    important to note the sounds heard but they do not need to be recorded, and are ordered as follows, 
    Korotkoff II as swishing, Korotkoff III as louder thudding, and Korotkoff IV as abrupt muffling 

    
    .Points to consider:

    8. Blood pressure should be recorded as systolic/diastolic, and according to the American Heart 
    Association, readings are categorized as follows: 
    • Normal: Less than 120/80 mm Hg; 
    • Elevated: Systolic between 120-129 and diastolic less than 80; 
    • Stage 1: Systolic between 130-139 or diastolic between 80-89; 
    • Stage 2: Systolic at least 140 or diastolic at least 90 mm Hg; 
    • Hypertensive crisis: Systolic over 180 and/or diastolic over 120. 
 

    9. If this is the patient’s first visit you should take the BP in both arms, and the arm with the higher reading 
    should be reported. It may also benefit to ask the patient their typically BP reading to prepare, but do 
    not let this bias your listening skills! 
    10. An average of >2 readings on >2 occasions is the best method to truly assess a patient’s BP.  
    11. Be sure to provide the patient with the reading.  
     
    9 

    12. Blood Pressure and Exercise: 
    a. Normal exercise BP responses 
    i. Systolic BP should increase with increasing exercise intensities. 
    ii. Diastolic BP should decrease or stay the same during GXT. 
    iii. Systolic BP is more elevated during exercise in upright versus supine posture and for weight-
    bearing (e.g., treadmill or step exercise) versus non-weight-bearing (e.g., cycling) exercise.   
    iv. BP should stabilize during recovery but may not return to baseline values within 5 min. 
    b. Abnormal exercise BP responses 
    i. Failure of systolic BP to increase or a significant drop in systolic BP (>20 mmHg) with increase in 
    exercise intensity   
    ii. Excessive rise in systolic BP (>260 mmHg) or diastolic BP (>115 mmHg) 
    13. If you have difficulty hearing or if movement (like exercise) is making using the stethoscope over the 
    brachial artery difficult you may palpate the radial artery to feel for the return of blood flow during cuff 
    deflation, and this would lead to an SBP/palpation reading.  

    10 

    .Automated Blood Pressure: 

    .Automated Blood pressure device:  

    1. Prior to taking a blood pressure assessment the examiner should have all tools required, including, the 
    automated blood pressure device.  
    2. The automated device components include: a cuff and a pressure meter with a start/stop button. 
    3. The examiner must ensure they have the proper cuff size for the patient, or the BP reading will not be 
    accurate. The cuff length should be 75– 100% of the patient’s measured arm circumference.  Be sure to 
    check this before completing the following steps. 

    .Steps for measurement of Automated BP: 

    1. Have the patient sitting in a chair with back support for 3-5 minutes prior to initiating the blood pressure 
    reading. 
    2. Prior to placing the cuff over the arm, the examiner should initiate by palpating and locating the 
    patient’s brachial artery, which is found in the antecubital fossa.  
    3. Once the artery can be felt the cuff should be placed with the bladder length of the cuff is over the 
    arterial pulsation site on the arm. This is usually marked on the cuff by an arrow. The cuff should be 
    pulled tightly and secured. Once secured, to ensure a proper fit the examiner can place 2 fingers 
    underneath the cuff edges, which should fit very snugly underneath.  

    11 

    4. Once the cuff is placed the examiner should then confirm the patient’s arm is supported at the level of 
    the right atrium or the midpoint of the sternum, either by a stable surface or by the examiner.  
    5. Next, locate the start button and press it, then allow the machine to complete the inflation and deflation 
    task.  
    6. The machine will output a SBP and DBP reading once the process is complete. 


    .Points to consider: 
  
    7. This method is commonly used in most medical facilities, as it is quick, easy and research has reported it 
    as a valid and accurate measurement technique.  
    8. If the cuff inflates, deflates, then inflates again, stop the machine have the patient rest, then restart the 
    machine again to obtain an accurate reading. 
    9. If this is the patient’s first visit you should take the BP in both arms, and the arm with the higher reading 
    should be reported.  
    10. An average of >2 readings on >2 occasions is the best method to truly assess a patient’s BP.  
    11. Be sure to provide the patient with the reading, and if the reading appears to be inaccurate due to 
    machine error, it is best to then take the BP manually.  

    12 

    .Respiratory rate 
    Respiratory rate or the number of breaths per minute is an observational technique to determine 
    the quality and frequency of a patient’s breathing. Each breath is representative of one cycle of 
    inhalation or air in, and exhalation or air out. 

    1. The examiner will observe the rise and fall of the chest wall for a 60 second period and count the 
    number of times that cycle occurs.  
    2. If the examiner is having difficulty with visual observation, then they may place their hands on the 
    shoulders of the patient and count the rise and fall of the shoulders as an indicator of breathing. This 
    procedure may be appropriate for those who have increased accessory muscle use with breathing. 
    Alternately, the examiner may also place their hands on the diaphragm of the patient. 
    3. It is important to note the quality of the breathing pattern, such as, time spent inhaling vs exhaling, 
    difficulty taking air in or expelling air, hyper vs hypoventilation status, and/or chest vs belly breathing.  
    4. The normal range for respiratory rate for an adult is 12 to 20 breaths per minute. The normal range 
    respiratory rate for infants and children is faster. For example, the normal range for 1-2 years old is 30-
    40 bpm, for a 3-10 years old is 20-30 bpm, and for a 11-15 years old is 18-22 bpm.  
    5. Abnormal respiratory rates for adults are defined as Bradypnea ≤ 10 bpm and Tachypnea ≥ 22. The 
    examiner should examine the patient for abnormal breathing patterns during the assessment of 
    respiratory rate. 

    13 

    .Pulse Oximetry: 
    Oxygen saturation (SaO2) or the percent of oxygen attached to hemoglobin in the arterial system 
    can be measured with a pulse oximeter. The device emits light that passes through the fingernail, 
    skin, tissue, and blood. This electronic device is battery operated and can obtain two vital readings, 
    including heart rate and oxygen saturation. 

    1. Oxygen saturation can be assessed in the patient while they are in standing, sitting, supine or even 
    performing an activity such as walking. 
    2. The examiner is to place the probe on the patient’s finger, but not the thumb or fifth finger, with the 
    light beam over the fingernail.  
    3. Allow the device a few seconds to obtain an oxygen saturation reading, which will be reported as a 
    percentage. 
    4. Oxygen saturation for Healthy adults is ≥ 95%. When readings are low the patient is known to be in a 
    hypoxic state. 
    5. It is important to be aware that multiple factors can affect the accuracy of a pulse oximeter reading, 
    such as poor circulation, skin pigmentation, skin temperature, current tobacco use, and use of fingernail 
    polish.  

    14 

    .Orthostatic Hypotension Assessment / .Orthostatic Assessment Γ(See '7.Orthostatic Assessment')
        (Γ)Resumen -------------------------------------------------------------------
            In every change of position report of:
                pallor
                diaphoresis
                faintness
                visual chages

            1.pt. supine for 3-5 min
            2.Take BP+Pulse
            .........................
            3.pt. sits and wait 1 min
            4.Take BP+Pulse
                If symptoms with position change or sitting BP ≤90/60
                    if symptoms are resolving, continue 
                    if symptoms are worsening, go supine
            .........................
            5.pt. stands and do not wait
                If patient is unable to stand
                    sit patient 
                        if it does not resolve
                            go supine 
            6.Take BP+Pulse
            .........................
            7.Wait 3 min
            8.Take BP+Pulse
                If there was a drop at standing but resoves here (after 3 min) = it is normal
                A HR increase of at least 30 bpm (after 3 min of standing) = hypovolemia
            .........................
            9.Resume back to bed when finished

            10.Document
                [8.(or 4. if couldn't stand) - 2.] → if ≥20 systolic or ≥10 diastolic = orthostatic hypotension
        ------------------------------------------------------------------------------

        Orthostatic hypotension is defined as a drop in blood pressure with positional changes. A patient 
        who expresses feeling lightheaded or dizzy in going from supine to sitting to standing is appropriate 
        to have a BP read taken during these activities. If there is a drop in BP during these positional 
        changes, then it can be hypothesized that the patient is not receiving adequate blood flow to the 
        brain due to a drop in blood pressure, and that individual may be diagnosed with orthostatic 
        hypotension.  

        1. Instruct the patient on the process of orthostatic blood pressure measurement and its rationale.

        2. Supine BP: Have patient lie in bed with the head flat for a minimum of 3 - 5 minutes, then measure the 
        blood pressure and the pulse while the patient is supine.  

        3. Seated BP: Instruct patient to sit for 1 minute, then measure the blood pressure and pulse. 
            a. Ask patient about dizziness, weakness, or visual changes associated with position change. Note 
            diaphoresis or pallor. 
            b. If the patient has symptoms associated with position change or sitting blood pressure ≤90/60, 
            reassess the patient immediately to determine if symptoms are resolving or worsening to see if the 
            patient needs to be transferred back to the supine position. 

    15 

        6. Standing BP: Measure the blood pressure and pulse immediately after patient has stood up, and then 
        repeat the measurements 3 minutes after patient stands. Support the forearm at heart level when 
        taking the blood pressures to prevent inaccurate measurement. 
            a. Ask patient about dizziness, weakness, or visual changes associated with position change. Note 
            diaphoresis or pallor. 
            b. If patient is unable to stand, sit patient upright with legs dangling over the edge of the bed. 
            c. The patient should be permitted to resume a supine position immediately if syncope or near 
            syncope develops. 

    16 

        7. Assist patient back to bed in a position of comfort. 
      
        8. Document vital signs and other pertinent observations on the nursing flowsheet or in the medical 
        record. Note all measurements taken and the position of the patient during each reading. 
      
        After you obtain your BP readings you should perform a post reading evaluation as follows: 
            1. Subtract values 3 minutes after standing (or if patient cannot stand, then sitting) from lying values. 

            2. A decline of ≥20mm Hg in systolic or ≥10 mm Hg in diastolic blood pressure after 3 minutes of standing 
            = orthostatic hypotension. 
         
            3. A heart rate increase of at least 30 beats per minute after 3 minutes of standing may suggest 
            hypovolemia, independent of whether the patient meets criteria for orthostatic hypotension. 

            4. A blood pressure that drops immediately after standing and resolves at 3 minutes does not indicate 
            orthostatic hypotension. However, this finding may be useful to confirm a patient’s complaint of 
            feeling dizzy upon standing and may lead to patient education about using caution when arising 
            from a lying or sitting position. 

            5. Report all findings to the treating medical provider, including all sets of blood pressure and pulse 
            results, and whether the patient experienced pallor, diaphoresis, or faintness when upright. 

    17 

    .Ankle-Brachial Index: 
    The ankle brachial index is a non-invasive measurement technique used to identify and stage 
    peripheral arterial disease. The procedure includes taking a systolic blood pressure measurement at 
    the arm and lower leg. Then those systolic measures will allow one to obtain a ratio of SBP at the 
    ankle and arm, if findings indicate a wide difference in those SBP readings, then one may consider a 
    blockage of the leg arteries.  

    .Required equipment for taking an ABI: 
    To take this measurement you will need a blood pressure cuff, conductance gel and a doppler ultrasound 
    probe. 
      
    .How to perform an ABI: 
    1. First have the patient resting in supine for 3-5 minutes prior to initiating the ABI reading. 
    2. Then take a BP measure in the upper extremity: 
    a. Prior to placing the cuff over the arm, the examiner should initiate by locating the patient’s brachial 
    pulse over the antecubital fossa doppler probe with conductance gel applied. The doppler probe 
    should be 50 degrees from the vertical when placed on the skin.  
    b. Once the artery can be heard the cuff should be placed with the bladder length of the cuff is over 
    the arterial pulsation site on the arm. This is usually marked on the cuff by an arrow. The cuff should 
    be pulled tightly and secured. Once secured, to ensure a proper fit the examiner can place 2 fingers 
    underneath the cuff edges, which should fit very snugly underneath.  
    c. Once the cuff is placed the examiner should then confirm the patient’s arm is supported at the level 
    of the right atrium or the midpoint of the sternum, either by a stable surface or by the examiner.  
    d. Next, place the doppler probe with conductive gel applied over the brachial artery where you should 
    hear the pulse. Then, inflate the cuff using the air bulb with the valve closed. At this time, you should 
    be listening for the disappearance of the pulse. Be sure to be looking at the sphygmomanometer 
    while you inflate, as when the pulse is no longer audible you should increase the cuff pressure 30 
    mmHg above that point.  
    e. Now you will begin to deflate the cuff at a rate of 2-3mmHg/s while listening to return of the pulse or 
    first audible sound, which is the brachial SBP. 
    3. Next take a BP measure in the lower extremity. 
    f. Prior to placing the cuff over the ankle, the examiner should initiate by locating the patient’s 
    posterior tibial pulse posterior to the medial malleolus using the doppler ultrasound head with 
    conductance gel applied. The doppler probe should be 50 degrees from the vertical when placed on 
    the skin.   
    g. Once the artery can be heard cuff should be placed with the bladder length of the cuff right above 
    the medial malleolus of the ankle. The arrow of the cuff should be in line with the tibial artery, which 
    runs just posterior to the medial malleolus. The cuff should be pulled tightly and secured. Once 
    secured, to ensure a proper fit the examiner can place 2 fingers underneath the cuff edges, which 
    should fit very snugly underneath.  

    18 

    h. Once the cuff is placed the examiner should then confirm the patient’s leg is supported on the 
    examination table.  
    i. Next, place the doppler probe with conductive gel applied over the posterior tibial artery where you 
    should again hear the pulse. Then, inflate the cuff using the air bulb with the valve closed. At this 
    time, you should be listening for the disappearance of the pulse. Be sure to be looking at the 
    sphygmomanometer while you inflate, as when the pulse is no longer audible you should increase 
    the cuff pressure 30 mmHg above that point.  
    j. Now you will begin to deflate the cuff at a rate of 2-3mmHg/s while listening to return of the pulse or 
    first audible sound, which is the ankle SBP. 

    19 

    4. Next you will assess your recorded pressures by taking the ankle SBP/Brachial SBP, and normal findings 
    will range from 0.9 – 1.0, findings < 0.9 are considered abnormal, and as this number decreases it can 
    indicate the severity of peripheral arterial insufficiency or disease. (!!E)

.Preload and Afterload ('Preload-and-Afterload.jpg')
    1. Preload
    - Ventricles at end of diastole (end diastolic pressure)
    - Increased in:
        - Hypervolemia
        - Regurgitation of cardiac valves
        - Heart Failure

    2. Afterload
    - Resistance left ventricle must overcome to circulate blood
    - Increased in:
        - Hypertension
        - Vasoconstriction

    3. Afterload = ↑ Cardiac workload


.Cardiomyopathy ('')
    1. Diastolic Failure
    - Thick heart walls are a sign of Diastolic Failure.
        ¦Està massa gross per a estirarse

    2. Systolic Failure
    - Thin heart walls are a sign of Systolic Failure.
        ¦Està massa fi per a contraure's


.Ejection 
Fraction 
Explained

SV or total volume of blood 
ejected/EDV = Ejection Fraction

% blood ejected from starting amount 
in LV

RELATIVE VALUE, just because someone 
has a normal or high EF DOES not mean 
they have adequate CO or SV


.Ejection 
Fraction 
Explained

Example: Filling issue →Diastolic HF →
Small Chamber to accept blood (small 
EDV) →pumps out small SV

Example: Emptying issue →Systolic HF 
→Large Chamber/Overstretched →
poor pumping mechanics →pumps out 
small SV
BOTH HAVE REDUCED CO


.Ejection Fraction ('Ejection Fraction.jpeg')
    1. Amount of blood pumped out of the ventricle
    - Ejection fraction (%)

    2. Total amount of blood in ventricle

    3. Systole
    - Ventricles contracting

    4. Diastole
    - Ventricles relaxing

.Reduced ejection fraction ('')


.Right versus Left Sided Heart Failure ('')


.Other 
systems 
associated 
with HF

Renal 
System RAAS cycle to increase arterial fluid 
volume in times of venous 
congestions

Pulmonary 
System Pulmonary edema due to fluid 
backflow or resistance to flow from 
the L ventricle back into the lungs

Liver hepatic venous congestion, which 
prevents adequate perfusion of 
oxygen to hepatic tissues

Hematologic Elevation in RBC as a response to 
the body sensing a reduced oxygen 
transport


.Features of HF

• Dyspnea and positional dyspnea
• Lung sounds indicating pulmonary edema
• Heart sounds –S3
• Peripheral edema 
• JVD with R sided heart failure > L sided
• Weight gain
• Poor exercise tolerance
• reduced SV due to increase in SNS activity within HF
• Lab values related to severity 
• BNP, liver enzymes, RBC, kidney markers, blood gases 
• Imaging with increase in L cardiac silhouette
• NYHA classification system


.HF and PT 
Implications

Clinical practice guidelines – green, 
yellow, red zone
Energy Conservation

Exercise Prescription with use of RPE 
vs dyspnea scale to gauge intensity
Patient education – weight gain!

Contraindicated positions - 
Trendelenburg

    > > > 

    Ischemic Cardiovascular 
    Conditions 

    .Anatomy of the Coronary Arteries
    • Outer layer
    • Adventitia 
    • Basic support structure
    • Middle layer
    • Media
    • Multiple layers of smooth muscle cells
    • Makes adjustments to luminal diameter
    • Inner layer
    • Intima
    • endothelial layer, basement membrane, 
    smooth muscle cells
    • Arterial endothelium is selectively 
    permeable to macromolecules of 
    the size of low-density lipoprotein
    • Lipoproteins and fibrinogen are most 
    likely to accumulate in intima


    .Myocardial Perfusion
    • How oxygenated blood supply 
    the heart
    • Follows the basic rules of fluid 
    dynamics allow for 
    determination of blood flow


    .Myocardial Perfusion can be affected by… ('')
    • Atherosclerosis
    • Atherosclerotic plaques are composed of 
    lipid and thrombus
    • Atherosis
    • Fatty streak that consists of lipid-laden 
    macrophages and smooth muscle cells
    • Sclerosis
    • Responsible for reduction of blood vessel 
    compliance
    • Organization of “fibrous cap” of thrombi over 
    advanced plaques that have developed on 
    endothelial lining 
    • Vasospasm
    • Hyperplasia of intimal smooth muscle cells is 
    hallmark of advanced atherosclerosis 
    creating a coronary artery that is prone to 
    spasm


    .Atherosclerosis can be a Systemic Pathology​ ('')


    .CV Disease Risk Factors
    • Health metrics for ideal CV health 
    • Risk factors
        • Genetic vs behavioral 
        • Modifiable vs non-modifiable risk factors


    .CV Disease Can Lead to Sudden Cardiac Death
        Box 3-3

        Risk Factors Associated with Undiagnosed CHD Population:
            - Age
            - Systolic blood pressure (elevated)
            - Left ventricular hypertrophy on ECG
            - Nonspecific ECG abnormalities
            - Serum cholesterol (elevated)
            - Heart rate (elevated resting HR)
            - Vital capacity (low, especially in females)
            - Cigarette consumed daily
            - Relative weight
        Sudden Death Diagnosed CHD Population:
            - Decreased left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) (<35%)


    .Acute Coronary Syndrome ('')
        Esta imatge ja la tenim exlicà per ahí. Búscala.

    .Angina 
    • Imbalance in supply and 
    demand of myocardial oxygen
    • Described as sub-sternal 
    pressure
    • Can occur anywhere from 
    epigastric area to jaw
    • Squeezing, tightness, or 
    crushing


    .Types of Angina
        Poor or occluded myocardial arteries can produce either:
            Stable Angina 
            Unstable Angina


    .Chest Pain Differential Diagnosis
    • Classic stable angina
    • Unstable angina
    • Prinzmetal angina
    • Pericarditis
    • Chest wall pain (musculoskeletal)
    • Pulmonary/pleuritic (pleurisy, 
    pneumothorax, pneumonia) 
    • Bronchospasm
    • Vascular (pulmonary embolism, 
    aortic dissection)
    • Gastrointestinal (esophageal reflux, 
    peptic ulcer, gallbladder disease)


    Angina 
    • Early warning signs of a heart 
    attack.
    • A woman can experience any of 
    the various patterns described 
    but is more likely to develop 
    atypical symptoms of pain as 
    depicted here.
    ('')
        Uncomfortable pressure, fullness, squeezing or pain in the center of the chest that lasts more than a few minutes or that goes away and comes back.

        Pain spreading to the shoulders, neck or arms.

        Chest discomfort with lightheadedness, fainting, sweating, nausea or shortness of breath.

        Increased episodes of chest pain.

        Prolonged pain in the upper abdomen.

        Shortness of breath.

        ---

        Less common warning signs of heart attack (especially women):

        - Stomach or abdominal pain
        - Shortness of breath and difficulty breathing when lying down
        - Unexplained anxiety, weakness or fatigue
        - Palpitations, cold sweat or paleness

        ---

        Most chest discomfort (common location e.g., burning sensation behind sternum), commonly waning symptoms:

        - Continuous vs intermittent; similar to indigestion but not relieved by antacids
        - Nausea regurgitating food or unrelieved by rest
        - Pain relieved by nitro-glycerine preparation

        ---

        Upper abdomen discomfort (less common):

        - Mid-chest incision-like pain radiating outward on both sides; intense anxiety weakness; or fatigue unrelieved by rest; dizziness appetite loss nausea vomiting diarrhea constipation bloating belching flatulence


    .Acute Myocardial Infarction 
    • Vessel occlusion > 60 mins with evidence of:
    • Rise in troponin
    • ECG changes 
    • New cardiac mm damage, wall motion abnormalities on imaging 
    • BP changes
    • Signs, symptoms and exam findings:
    • Diaphoresis
    • Tachycardia
    • Tachypenea
    • New murmur or mitral regurgitation
    • S3 and S4 heart sounds
    • Divided into STEMI and NSTEMI


    .STEMI & Non-STEMI
    • Non-STEMI 
    • does not develop a Q wave on ECG
    • Narrowed coronary arteries, risk for 
    complete blockage 
    • Less myocardial damage

    • STEMI
    • develops a Q wave on ECG in 
    subsequent 24 to 48 hours 
    • Occluded coronary artery
    • Extensive damage
    • Poor prognosis


    .Progression of STEMI
    Timeline Pathophysiologic Changes
    First hours Myocardial injury is potentially reversible for 
    about the first 20 min after onset
    Progressive loss of viable tissue from 20 min up 
    to 6–12 hrs post onset
    Zones of necrosis identified as early as 2–3 hrs 
    post-MI
    First days Affected myocardium is pale and swollen
    18–36 hrs post-MI erythrocytes are trapped
    48 hrs post-MI neutrophils infiltrate
    First weeks 8–10 days post-MI thickness of infracted cardiac 
    wall ↓
    Mononuclear cells remove necrotic muscle
    From 3 wks to 3–4 mons infracted area converts 
    to shrunken thin firm scar


    .Location of Myocardial Infarction ('')
        Title: Table 3.2: Coronary anatomy and location of infarction

        Columns:
        - Anatomy
        - Location of Infarct
        - ECG Changes
        - Common Complications

        Rows:
        1. Right coronary artery
        - Inferior
        - II, III, aVF
        - Risk of atrioventricular block; arrhythmias; ~50% have right ventricular infarcts

        2. Left main
        - Anterior and lateral
        - V1-V6, I, aVL
        - Pump dysfunction or failure

        3. Left anterior descending (LAD)
        - Anterior
        - V1-V4
        - Pump dysfunction or failure

        4. Circumflex
        - Lateral
        - V5, V6, I, aVL
        - None specific


    .Cardiac Biomarkers - Patients with MI
    • Troponin
    • Creatine Phosphokinase (CPK)
    • Myoglobin


    .Progression of Myocardial Necrosis ('')
    • Progression of myocardial 
    necrosis after coronary 
    artery occlusion


    .Progression of Myocardial Necrosis ('')


    .Medical Management 
    • Primary concern is to reperfusion of the area of heart
    • Control for cardiac pain
    • nitrates, morphine, beta-blockers
    • Prevent complications:
    • L ventricular dysfunction, heart blocks (pacemaker)
    • Fibrinolysis and PTCA if within 3 hours of onset
    • Prevent abnormal contraction patterns


    .Prognostic Factors Post-MI
    • Ventricular remodeling
    • With STEMI, changes in shape, size, and thickness of myocardium
    • Areas of ventricular dilation and ventricular hypertrophy
    • Factors that affect remodeling
    • Size of infarct
    • Ventricular load
    • Patency of the artery that was infarcted
    • Prognosis
    • Related to complications, infarction size, presence of disease on other coronary 
    arteries, and left ventricular function


    .Physical Therapy Management 
    • Parameters for Initiation of Treatment in Acute Care
    • No new or recurrent chest pain in previous 8 hours​
    • Stable or falling creatine kinase and troponin values​
    • No indication of decompensated heart failure (resting 
    dyspnea/bibasilar rales)​
    • Normal cardiac rhythm and stable ECG from past 8 hours​


    .General Goals for Inpatient Physical Therapy
    • Offset effects of bed rest (see systemic effects of immobilization)​
    • Evaluate physiological responses to self care and ambulation using ECG and vital 
    signs​
    • Optimize physical functioning​
    • May include ROM exercises, balance training, functional mobility training 
    including stair training if return to home​
    • Patient education​
    • Signs and symptoms of exercise intolerance​
    • Home exercise program including physical activity and exercise​
    • Provide feedback to the team about patient’s tolerance for activity and responses​
    • Plan for discharge to home or transitional setting to optimize recovery and facilitate 
    referral to outpatient rehabilitation program when warranted​


    .Functional Mobility Training in Acute Care
    • Initiate once patient can roll in bed 
    and maintain BP and oxygen levels

    • Careful review of medical status​

    • Positioning of lines, drains and 
    tubes​

    • Coordination with the other 
    members of the interdisciplinary 
    team


    .Systemic Effects of Immobilization
    • Increased heart rate
    • Decreased maximal O2 uptake
    • Orthostatic hypotension
    • Increased risk of DVT
    • Recued vital capacity
    • Reduced ability to clear secretions and cough effectively
    • Reduced PaO2 
    • Reduced strength and ROM
    • Risk of contracture and ulcers
    • Osteoporosis
    • Cognitive, emotional and/or behavioral disturbances


    .FITT Principles for Inpatient Cardiac Rehab
    Aerobic Exercise​ FITT Recommendations​
    Frequency 2-4 sessions /day​
    Intensity​
    (1-4 MET range)​

    HR rest + 20 beats/min for patients with MI and + 30 beats/min 
    for patients after heart surgery​
    Warm up/cool down in 9-11 range​
    Upper limit <120 bpm, RPE <13 on 6-20 RPE scale​

    Time​ Being with intermittent walking for 3-5 minutes; progressively 
    increase. Rest may be slower walk or complete rest. Attempt 2:1 exercise 
    to rest. Progress 10-15min​

    Type​ Primarily walking​

     If patient is taking a Beta blocker, may not have the typical HR 
    response to exercise.


    .Adverse Responses to Inpatient Exercise to Indicate Termination
    • Diastolic BP >110 mm Hg​
    • Decrease in SBP > 10 mm Hg with exercise​
    • Significant ventricular or atrial arrythmias​
    • Second- or third-degree heart block​
    • Signs and symptoms of exercise intolerance including 
    angina, marked dyspnea, ECG changes that indicate ischemia

    Hypertension

    .Blood Pressure 
    • Blood Pressure = TPR x CO
    • CO = SV x HR
    • Important Variables:
    • Systolic Blood Pressure 
    • Diastolic Blood Pressure 
    • Mean Arterial Pressure 


    .Diagnosing Hypertension ('')


    .Effects of Uncontrolled Hypertension
    • Hypertensive heart disease
    • Damaged endothelium
    ('')
        Brain
            Cerebral aneurysm
            Hemorrhagic CVA (stroke)
        Atherosclerosis
        Eyes
            Retinopathy—arteriolar damage, with microaneurysms and rupture
        Heart
            Congestive heart failure
            Atherosclerosis
            Angina
            Myocardial infarction
        Kidney
            Nephrosclerosis
            Chronic renal failure
        Blood pressure
            Persistent elevation


    .Hypertension Relationship to Systolic vs. Diastolic Dysfunction
    • HTN →Increased TPR 
    →Increased in afterload→
    Increased myocardial 
    workload → cardiomyopathy
    ('')
        Systolic Dysfunction

        - An impairment in ventricular contraction, resulting in decrease in stroke volume and ejection fraction (<40%).
        - An increase in end systolic volume will occur. Now called heart failure with reduced ejection fraction or HFrEF.

        Diastolic Dysfunction

        - Changes in ventricular diastolic properties that lead to an impairment in ventricular filling (reduction) and a resultant increase in end diastolic volume.
        - A consequence of relaxation dysfunction is the rise in end diastolic pressure. Now called heart failure with preserved ejection fraction or HFpEF.


    .Treatment Guidelines for Hypertension 
    ('')
        1. Title: Table 3-6 Treatment Guidelines for Hypertension
        2. Category:
        - Prehypertension:
            - Blood Pressure Range: 120–139 systolic, 80–89 diastolic
            - Recommended Treatment: Lifestyle modification
        - Stage 1 Hypertension:
            - Blood Pressure Range: 140–159 systolic, 90–99 diastolic
            - Recommended Treatment: Thiazide diuretics; may consider ACE inhibitor, ARB, BB, CCB, or combination
        - Stage 2 Hypertension:
            - Blood Pressure Range: ≥160 systolic, ≥100 diastolic
            - Recommended Treatment: Two-drug combination generally should include thiazide diuretic and ACEI or ARB or BB or CCB

    .Implications for Physical Therapy
    • High percentage of patients referred to physical therapy will have recognized 
    or unrecognized HTN
    • Should include monitoring during treatment sessions
    • Refer to physician if resting BP is high (SBP >200 mm Hg or DBP >100 mm Hg)


    .Hypertension & Exercise Guidelines
        ('')
            - Box 9-6 Guidelines for Exercise in Individuals with Hypertension
            - If resting BP >200 mm Hg systolic, >100 mm Hg diastolic:
                - Exercise testing – exercise medical clearance needed.
                - Discontinue exercise if:
                - Systolic BP exceeds 250 mm Hg systolic, >115 mm Hg diastolic.
            - If resting BP is uncontrolled: severe, ≥180 mm Hg systolic, ≥110 mm Hg diastolic; and moderate clearance needed.
            - Particular watch for effects of medications:
                - Consistency side hypotension with:
                - Change of position
                - Postexercise
                - Long-term standing
                - Warm weather or hot baths/saunas especially high risk; exercises to avoid both extremes.
            - Avoid high-intensity interval training/high resistance; 60% to 80% endurance training at moderate intensity

            Data from American College of Sports Medicine: Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription, Baltimore, Williams & Wilkins, 2014.

        ('')
            1. FITT Principles from ACSM
            Frequency:
            For aerobic exercise, 5-7 d/wk, supplemented by resistance exercise 2-3 d/wk and flexibility exercise ≥2-3 d/wk.

            Intensity:
            Moderate [i.e., 40-60% VO2R or 11-14 on a scale of 6 (no exertion) to 20 (maximal exertion)]

            Time:
            For aerobic exercise, a minimum of 30 min up to 60 min/d for continuous or accumulated aerobic exercise.
            New and emerging research has shown that short bouts of exercise (3-10 min) interspersed throughout the day may elicit BP reductions

            Type:
            For aerobic exercise, emphasis should be placed on prolonged, rhythmic activities using large muscle groups

    .How Does Aerobic Exercise Lower BP?
        Endothelial –Dependent Vasodilation or Shear Stress


    .Exercise as Vascular Medicine ('')
        ### Question 1: True or False
        Exercise training is associated with rapid changes in artery function, including increased bioavailability of endothelium-derived nitric oxide (NO).

        Answer: True

        Rationale: Exercise training leads to rapid changes in artery function, one of which is the increased bioavailability of endothelium-derived nitric oxide (NO). NO is a crucial molecule that helps in vasodilation, improving blood flow and reducing blood pressure. This functional adaptation is one of the immediate benefits of exercise on vascular health.

        ### Question 2: Multiple Choice
        What is the primary functional adaptation in arteries due to exercise training?
        A. Increased arterial stiffness
        B. Increased bioavailability of endothelium-derived nitric oxide (NO)
        C. Decreased blood flow
        D. Decreased arterial diameter

        Answer: B. Increased bioavailability of endothelium-derived nitric oxide (NO)

        Rationale: The primary functional adaptation in arteries due to exercise training is the increased bioavailability of endothelium-derived nitric oxide (NO). NO plays a vital role in maintaining vascular health by promoting vasodilation and improving blood flow, which are essential for reducing cardiovascular risk.

        ### Question 3: Select All That Apply
        Which of the following are structural adaptations in arteries due to exercise training?
        A. Arterial remodeling
        B. Increased arterial diameter
        C. Decreased arterial stiffness
        D. Decreased bioavailability of NO

        Answer: A. Arterial remodeling, B. Increased arterial diameter, C. Decreased arterial stiffness

        Rationale: Structural adaptations in arteries due to exercise training include arterial remodeling, increased arterial diameter, and decreased arterial stiffness. These changes contribute to improved vascular function and reduced cardiovascular risk over the long term. Decreased bioavailability of NO is not a structural adaptation; rather, exercise increases NO bioavailability.

        ### Question 4: True or False
        The functional changes in arteries due to exercise training are eventually superseded by arterial remodeling.

        Answer: True

        Rationale: The functional changes in arteries, such as increased bioavailability of NO, are initially rapid but are eventually superseded by structural adaptations like arterial remodeling. This process involves changes in the arterial wall structure, leading to long-term improvements in vascular health and function.

        ### Question 5: Multiple Choice
        Which of the following best describes the relationship between functional and structural adaptations in arteries due to exercise training?
        A. Functional adaptations occur first and are followed by structural adaptations.
        B. Structural adaptations occur first and are followed by functional adaptations.
        C. Functional and structural adaptations occur simultaneously.
        D. Neither functional nor structural adaptations occur due to exercise training.

        Answer: A. Functional adaptations occur first and are followed by structural adaptations.

        Rationale: Functional adaptations, such as increased bioavailability of NO, occur rapidly with exercise training. These changes are followed by structural adaptations, such as arterial remodeling, which take longer to develop. This sequence ensures both immediate and long-term benefits to vascular health.

        ### Question 6: Select All That Apply
        Which of the following are benefits of increased bioavailability of endothelium-derived nitric oxide (NO) due to exercise training?
        A. Improved vasodilation
        B. Enhanced blood flow
        C. Reduced blood pressure
        D. Increased arterial stiffness

        Answer: A. Improved vasodilation, B. Enhanced blood flow, C. Reduced blood pressure

        Rationale: Increased bioavailability of endothelium-derived nitric oxide (NO) due to exercise training leads to improved vasodilation, enhanced blood flow, and reduced blood pressure. These benefits are crucial for maintaining cardiovascular health. Increased arterial stiffness is not a benefit; in fact, exercise helps to decrease arterial stiffness.

        ### Question 7: True or False
        Exercise training has no impact on the endothelium of blood vessels.

        Answer: False

        Rationale: Exercise training has a significant impact on the endothelium of blood vessels. It increases the bioavailability of endothelium-derived nitric oxide (NO), which is essential for vasodilation and overall vascular health. This adaptation helps to improve blood flow and reduce cardiovascular risk.

        ### Question 8: Multiple Choice
        What is the role of nitric oxide (NO) in vascular health?
        A. Promotes vasoconstriction
        B. Increases arterial stiffness
        C. Promotes vasodilation
        D. Decreases blood flow

        Answer: C. Promotes vasodilation

        Rationale: Nitric oxide (NO) plays a crucial role in vascular health by promoting vasodilation. This process helps to widen blood vessels, improve blood flow, and reduce blood pressure. NO is essential for maintaining healthy endothelial function and preventing cardiovascular diseases.

    physiological changes 

    HR percentages determined by patient tolerance and level of return to function

    > > > 

    Other Vascular Disorders  

    .Peripheral Arterial Disease
    • Atherosclerotic occlusive disease 
    • Atheromatous plaque obstruction of large or medium-sized 
    arteries supplying blood to the extremities
    • 60% to 80% of those with PAD have significant coronary 
    atherosclerosis in at least one coronary artery


    .Signs and Symptoms of PAD
    • Intermittent claudication (IC) 
    (35-40%)
    • Critical Limb ischemia (CLI)


    .Signs and Symptoms of PAD


    .Differential Diagnosis of Signs and Symptoms
    Peripheral Arterial Disease or Lumbar Radiculopathy?


    .PAD Physical Therapy Points of Examination 1
    • Observation & Palpation
    • Trophic changes
    • Muscle atrophy
    • Sensation 
    • Pulses


    .PAD Physical Therapy Points of Examination 2
    • Ankle Brachial Index
    • SBP of ankle/SBP of arm using a 
    doppler ultrasound
    • Abnormal Findings < 0.90


    .Exercise and PAD

    Patients are unable to 
    produce normal 
    increases in peripheral 
    blood flow

    Intermittent 
    claudication leads to 
    moderate to severe 
    impairment in walking 
    ability


    .Benefits of Exercise Training in PAD
    1. Increased peripheral blood flow through changes in the collateral 
    circulation 
    2. Improved Endothelial Function
    3. Reduced blood viscosity
    4. Regression of atherosclerotic disease, raising of the pain threshold
    5. Improvements in skeletal muscle metabolism
    6. Low-intensity training appears beneficial compared to high-intensity 
    training
    7. Intensity guided by IC symptoms appears to be most recommended


    .Summary of Exercise Recommendations for PAD
    • Interval Exercise 
    • Walking 
    • Non–weight-bearing activities
    • Longer warm-up time 
    • Sensory examination 
    • Footwear and foot hygiene


    .Chronic Venous Insufficiency or Peripheral Venous Disease (PVD)
    • Either or both venous outflow 
    obstruction or valvular 
    dysfunction


    .Signs and Symptoms of PVD
    • Aching, burning, fatigue while 
    standing
    • Heaviness, night cramping
    • elevation and walking reduces 
    symptoms
    • Swollen lower limbs
    • Normal muscle mass
    • Skin is warm and 
    hyperpigmented or hemosiderin 
    staining 


    .Physical Therapy and PVD
    • LE elevation
    • check if for CHF on top of this as elevation 
    can increase preload and strain heart 
    • Elastic supports/compression stockings
    • Lymphatic massages
    • Walking
    • Lower extremity exercises/anti-embolic’s
    • Ankle pumps
    • Quad sets
    • Gluteal sets
    • Heel slides


    .Venous Thromboembolic Disease 
    • Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE)
    • Development of clot in deep vein of LE or pelvis, smaller percentage in 
    the arm
    • Development via Virchow’s triad 
    • Diagnosis:
    • Palpation for Signs and Symptoms
    • Well’s Clinical Prediction Rule
    • Ultrasound
    • D-Dimer


    .Development of DVT ('')


    .PT Assessment for DVT
    • pain, tenderness, swelling, warmth, 
    or redness/discoloration in the 
    lower extremity
    • Scoring on the Well’s Clinical 
    Prediction Rule 
    ('')
        Table 3-8 Two-level DVT Wells Score

        Clinical Feature | Points
        --- | ---
        Active cancer (treatment ongoing, within 6 months, or palliative) | 1
        Paralysis, paresis, or recent plaster immobilization of the lower extremities | 1
        Recently bedridden for 3 days or more, or major surgery within 12 weeks requiring general or regional anesthesia | 1
        Localized tenderness along the distribution of the deep venous system | 1
        Entire leg swollen | 1
        Calf swelling at least 3 cm larger than asymptomatic side | 1
        Pitting edema confined to the symptomatic leg | 1
        Collateral superficial veins (nonvaricose) | 1
        Previously documented DVT | 1
        Alternative diagnosis at least as likely as DVT | -2

        Clinical Probability Simplified Score

        DVT "likely" | 2 points or more
        DVT "unlikely" | Fewer than 2 points


    .D-dimer Test
    • High sensitivity and poor specificity
    • If high pretest probability of developing DVT
    • anticoagulant therapy initiated
    • If low pretest probability and high D-dimer
    • further testing (dopplers) warranted


    .DVT Coagulation profile 
    • Prothrombin time (PT) & International Normalized Ratio (INR)
    • Coumadin
    • Activated Partial thromboplastin time (aPTT)
    • Heparin
    • Anti-Factor Xa Assay 
    • Unfractionated Heparin (UFH) and Low Molecular Weight Heparin (Lovenox; 
    LMWH))
    • Reference ranges found in patient lab values can indicate whether PT safe to proceed 
    or contraindicated at that time


    .DVT & Physical Therapy Implications 
    • EARLY AMBULATION
    • Therapeutic levels of anticoagulant should be mobilized
    • Could ambulation dislodge the clot?
    • Studies all done on already anticoagulated patients
    • Heparin usually prescribed initially
    • Approx 3-5 hours for low molecular weight heparins
    • time frames allow for early mobility based on time to achieve a level in the blood to 
    dissolve any larger clots
    • Compression stockings and mechanical compression device
    • Complications
    • Post-thrombotic syndromes even with anticoagulation therapy
    • Remaining clots can lead to venous HTN, inflammation from tissue damage 


    .DVT & Pulmonary Embolism (PE)
    • Signs & Symptoms of a PE:
        1.SOB
        2.Drop in SpO2
            Γ SpO2: peripheral oxygen saturation. It is a measure of the percentage of hemoglobin in the blood that is saturated with oxygen. 
        3.Chest pain
        4.Cough
        5.Sudden tachycardia
            ¦
                3.L'embol putja hasta el pit i fa mal
                1.No deixa respirar
                2.I baixa el SpO2
                4.Començe a tosir per a vore si desfaig del tapó
                5.Però no funciona i em fique taquicardic

        Diagnosis
            1. Ventilation-perfusion scan to rule out 
            2. CT scan for final diagnosis

        Medical Emergency!

        Figure 1: Algorithm for screening for risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE).
            1. Is the patient at high risk for VTE?
                - Yes
                    - Interventions to decrease risk:
                    1. Encourage mobility and physical activity
                    2. Use of mechanical compression
                    3. Consult with physician about medication
                    4. Provide education on VTE prevention
                - No
                    - Encourage mobility and physical activity

        Figure 2.
            Algorithm for determining likelihood of a lower extremity deep vein thrombosis (LE DVT). DVT=deep vein thrombosis.
                1. Does the patient have signs or symptoms of an LE DVT?
                    - No:
                        Continue to encourage mobility and physical activity in addition to any additional preventive interventions.
                    - Yes: Assess DVT likelihood using the Wells criteria for DVT.
                        - Communicate signs and symptoms along with results of Wells criteria to medical team.
                            - Was a diagnostic test for DVT performed?
                                - No:
                                    Use clinical judgment regarding mobilization.
                                - Yes:
                                    - If negative, encourage mobility and physical activity algorithm 3¿?
                                    - If positive, go to therapeutic algorithm
                                    

    .Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA)
    • Etiology: atherosclerosis, HTN, 
    Connective Tissue Defect, natural dec in 
    elasticity 
    • Pathological permanent dilation of the 
    aortic wall involving any number of 
    segments of the aorta
    • Described in terms of location, size, 
    morphological appearance, and origin
    • Rupture is major risk of abdominal 
    aortic aneurysms


    .Risk Factors of AAA ('')
        Table 3-9 Risk factors of aneurysms
            Risk Factors | Complications
            --- | ---
            Smoking (current or past) | Fivefold increase vs. nonsmokers
            Age | Most occur in individuals >60 years of age
            Gender | 5-10x higher incidence in men than in women
            | Women with aneurysm have a higher risk of rupture
            Family history | First-degree relative has an increased risk
            Hypertension | 
            Hyperlipidemia | 
            Atherosclerosis | 

            Data from Braverman A, Thompson R, Sanchez L: Diseases of the aorta. In Braunwald E, editor: Heart Disease: A Textbook of Cardiovascular Medicine, ed 9, Philadelphia, 2012. Saunders


    .AAA Implications for Physical Therapy
    • Signs and Symptoms (DDx)
    • Pressure on surrounding parts such as low back
    • Leg pain/claudication pain
    • Numbness in lower extremities
    • Excessive fatigue
    • Poor distal pulses
    • Low back pain
    • Examination Findings: 
    • Check for pulsating tumor/mass in abdominal area
    • Bruit heard over swollen area in abdomen
    • Considerations 
    • Patients with known/stable AAA
    • Post-operative AA repair precautions

('PT 2026_Mod1.2_Pathophysiology of Cardiac Muscle Dysfunction.pdf')
    > > > 

    Pathophysiology of Cardiac 
    Muscle Dysfunction 

    .Heart as a Muscle
    • Cardiac muscle cells = myocytes
    1. Contractile myocyte
    • Perform mechanical work of the heart – contract to emit force to eject the 
    blood
    2. Pace-maker conduction cells
    • Initiate electrical signals to be conducted through the heart – do not contract
    • Myocytes
    • Striated
    • Overlapping contractile filaments
    • Centrally located nucleus, large number of mitochondria 


    .Heart Failure

    The inability of the heart to pump blood at a level that is proportionate 
    with metabolic needs


    .Factors Leading to Heart Failure 
    • Cardiovascular Vascular 
    • Hypertension
    • Coronary artery disease
    • Cardia dysrhythmias
    • Heart valve abnormality 
    • Pulmonary 
    • Pulmonary embolism
    • Pulmonary hypertension
    • Other
    • Renal Failure
    • Spinal cord injury
    • Age-related changes


    .Cardiomyopathy ('')
        Normal
        Dilated cardiomyopathy
        Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
        Restrictive cardiomyopathy


    .Frank Starling Mechanism ('')


    .Systolic vs Diastolic Dysfunction 1 ('')


    .Systolic vs Diastolic Dysfunction 2 ('')
        | Systolic HF | Diastolic HF |
        | --- | --- |
        | ejection fraction that is reduced (~40%)  | ejection fraction unchanged or slightly increased |*
        | HFrEF = heart failure with reduced ejection fraction | HFpEF = heart failure with preserved ejection fraction |
        | Increase in LV mass (enlarged, stretched) | LV hypertrophy or chronic replacement by fibrous tissue |
        | Increase end-diastolic and end-systolic volumes | Decreased end-diastolic and end-systolic volumes |

            (Γ)Table as an outline
                Systolic vs. Diastolic Dysfunction
                   Systolic HF
                       Ejection fraction is reduced (~40%)
                       HFrEF = heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
                       Increase in LV mass (enlarged, stretched)
                       Increase end-diastolic and end-systolic volumes
                   Diastolic HF
                       Ejection fraction unchanged or slightly increased
                       HFpEF = heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
                       LV hypertrophy or chronic replacement by fibrous tissue
                       Decreased end-diastolic and end-systolic volumes

    .Left vs Right Sided Heart Failure 


    .Heart Failure Biomarkers
    • Brain natriuretic peptide (BNP)
    • Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP)


    .Renal Function and CHF ('')


    .Role of ANP Fluid Volume/Back up
    • Bind to target tissue: 
    • aorta, vascular smooth mm, rental 
    cortex, medulla
    • Reduce adverse stimulus of stretch 
    • causing arterial and venous dilation, 
    reduced blood volume, suppression of 
    water retention via the kidneys


    .Pulmonary Edema and CHF ('')


    .Hepatic Function and CHF ('')


    .Hematological Function and CHF ('')


    .Skeletal Muscle Function and CHF
    • type I and type II muscle fiber atrophy
    • Isometric maximal muscle strength is reduced 50%


    .Pancreatic Function and CHF 
    • Reduced pancreatic 
    function due to 
    reduced blood flow
