3.5. Lecture: Clinical Manifestations and Management of Heart Failure
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

('Clinical Manifestations and Management of Heart Failure.pdf')
    > > > 

    Clinical Manifestations and 
    Management of Heart Failure

    .Clinical Manifestations of Heart Failure
    • Dyspnea 
    • breathlessness or air hunger
    • Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
    • unexplained episodes of shortness of breath occur in supine 
    position
    • Orthopnea
    • development of dyspnea in recumbent position
    • Breathing patterns
    • rapid respiratory rate at rest with quick and shallow breaths


    .Clinical Manifestations of Congestive Heart Failure
    • Crackles
    • abnormal breath sounds that occur 
    during inspiration 
    • Heart sounds
    • S3 indicates a noncompliant left 
    ventricle and is associated with CHF
    • Occurs during diastole after S2
    • Peripheral edema
    • retention of fluid; pitting edema 
    (graded 1+ to 4+; time of skin 
    rebound)
    • Jugular venous distention
    • results from fluid overload


    .Clinical Manifestations of Congestive Heart Failure 1
    • Pulsus alternans
    • mechanical alteration of femoral or radial pulse
    • Changes in extremities
    • may become cold and appear pale and cyanotic
    • Weight gain
    • as total body fluid volume increases, so does total body weight
    • Sinus tachycardia 
    • Decreased exercise tolerance


    .Clinical Manifestations of Heart Failure 2
        .Radiological findings in congestive heart failure
        • Evaluation of size and shape of 
        cardiac silhouette (left VEDV)
        • Presence of interstitial, 
        perivascular, alveolar edema 
        (fluid in lungs)

        .Laboratory findings in congestive heart failure:
        • BNP & ANP
        • Erythrocyte sedimentation rate
        • Liver enzymes (AST, bilirubin, 
        LDH-5)
        • Kidney markers (BUN, 
        creatinine)
        • Blood gases as related to lung 
        and kidney dysfunction

        .Echocardiography
        • Left ventricular ejection fraction
        • Structure of LV 
        • Other structural abnormalities


    .Exercise Tolerance in Heart Failure  
    • Increased tachycardia at submaximal loads
    • Decrease in SBP 
    • ECG signs of myocardial ischemia with angina
    • Quick onset of dyspnea and fatigue
    • Lower maximal work loads
    • Chronotropic incompetence 


    .6 MWT and Heart Failure
    Those ambulating < 468m poorer 
    short-term survival


    .NYHA Classification ('')
                | AHA/ACC Stage | Description                                                                 | NYHA Class | Description                                                                                                           |
        |---------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
        | Stage A       | At high risk for developing HF. No Identified structural or functional abnormality, no signs or symptoms of HF. | N/A        | Not applicable                                                                                                        |
        | Stage B       | Structural heart disease that is strongly associated with the development of HF but no signs and symptoms of HF. | N/A        | Not applicable                                                                                                        |
        | Stage C       | Symptomatic HF, associated with underlying structural heart disease.        | I          | No limitation in physical activity; ordinary physical activity does not cause fatigue, palpitations, or dyspnea.      |
        |               |                                                                             | II         | Slight limitation of physical activity; comfortable at rest but ordinary activity results in fatigue, palpitations, or dyspnea. |
        |               |                                                                             | III        | Marked limitation of physical activity; comfortable at rest but less than ordinary activity results in fatigue, palpitations, or dyspnea. |
        |               |                                                                             | IV         | Symptoms at rest; unable to do any physical activity without symptomology.                                            |
        | Stage D       | Advanced structural disease with marked symptomology at rest despite maximal medical therapy. | N/A        | Not applicable                                                                                                        |


    .Medical Management & Treatment 1
    • Proper prescription of physical activity
    • Dietary Recommendations
    • Restriction of sodium intake
    • Pharmacological Agents 
    • Diuretics
    • Digoxin or positive ionotropic agents
    • Vasodilators 
    • Anticoagulants 


    .Medical Management & Treatment 2
    • ICD implantation
    • Cardiac resynchronization 
    therapy


    .Mechanical Management 
    • Dialysis and ultrafiltration
    • Assisted circulation via intra-
    aortic balloon counter-pulsation 
    using a pump (IABP)
    • Ventricular assist device


    .Surgical Management 
    • Left ventricular muscle flap 
    or cardiomyoplasty
    • Cardiac transplantation via 
    Xenograft or Allograft


    .Significant predictors of survival
    • Decreasing LVEF
    • Decreasing peak exercise oxygen uptake
    • Widened QRS on 12-lead ECG
    • Chronic hypotension
    • Resting tachycardia
    • Renal insufficiency
    • Intolerance to therapy
    • Refractory volume overload


    .Physical Therapy Assessment
    • Thorough assessment including an interview, vitals, & 
    cardiopulmonary assessment
    • PT cardiopulmonary assessment may include:
    • Heart sounds
    • Lung sounds
    • Palpation
    • Observation


    .Rehabilitation and Exercise in HF
    • Supervised Exercise Training 
    • Cardiac rehabilitation 
    Programs
    • Exercise prescription and 
    exercise modalities in HF


    .Guidelines for Exercise Training in CHF 1
    • Relative criteria necessary 
    for the initiation of an 
    aerobic exercise training 
    program


    .Guidelines for Exercise Training in CHF 2
    • Relative criteria indicating a 
    need to modify or terminate 
    exercise training


    .Heart Failure Clinical Practice Guidelines ('')
        | Zone Color  | Signs and Symptoms                                                                 | Physical Therapist Recommendations                                                                 |
        |-------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
        | Green zone  | - No shortness of breath<br>- No swelling<br>- No weight gain<br>- No chest pain<br>- No decrease in your ability to maintain your activity level | Continue activity and therapy as tolerated.                                                        |
        | Yellow zone | - Weight gain of 2-3 lbs in 24 hrs<br>- Increased cough<br>- Peripheral edema: increased distal extremity swelling<br>- Increase in shortness of breath with activity<br>- Orthopnea: increase in the number of pillows needed to sleep comfortably at night | Symptoms may indicate an adjustment in medications and therefore warrants communication with the physician. |
        | Red zone    | - Shortness of breath at rest<br>- Unrelieved chest pain<br>- Wheezing or chest tightness at rest<br>- Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea: requiring to sit in chair to sleep<br>- Weight gain or loss of more than 5 lbs in 3 days<br>- Confusion | Symptoms indicate overt decompensation and an immediate visit to the emergency department or physician office. |


    .Exercise Prescription Considerations
    • Must consider the FITT principle 
    • Consider HF Patients with:
    • Intravenous ionotropic agents
    • Left Ventricular Assistive Devices


    .Breathing Interventions


    .Energy Conservation
    • Goal is to decrease 
    workload on heart 
    without loss of function
    ('')
        | Zone Color  | Signs and Symptoms                                                                 | Physical Therapist Recommendations                                                                 |
        |-------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
        | Green zone  | - No shortness of breath<br>- No swelling<br>- No weight gain<br>- No chest pain<br>- No decrease in your ability to maintain your activity level | Continue activity and therapy as tolerated.                                                        |
        | Yellow zone | - Weight gain of 2-3 lbs in 24 hrs<br>- Increased cough<br>- Peripheral edema: increased distal extremity swelling<br>- Increase in shortness of breath with activity<br>- Orthopnea: increase in the number of pillows needed to sleep comfortably at night | Symptoms may indicate an adjustment in medications and therefore warrants communication with the physician. |
        | Red zone    | - Shortness of breath at rest<br>- Unrelieved chest pain<br>- Wheezing or chest tightness at rest<br>- Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea: requiring to sit in chair to sleep<br>- Weight gain or loss of more than 5 lbs in 3 days<br>- Confusion | Symptoms indicate overt decompensation and an immediate visit to the emergency department or physician office. |

        | 10 Maximal                           | 10 Maximal                             |

//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
3.6. Cardiovascular Conditions Self-Assessment
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////// (!!Q)

(See ANKI: 'T01_CP_inCan_M01_U01_01c', 'T01_CP_inCan_M01_U02_01b', could be more)

Question 1
0 / 
Which of the following components of the ECG impulse represents the ventricular depolarization? 
  P wave 
  P-R segment 
Correct!
  QRS complex 
  ST segment 
The QRS complex is the electrical stimulus of ventricular depolarization and is normally followed closely by ventricular contraction 

 
Question 2
0 / 
A single-lead tracing or rhythm strip can be used to determine all of the following EXCEPT: 
  Heart rate 
  Heart rhythm 
  Presence of arrhythmia 
Correct!
  Presence of ischemia 
The single-lead tracing or rhythm strip can be used only to determine heart rate, rhythm, or the presence of arrhythmia. If hypertrophy, ischemia, or infarction is susp ected, then a 12-lead ECG should be obtained. 

 
Question 3
0 / 
When a therapist is assessing the cardiac cycle for rhythm and rate disturbances, which of the following assessment approaches is used to evaluate the P-R interval? 
Correct!
  Is the duration between 0.12 and 0.20 second? 
  Is the duration between 0.06 and 0.10 second? 
  Is it regular? 
  Does one occur before every QRS? 
When evaluating the P-R interval, the therapist determines whether it has a normal duration of 0.12 to 0.20 second. 

 
Question 4
0 / 
A premature ventricular complex that occurs every third beat on an ECG is named: 
  Bigeminy 
Correct!
  Trigeminy 
  Unifocal 
  Paired 
When analyzing PVCs occurring on a patient’s ECG it is important to note when and how frequent they occur. When you see one happening every 3rd beat or QRS, QRS, PVC, then you would name that a trigeminy. A Bigeminy is when every other beat is PVC, a Unifocal is when all PVCs appear identical in configuration, and a Paired is when two PVCs are together 

 
Question 5
0 / 
The development of mural thrombi secondary to the coagulation of blood in the heart chamber subsequently leading to a potential stroke occurs in which of the following heart arrhythmias?  
  Atrial flutter 
Correct!
  Atrial fibrillation 
  Atrial tachycardia 
  Sinus pause or block 
Atrial fibrillation has the potential for developing mural thrombi because of the coagulation of blood with fibrillating atria. Mural thrombi may lead to emboli. 

 
Question 6
0 / 
A 68-year-old male collapses in his yard while mowing. The EMTs immediately obtain an ECG strip that reveals grossly irregular up and down fluctuations of the baseline in an irregular zigzag pattern. Which of the following arrhythmias is potentially occurring? 
  Ventricular tachycardia 
Correct!
  Ventricular fibrillation 
  Atrial flutter 
  Atrial fibrillation 
An ECG of a ventricular fibrillation results in a picture of grossly irregular up and down fluctuations of the baseline in an irregular zigzag pattern. 

 
Question 7
0 / 
Which of the following changes on an ECG BEST indicate a period of ischemia? 
  ST-segment elevation 
Correct!
  ST-segment depression 
  Enlarged QRS complex 
  Presence of a significant Q wave 
Ischemia is classically demonstrated on the 12-lead ECG with T wave inversion or ST-segment depression.

        .Diagnoses Review Group Activity
            INSTRUCTIONS
                -In this activity you will determine how a specific diagnosis will impact the specified variables as listed in the table. This about whether these variables increase or decrease and how that may affect exercise tolerance. Please have an explanation as to why this may occur. When completed, we will come back to discuss.

            Hypertension
                Stroke Volume
                Heart Rate
                Left Ventricular Contractility 
                Cardiac Output
                Exercise Tolerance
            Myocardial Infarction of the Left Ventricle
                Stroke Volume
                Heart Rate
                Left Ventricular Contractility 
                Cardiac Output
                Exercise Tolerance
            Systolic Heart Failure
                Stroke Volume
                Heart Rate
                Left Ventricular Contractility 
                Cardiac Output
                Exercise Tolerance
            Diastolic Heart Failure
                Stroke Volume
                Heart Rate
                Left Ventricular Contractility 
                Cardiac Output
                Exercise Tolerance

            Reminder:
                Stroke Volume: Amount ejected per beat (=End diastolic volume – end systolic volume)
                Heart Rate: Beats per minute or SA node stimulation
                Cardiac Output: Amount of blood pumped by each ventricle per minute (L/min)
                Contractility: Force of myocardial contraction independent of preload and afterload

    - reduced Thrombopoietin (TPO) production - 16%
    - increased glucose levels - 0%
    - increased ANP production - 8%

3.10. Module 3 Quiz

Question 1
Which of the following interventions would result in the highest survival rate from ventricular fibrillation sudden cardiac arrest?

  Immediate CPR and AED shock within 3 to 5 minutes
  AED shock within 15 minutes
  Entry into emergency medical system within 15 minutes
  Administration of CPR within 10 minutes

  Immediate CPR and AED shock within 3 to 5 minutes 
Early CPR and rapid defibrillation combined with early advanced care can produce high long-term survival rates for witnessed cardiac arrest. If bystanders provide immediate CPR and the first shock is delivered within 3 to 5 minutes, the reported survival rates from ventricular fibrillation cardiac arrest are as high as 48% to 74%.

Question 2
Which of the following clinical cues exhibited by a patient with stable angina should alert the health care provider to notify the patient’s physician?

  Reports chest discomfort several times a week.
  Reports chest discomfort in morning that was relieved with minor activity.
  Reports chest discomfort at a lower level of activity than usual.
  Reports chest discomfort resolution with rest or decrease of activity intensity.

  Reports chest discomfort at a lower level of activity than usual. 
Clinical clues to the development of unstable angina that should alert the health professional to notify the patient’s physician include angina at rest, occurrence of typical angina at lower level of activity than usual, angina several times a day versus a week, evidence of loss of previously present myocardial reserve, or angina that occurs in the morning that is worse with minor activity. 

Question 3
Which of the following peripheral muscular adaptations that occurs with aerobic exercise would benefit the patient with intermittent claudication the MOST?
  Improvements in anaerobic metabolism
  Increased blood viscosity
  Reduced pain threshold
  Increased collateral circulation or capillary density

  Increased collateral circulation or capillary density 
Mechanisms that have been postulated to account for improvements in rest pain with patients diagnosed with intermittent claudication include increased peripheral blood flow through changes in collateral circulation, reduced blood viscosity, regression of atherosclerotic disease, raising of pain threshold, and improvements in skeletal muscle metabolism.   

Question 4
Which of the following pathological conditions will result in scar formation with associated decreased contractility and reduced relaxation in the myocardial tissue?

  Myocardial Infarction
  Renal failure
  Angina
  Hypertension

Myocardial Infarction
Actual injury to myocardial tissue from an infarction may result in scar formation and decreased contractility as well as reduced relaxation.

Question 5
According to the Frank–Starling mechanism, an insignificant ventricular end-diastolic volume will result in which of the following changes in heart function?

  No Change in filling pressure
  Decrease in ventricular mechanical performance
  Increase in stroke volume producing an elevated blood pressure
  Increase in stretch of the myocardium

  Decrease in ventricular mechanical performance 
This a question you need to read carefully to determine what it is asking first and foremost. The Frank–Starling mechanism explains the relationship between ventricular filling pressure (or end-diastolic volume) and ventricular mechanical activity. An optimal filling pressure (or ventricular end-diastolic volume) exists and if exceeded or insignificant will decrease ventricular mechanical performance. Stroke volume is the result of an optimal degree of myocardial stretch as well as that of myocardial contractility.

Question 6
Which of the following statements BEST describes the term diastolic heart failure?

  .Inability of the ventricles to accept the blood ejected from the atria
  .Loss of contracting myocardium because of anterior myocardial infarction
  .Change in filling due to replacement of infarcted area with distensible fibrous tissue
  .Impaired contraction that produces an inefficient expulsion of blood
  .The inability of the ventricles to accept the blood ejected from the atria during rest or diastole, such as due to the replacement of an infracted area with nondistensible fibrous scar tissue (which does not readily or adequately accept the blood ejected into the left ventricle from the left atria producing diastolic failure).

Inability of the ventricles to accept the blood ejected from the atria 


Question 7
A patient with congestive heart failure is being seen by a physical therapist for exercise progression. The patient is currently taking beta-blocker medication. Which of the following methods to monitor exercise intensity is MOST appropriate for this patient?

  Blood Pressure Response
  Patient Observation
  Rating of Perceived Exertion
  Heart Rate Response

Rating of Perceived Exertion
More patients with CHF and CMD are being prescribed beta-blockers, which often cause little or no change in resting and exercise heart rates. The Borg rating scale is a good clinical tool for monitoring intensity and assisting the clinician with the appropriate time to progress the exercise.
    What is CMD? ¿?
    Explain the rationale
        Rating of Perceived Exertion is the most appropriate method to monitor exercise intensity for a patient with congestive heart failure taking beta-blocker medication.

        Rationale: Beta-blockers affect heart rate response, making it an unreliable indicator of exercise intensity for patients taking these medications. The Rating of Perceived Exertion (RPE), such as the Borg scale, allows patients to subjectively gauge their level of exertion. This method is particularly useful for patients with congestive heart failure on beta-blockers because it doesn't rely on heart rate and takes into account the patient's overall feeling of exertion, including factors like breathlessness and muscle fatigue.

Question 8
A patient with NYHA class II congestive heart failure is currently receiving physical therapy. Instruction about energy conservation will be included in the patient education session. Which of the following recommendations would be appropriate for this patient?

  Complete several tedious tasks at one time .
  Stop and rest when you get tired.
  Alternate easy tasks with difficult tasks, plan for rest.
  Keep the living environment setup the same .

Alternate easy tasks with difficult tasks, plan for rest.
Table 4-R provides a number of recommendations for energy conservation. Of the answers choices, answer (C) is correct as it recommends alternating easy tasks with difficult tasks to help a patient maintain an overall low intensity with rest incorporated. Answer (A) is incorrect; it should be stop to rest before you get tired; answer (B) is incorrect; you should spread out tedious tasks; answer (D) is incorrect; you should make changes in the environment to make activities easier such as keeping items within easy reach.

Question 9
A noncompliant left ventricle that occurs as blood passively fills a poorly relaxing ventricle during early diastole and is considered the hallmark of congestive heart failure describes which of the following heart sounds?
  S4
  S3
  S2
  S1

S3 is heard during early diastole (after S2) and indicates a noncompliant left ventricle that occurs as blood passively fills a poorly relaxing left ventricle that appears to make contact with the chest wall. The presence of S3 is considered a hallmark of CHF.


Question 10
You are working with a patient who has Class III NYHA CHF in the physical therapy clinic, and they express some breathlessness completing a load of laundry, which includes loading the washer, loading the dryer and folding the clothing. You decide it is important to instruct some energy conservation techniques. All of the following are appropriate energy conservation instructions for this patient, EXCEPT:

  “when you can, delegate this activity to family members in your home”
  “sit while performing the folding of the laundry”
  “make sure to push through to completion, even when you are breathless”
  “plan ahead, and ensure you have rest breaks between each of the laundry tasks”

“make sure to push through to completion, even when you are breathless” 
See box 4-8 in the Hillegass test for energy conservation suggestions, but you should not tell a patient with CHF to push through when breathless, as this is a sign of possible acute heart failure leading to reduced cardiac output, venous congestion and/or fluid backflow into the lungs.  This may be concerning, especially with a patient at Class III, where they may start to have marked limitation in activity and be more comfortable at rest.
    ('hillegass Essentials of Cardiopulmonary Physical Therapy 4th.pdf')
        BOX 4-7 Energy conservation techniques for individuals with heart failure
            • Sit while working whenever possible.
            • Before you get tired, stop and rest.
            • Spread tedious tasks out throughout the week.
            • Do the tasks that require the most energy at times that you have the most energy.
            • Alternate easy tasks with difficult tasks, and plan a rest period.
            • Devote a portion of your day to an activity you enjoy and find relaxing.
            • Keep items within easy reach.
            • Plan ahead so you don’t have to rush or push yourself hard.
            • Decide activities that are not necessary for you to do, and delegate to other family members or caregivers; share the work.

    Quiz M05
        Which lab value is considered gold standard for diagnosing a cardiac injury?
                Creatinine
                Troponin
                Triglycerides
                BNP

                Troponin
                    Troponin is considered the gold standard measure for diagnosing cardiac injury, specifically myocardial infarction. Troponin a preferred biomarker with high cardiac tissue specificity, and should be monitored as they trend upward.

                    Here's why the other options are incorrect:
                        Creatinine: ¦Kreatine (K) = Kidney (K)
                            Creatinine is primarily used to assess kidney function, not cardiac injury. While kidney dysfunction can be associated with heart problems, creatinine levels do not directly indicate cardiac damage.

                        Triglycerides:
                            Triglycerides are a type of fat in the blood. While high levels can be a risk factor for heart disease, they do not directly indicate acute cardiac injury. Triglyceride levels are more useful for assessing long-term cardiovascular risk rather than diagnosing acute cardiac events.

                        BNP (Brain Natriuretic Peptide):
                            While BNP is related to heart function, it is primarily used to diagnose and monitor heart failure. It rises in response to increased stretching of the heart muscle, which occurs in heart failure. However, it is not as specific or sensitive as troponin for diagnosing acute myocardial injury or infarction.

            Which of the following lab values is associated with hepatic or liver tissue can trend upward when a patient has increased fluid volume due to congestive heart failure?
                Creatine Phospohokinase (CPK)
                Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN)
                Albumen
                Troponin

                Albumen ¦Cuan més aigua en el fetge, més fesols (alubias) creixen | Fetge = Fesols
                    Γ Única que es referix a molt de fluit, en conter de poc
                    Albumen is a lab value that is associated with the liver, and can be elevated in instances of high fluid volume with cardiac insufficiency. Troponin and CPK are both cardiac specific lab values, and BUN is a kidney specific.

                    Γ Albumen is the correct answer because it's produced by the liver and its levels can be affected by liver function and fluid status. In congestive heart failure, increased fluid volume can lead to hemodilution, which may result in lower albumin levels. Additionally, liver congestion due to right-sided heart failure can impair albumin production. Therefore, albumin levels can be a useful indicator of both liver function and fluid status in heart failure patients.

                    Explanation for incorrect answers:
                        Creatine Phosphokinase (CPK):
                            CPK is primarily associated with muscle damage, not liver function or fluid volume. It's typically elevated in conditions like myocardial infarction, muscle injuries, or certain neuromuscular disorders. It's not directly related to congestive heart failure or fluid volume changes.

                        Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN): ¦Buny = Conill = els rinyons pareixen que tenen dos orelletes en la part de dalt
                            While BUN can be elevated in heart failure due to decreased renal perfusion, it's primarily a marker of kidney function, not liver function. BUN levels can be affected by various factors including dehydration, high protein intake, and certain medications, but it's not specifically associated with liver tissue or fluid volume in the context of heart failure.

                        Troponin:
                            Troponin is a cardiac-specific marker used to diagnose myocardial injury or infarction. It's not associated with liver function or fluid volume changes in heart failure. Elevated troponin levels indicate damage to heart muscle cells, but they don't directly reflect fluid status or liver function.

            Which of the following BNP lab values would indicate the presence of heart failure with a marked limitation in activity and the patient will report that they only feel comfortable at rest?
                240 pg/mL
                350 pg/mL
                680 pg/mL
                1000 pg/mL

                680 pg/mL
                    BNP > 600 is considered NYHA class III CHF, and patients will demonstrate marked limitation in activity due to severe heart failure symptoms, even during less-than ordinary activity (walking short distances 20-100m), and comfortable only at rest.

                    Explanation for incorrect answers:
                        240 pg/mL:
                        This BNP level is too low to indicate marked limitation in activity due to heart failure. BNP levels below 400 pg/mL are generally associated with milder forms of heart failure or may even be within normal limits for some individuals.

                        350 pg/mL:
                        While this level suggests the presence of heart failure, it's not high enough to indicate marked limitation in activity where the patient only feels comfortable at rest. This level might be more consistent with mild to moderate heart failure.

                        1000 pg/mL:
                        Although this level certainly indicates severe heart failure, it's higher than necessary to indicate marked limitation in activity. A BNP level this high might suggest a more critical condition, possibly requiring immediate hospitalization or intensive care.

                        The value of 680 pg/mL is most appropriate for indicating heart failure with marked limitation in activity, where the patient only feels comfortable at rest. This level suggests significant ventricular dysfunction and correlates with New York Heart Association (NYHA) Class III-IV heart failure, where patients experience notable symptoms even with minimal exertion or at rest.

Module 4: Cardiovascular Diagnostic Testing & Immersion Preparation (Vitals Assessment)

//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
4.0. Module Introduction
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

This module is presented in two units. Unit 1 you will begin to explore cardiovascular diagnostic testing. This module will include clinical laboratory studies, non-invasive diagnostic testing, and other imaging modalities that can give the medical team, including the PT, a clear objective information about a patient’s current cardiovascular status. You will discover how lab values and imaging results can impact a PT treatment and plan of care, and how to utilize those results to modify exercise for an individual with cardiopulmonary disease. In Unit 2 you will start to prepare for immersion in Module 7 by reviewing the lab manual and videos of how to take vitals as part of the PT cardiopulmonary assessment.  

Learning Objectives
By the end of this week, you will be able to: 

Interpret the results of cardiovascular diagnostic tests including objective information derived from laboratory, diagnostic, and procedure data.
Create a physical therapy treatment plan based on degree of abnormality of laboratory values and provide rationale for postponing physical therapy intervention when a patient has critical lab values. 
Determine modifications and appropriateness for exercise based on cardiovascular lab values and diagnostic testing.
Analyze lab values that may change based on the inter-relationship of the cardiovascular system with other bodily systems.
Identify individuals that may be at increased risk of a coronary event or heart failure and demonstrate how these findings would impact clinical monitoring and physical therapy interventions.

    .Why does a PT care about lab values?
    • Provides objective information about a patient condition
    • Enables formulation of our plan of care and mobility recommendations
    • weighing anticipated benefit of a therapy intervention vs the potential risk 
    to the patient.
    • longer-term consequences over the episode of care, should be assessed
    • Awareness of physiological changes that might occur whenever a lab value is 
    out of range. 
    • Awareness of clinical implications if a value should fall into the critical range.


    .Understanding Lab Values
    Trends

    Risk vs Benefit 
    Considerations

    Acute vs Chronic 
    Considerations

    Gender, Race, and Culture 
    Considerations

    Age Considerations


    .Complete Blood Count (CBC)
    • Common blood test to get a basic patient picture
    • Results regarding the concentration of:
    • Red blood cells (RBC) or Hematocrit (HCT)
    • Hemoglobin (Hgb)
    • White blood cells (WBC)
    • Platelets (Plt)


    .Red Blood Cells or Hematocrit (%) 
    • Account for 45% of whole blood and most of blood’s viscosity
    • Main function
    • Carry O2 and Co2 via Hgb molecules inside RBC
    • Formed in bone marrow of adults
    • Signaled by various endocrine glands and kidneys to stimulate production
    • Nutritional supply of Iron, vit b12, folic acid are necessary for RB formation
    • Hct BEST measure of RBC:
    • Hematocrit test indicates the percentage of blood by volume that is composed of red blood cells
    • Value important as it may have a “relative” increase in RBC
    • Assess blood loss and fluid balance
    • Reference Values:
    • Male: 42-52%
    • Female: 37-47%


    .Polycythemia 
    • Increased RBC or HCT
    1. Primary (p. Vera)
    • Bone marrow disorder
    • Synthesizes more RBCs then normal
    • Tx: suppress bone marrow
    2. Secondary
    • Kidneys signaled to release erythropoietin & inc RBC production in bone marrow
    • Compensation to inc O2 carrying capacity when senses limited O2 or hypoxia
    • COPD or CHF
    • High altitude
    3. Relative
    • Could occur d/t dehydration (HCT & RBC values required to help indicate this)


    .Polycythemia & PT Implications
    Symptoms
    • Fatigue, Headache, Dizziness
    • Blurred vision & Paresthesia’s 
    • reduced blood flow or inc in blood viscosity 
    • Splenomegaly 
    • spleen working harder to recycle cells
    • HTN
    • Cyanosis or digital clubbing

    PT Implications
    • Discuss Smoking cessation 
    • address O2 issues 
    • High critical values (>60%) 
    • spontaneous blood clotting
    • Handling of patient near the spleen
    • Exercise tolerance
    • Symptom-based approach to intervention
    • Monitor symptoms 


    .Anemia
    • Reduced RBC or HCT
    • Acquired or Hemolytic
    • RBC destroyed (could be due to dialysis)
    • Post hemorrhagic 
    • Aplastic 
    • Deficient bone marrow
    • Iron, vitamin B12, folic acid deficiency
    • Inherited due sickle cell anemia 
    • cells being damaged or lysed as pass through the sickle cells

    .Anemia & PT Implications 
    Symptoms
    • Vague fatigue
    • Weakness
    • Dyspnea 
    • Dizziness
    • Pallor
    • Tachycardia
    • Angina (Esp if patient had CAD)

    PT Implications
    • Fluids
    • Blood transfusion needs
    • Low critical value (<15-20%)
    • Cardiac failure or death
    • Exercise Tolerance
    • Impaired endurance; progress slowly
    • Monitor VS, including SpO2 ; could be 
    tachycardic and/or orthostatic HoTN
    • <25%: symptoms-based approach 
    to intervention

    > > > 

    Important Lab Values to Consider

    .Lab Value Analysis

    Objective information about the patient’s status is derived from 
    laboratory, diagnostic, and procedure data

    Physical therapists must be able to identify and interpret the 
    results


    .Cardiovascular Diagnostic Lab Values
    1. Lipid Values
    2. Cardiovascular Specific
    3. Additional Lab Studies Related to Cardiac Function
    4. Coagulation Profiles


    .Blood Lipids
    • Hyperlipidemia
    • Considered a major risk factor for CAD
    • Serum cholesterol and triglycerides
    • Associated with ingestion of excess 
    amounts of saturated fat and 
    cholesterol
    • Breakdown consists of:
    • Total cholesterol
    • High-density lipoprotein (HDL)
    • Low-density lipoprotein (LDL)
    • Triglyceride estimates

    ('')
        Sure! Here is the exact transcription of the table from the image:

| Category | LDL Cholesterol (mg/dL) | Total Cholesterol (mg/dL) | HDL Cholesterol (mg/dL) |
|----------|-------------------------|---------------------------|-------------------------|
| Optimal  | <100                    |                           |                         |
| Near optimal/above optimal | 100-129               |                           |                         |
| Borderline high   | 130-159                | <200 Desirable            | <40 Low                 |
| High      | 160-189                 | 200-239 Borderline high   |                         |
| Very high | ≥190                    | ≥240 High                 | >60 High                |


    .Cardiovascular Specific Labs


    .Troponin
    • Gold standard for cardiac injury
    • 2 isoforms: 
    • troponin I & troponin T
    • Reference Ranges:
    • Normal <0.03 ng/mL 
    • MI > 0.10 ng/mL
    • PT considerations:
    • Monitor trends & wait for 2 consecutive down trending values 
    before initiating PT


    .Creatine Phosphokinase (CPK) 
    • Utilized if troponin is unavailable 
    • Isoenzyme that is released into the blood when skeletal, 
    brain, or cardiac muscle is injured
    • CK2-MB specific to cardiac muscle
    • Reference Ranges:
    • Normal = 30-170 U/L
    • Adult Males: 52-336 U/L
    • Adult Females: 38-176 U/L


    .Serum Enzymes & Myocardial Infarction
        Diagnosis of MI:
        • Troponin a preferred biomarker 
        with high cardiac tissue specificity
        • Elevations are 100% sensitive for 
        MI within 6-12 hours
        • Troponin I elevated 4-7d
        • Troponin T elevated 10-14d
        • CK-MB can lead to false positive 
        MI dx

        Prognosis after MI:
        • Level of troponin rise indicative of 
        mortality risk
        • High concentration of troponin 
        indicative of future heart failure 
        and cardiovascular death
        • Troponin T levels estimate infarct 
        size & L ventricular function


    .B-Type Natriuretic Peptide (BNP)
    • Protein produced by the 
    ventricles of the heart, 
    important in the diagnosis 
    of heart failure
    • This is released from the 
    ventricles during pressure or 
    volume overload
    • Strongest independent 
    predictor of CHF

    ('')
        BNP NYHA Classification
        BNP <100 pg/mL Indicates no heart failure

        BNP 100-300 
        pg/mL

        Class I: Cardiac disease, but no symptoms/no 
        limitations
        BNP >300 pg/mL Class II: Mild symptoms (mild SOB and/or angina) and 
        slight limitation during ordinary activity

        BNP >600 pg/mL Class III: Marked limitation in activity d/t symptoms, 
        even during less-than ordinary activity (walking short 
        distances 20-100m);  Comfortable only at rest.

        BNP >900 pg/mL Class IV: Severe limitations; Experience symptoms 
        even while at rest


    .Serum Enzymes and Congestive Heart Failure
    • BNP associated with staging and level of congestive heart failure
    • Atrial Natriuretic Peptide (ANP)
    • released when fluid backs up all the way into the atrium (inc atrial 
    pressure to release ANP)
    • BNP and ANP detection associated with mortality
    • Other values to consider with advanced CHF:
    • Increased BUN & Creatinine due to kidney compensatory mechanisms 
    with failing cardiac output
    • Increase in Hct due to hypoxia with lung edema
    • Reduced platelets due to liver damage


    .Additional Lab Studies Related to Cardiac Function


    .Clinical Laboratory Risk Factors for CAD
    • Homocysteine (type of amino acid found in blood) 
    • Low levels of folate and vitamin B
    • ≤13.0 µmol/L
    • Highly sensitive C-reactive protein
    • Low risk<1.0 mg/L
    • Avg Risk 1.0 – 0 mg/L
    • High Risk > 3.0 mg/L
    • If > 10.0 mg/L immediate evaluation for other heart related issues


    .Associated Kidney Values 
    • Important marker of cardiac function
    • If low CO kidneys will begin to work to maintain blood pressure
    • Lab values to track:
    • Increased sodium to increase H2O resorption 
    • Increased BUN & Creatinine due to reduced filtration/clearance


    .Associated Liver Values
    • When fluid volume increases there is possible hepatic 
    venous congestion, preventing adequate perfusion of O2 to 
    hepatic tissues
    • Lab Values that can trend upward:
    • Serum Albumen (Reference range: 3.5-5.2 g/dL)
    • Trends downward in primary liver disease
    • Serum bilirubin (Reference range: 0.3-1.0 mg/dL; Critical value: > 12 
    mg/dL)
    • AST (Aspartate Aminotransferase) (reference range 10 to 40 U/L)
    • LDH – 5 (reference range 100–190 U/L)

    Coagulation Profiles

    .Coagulation Profiles
    • Assess Serum Viscosity
    • Properties of fluid or blood to resist flow
    • Increased Blood Viscosity
    • Hypercoagulability 
    • Reduced Blood Viscosity 
    • Increased bleeding risk


    .Serum Viscosity
    • Examples of measures:
    • International Normalized Ratio (INR)
    • Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (aPTT)
    • Prothrombin Time (PT)
    • Anti-Factor Xa Assay
    • D-dimer
    • Implications for PT treatment


    .Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT)
        Risk Factors Presentation Considerations
            • Venous stasis
            • Bedrest
            • Paresis/paralysis
            • Vascular wall injury
            • Surgery
            • Prior DVT
            • Trauma/fracture
            • Hypercoagulable state
            • Cancer
            • Autoimmune disorder
            • Non-adherent thrombus may:
            • Extend
            • Embolize
            • Pulmonary Embolism (PE)
            • More likely for DVT located in proximal veins
            • Popliteal
            • Femoral 
            • Iliac

        Presentation
            • Signs and Symptoms are 
            diffuse and hard to 
            recognize
            • Symptoms of chronic DVT
            • Ulcers
            • Leg swelling
            • Skin breakdown

        Considerations
            • Size of clot
            • Chronic vs Acute
            • h/o PE have increased risk of new 
            PE
            • Stage of medical management
            • Co-morbidities
            • Pts with cardiopulmonary 
            compromise may be at > risk for 
            fatal PE
            • Proximal vs Superficial
            • Proximal DVT > risk for 
            development of PE


    .International Normalized Ratio (INR)
    • Assess effectiveness of 
    Coumadin
    • Physical Therapy 
    Implications:
    • >3.6 proceed with caution
    • >4.0 light exercise only
    • >5.0 check with medical team 
    prior to mobility 
    • 6.0 PT IS CONTRAINDICATED

    Range Level
    Normal Range 0.8-1.2
    Therapeutic Range for CVA 
    prophylaxis

    2.0-2.5

    Therapeutic Range (VTE, PE, a-fib) 2.0-3.0
    Therapeutic Range for higher risk 
    (prosthetic heart valve)

    2.5-3.5

    Therapeutic Range for lupus 
    anticoagulant

    3.0-3.5

    High risk for bleeding >3.6


    .Prothrombin Time (PT)
    • Assess effectiveness of 
    Coumadin
    • Not used as often as INR
    • Physical Therapy Implications:
    • utilize caution with mobility 
    when risk of bleeding
    • collaborate with the team

        Range Level
        Normal Range 11-13 
        seconds
        High risk for bleeding 
        into tissue

            >25 
            seconds


    .Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (aPTT)
    • Assess effectiveness of 
    Heparin 
    • PT implications
    • Must be in therapeutic ranges 
    prior to mobility 
    • Take caution and assess if 
    appropriate for mobility when 
    at increased risk for bleeding

        Range Level
        Normal Range 21-35 seconds
        >70 seconds 
        signifies 
        spontaneous 
        bleeding
        Therapeutic for
        effectiveness of 
        anticoagulant

            2-2.5x normal range 
            (60-109 seconds)
            Variability in 
            reagents


    .Anti-Factor Xa Assay
        • Assess effectiveness of heparin 
        therapy including low molecular 
        weight heparin and 
        unfractionated heparin
        • Treatment of known clot OR 
        as prophylactic treatment to 
        prevent clots
        • PT implications:
        • Clear to participate if:
        • On UFH > 3h
        • On LMWH >5h

            Therapeutic Ranges of: Level
            Low molecular weight 
            heparin LMWH

            0.5-1.2 IU/mL

            Unfractionated heparin 0.3-0.7 IU/mL
            Prophylactic Ranges of: Level
            Low molecular weight 
            heparin LMWH

            Unfractionated heparin 0.1-0.4 IU/mL


    .Mobilizing Patients with Known DVT

    • Consider if the patient is anticoagulated
    • If yes, consider the medication for anticoagulation and time 
    of administration
    • If the patient has achieved the therapeutic level of the 
    medication OR has achieved the time window necessary for 
    therapeutic changes, the patient may be appropriate for PT
    • Consult with the medical team when necessary
    • Specific guidelines in Hillegass, et al journal article

    to know if the patient is protected against clot or if they are not able to clot effectively when injured,

    when protected, they will have reduced risk of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, as well as being protected when having a known DVT.
    2:46
    Equally important is for the therapist to consider if the value is too high, that the patient may be at risk of bleeding and reduced clotting ability.
    2:58
    When this occurs, resistance exercise may be contraindicated because it would cause muscle micro tears that require clotting to stop the bleeding.
    3:09
    Furthermore, mobility may be on hold for abnormally high values for patient safety.
    3:19
    If the patient were to fall or bump into an object, they could have an adverse event associated with bruising or uncontrolled bleeding.
    3:26
    Next, we'll talk about deep vein thrombosis, which is a serious condition when a clot forms in a vein, typically in the lower extremities.
    3:36
    This condition is discussed in this presentation because patients at risk for
    3:45
    DVT or with a known DVT are often treated with medications to thin their blood.
    3:50
    And the lab values in this presentation are pertinent.
    3:57
    Risk factors for DVT include venous basis, vascular wall injury or a hyper coagulopathy state.
    4:01
    A non adherent clot can either extend, grow in size or mobilize.
    4:10
    Embolization means that it travels through the bloodstream lodges in a blood vessel and can block blood flow.
    4:19
    This condition can be life threatening because of the blockage in blood supply.
    4:28
    When an ambulance lodges in one of the pulmonary arteries, it is referred to as a pulmonary embolism.
    4:34
    A pulmonary embolism or PE is more likely to arise from a DVT that is located in the proximal vein, such as the poplar, teal, femoral or iliac.
    4:42
    A PE can be life threatening.
    4:54
    So it's important for the physical therapist to be alert to patients who have higher risk of DVT and symptoms of possible DVT.
    4:56
    The signs and symptoms of an acute DVT are diffuse and can be hard to recognize.
    5:07
    A patient may have leg pain or swelling or no symptoms at all.
    5:13
    When a patient has a chronic DVT, they may experience ulcers, chronic issues with leg swelling and even skin breakdown.
    5:19
    In future slides, we will talk about lab values that would be assessed in a patient who is at risk at DVT or who has an acute DVT.
    5:29
    The first lab test is called the international normalized ratio, which is commonly referred to as the INR.
    5:41
    The INR is used to assess the effectiveness of the medication, Coumadin.
    5:49
    Coumadin is an oral anticoagulant that is used to treat and prevent deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism.
    5:55
    This medication interacts with the vitamin K dependent activation of various clotting factors.
    6:04
    Lab value monitoring is important to make sure that anticoagulation is within a therapeutic or treatment range.
    6:12
    Too little anticoagulation can lead to reoccurrence of thrombosis, and too much anticoagulation can pose high risk for bleeding.
    6:21
    The dosing of the medication is patient specific,
    6:31
    which is why the INR must be closely monitored to determine coagulation, status and medication adjustment if needed.
    6:34
    Some diagnoses require higher levels of anticoagulation, as you can see in the suggested ranges on the right side of this slide.
    6:44
    A patient with a thrombus or a pulmonary embolism has a therapeutic range from 2 to 3,
    6:53
    while a patient with a prosthetic heart valve may have a higher range to prevent clotting around the valve.
    7:00
    Typically, a patient has higher risk of bleeding within INR greater than 3.6.
    7:07
    And in the case that the patient has a critical value, such as a value of six.
    7:14

    7:20

    7:25

    7:35

    7:45

    8:45

    8:57
    There are several important things for the physical therapist to consider when mobilizing a patient who's diagnosed with a deep vein thrombosis,
    9:05
    including an assessment of their coagulation profile to determine if they were in a therapeutic range.
    9:14

    9:22

    9:32

    > > > 

    Cardiovascular Diagnostic Tests & 
    Procedures 

    .Holter Monitor
    • Continuous 24-hour 
    electrocardiographic monitoring of a 
    patient’s heart rhythm
    • Essential to the diagnosis and 
    management of episodes of cardiac 
    arrhythmias and symptoms
    • If life threatening arrhythmias may be 
    referred to electrophysiological 
    specialist (ie. ventricular tachycardia)
    • PT Implications
    • Should be aware of results of Holter 
    monitoring
    • May need to postpone therapy until 
    treatment for arrhythmia is initiated Fig. 8.1. Holter monitoring is transcutaneous, with 
    multiple leads to record heart rhythm for 24 hours. 


    .Echocardiography 1

    Echo
    • Uses pulse of reflected ultrasound to evaluate 
    the functioning of the heart
    • Provides real-time images of beating heart:
    • size of ventricular cavity
    • Wall thickness
    • integrity of interatrial and intraventricular 
    septa
    • functioning of valves
    • motions of individual segments of ventricular 
    wall
    • Quantify volumes of left ventricle
    • SV and ejection fraction

    Contrast Echo
    • Use of intravenously injected contrast agent 
    with echocardiogram
    • Real time assessment of intracardiac blood 
    flow 
    • Enhanced image of intracardiac and 
    intrapulmonary shunts, endocardial wall, 
    ventricular wall thickness
    • Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) or 
    epicardial echocardiography can assess 
    distribution of cardioplegia and degree of 
    valvular regurgitation


    Echo Procedure Echo (top) 
    Contrast Echo (bottom)

    Echocardiography 2 ('') ('')


    .Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE)

    • Improved view of the heart and 
    mediastinum
    • Patient swallows probe (anesthesia 
    and sedatives)
    • Positioned @ end of esophagus 
    • Best option to detect 
    cardioembolic stroke risk or any 
    other heart type masses


    .Other Imaging Modalities

    Computed Tomography 
    (CT)
    • Used to identify 
    masses in 
    cardiovascular system 
    or to detect aortic 
    aneurysms or 
    pericardial thickening 
    (pericarditis)

    Single-Photon Emission 
    Computed Tomography 
    (SPECT)
    • Detect and quantify 
    myocardial perfusion 
    defects and 
    contractility defects
    • Used in conjunction 
    with radioactive 
    isotopes

    Electron Beam 
    Computed Tomography 
    (EBCT)
    • Used to detect calcium 
    in coronary arteries 
    and quantify coronary 
    atherosclerosis
    • Patients with coronary 
    calcifications may 
    identify those high risk 
    for future MI and CAD

    .Other Imaging Modalities

    Multigated Acquisition 
    Imaging
    • Calculates left 
    ventricular ejection 
    fraction
    • Noninvasive, can be 
    used on critically ill 
    cardiac patients

    Magnetic Resonance 
    Imaging
    • Used to evaluate 
    morphology, cardiac 
    blood flow, myocardial 
    contractility
    • Similar diagnostic 
    accuracy as PET 
    imaging, but more 
    available and less 
    expensive

    Magnetic Resonance 
    Angiogram
    • Uses magnetic and 
    radio wave energy to 
    take pictures of blood 
    vessels


    .Exercise Testing
        Used in diagnosis & management of patients with CAD
            • Involves systematically and progressively increasing O2 demand, evaluate the responses
            • Informal testing is performed to screen for exercise programs
        Maximal vs submaximal stress testing
            • Submaximal test is terminated on achievement of a predetermined end point
            • Maximal tests use patient’s maximal HR or terminate when patient is limited by symptoms
            • Maximal tests used to measure functional capacity and diagnose CAD
        Low-level exercise testing
            • Performed when patients are post-MI or CABG
            • Ex-induced ST-Segment depression of 2.0 mm or greater →indicator of prognosis after MI

    .Indications for Exercise Testing
    • Evaluation of chest pain suggestive of coronary disease
    • Evaluation of atypical chest pain
    • Determination of prognosis and severity of coronary artery disease
    • Evaluation of the effects of medical or surgical therapy of intervention
    • Evaluation of arrhythmias
    • Evaluation of hypertension with activity
    • Assessment of functional capacity
    • Screening to provide and exercise prescription
    • Providing motivation for lifestyle change to reduce the risk of 
    developing coronary artery disease 


    .Contraindications to Exercise Testing 
    ('')
        | BOX 8-7 Absolute contraindications to exercise testing | Relative contraindications to exercise testing |
        |--------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------|
        | Recent myocardial infarction (MI; less than 4 to 6 weeks after the MI for a maximal, symptom-limited test) in most clinical settings | Aortic stenosis |
        | Acute pericarditis or myocarditis | Known left main coronary artery disease (CAD or its equivalent) |
        | Resting or unstable angina | Severe hypertension (defined as systolic blood pressure > 165 mm Hg at rest, diastolic blood pressure > 110 mm Hg at rest, or both) |
        | Serious ventricular or rapid atrial arrhythmias (e.g., ventricular tachycardia, couplets, atrial fibrillation, or atrial flutter) | Idiopathic hypertrophic subaortic stenosis |
        | Untreated second- or third-degree heart block | Severe depression of the ST segment on the resting electrocardiogram |
        | Overt congestive heart failure (pulmonary crackles, third heart sound, or both) | Compensated heart failure |
        | Any acute illness | |


    .Example of Maximal Testing Protocol
        ('')
            | Stage | Time (min) | Speed (mph) | Grade (%) | Met^a |
            |-------|------------|-------------|-----------|-------|
            | I     | 3          | 1.7         | 10%       | 4 to 5|
            | II    | 3          | 2.5         | 12%       | 6 to 7|
            | III   | 3          | 3.4         | 14%       | 8 to 10|
            | IV    | 3          | 4.2         | 16%       | 11 to 13|
            | V     | 3          | 5.0         | 18%       | 14 to 16|
            | VI    | 3          | 6.0         | 20%       | 17 to 19|

            ^a MET, resting metabolic rate = 3.5 ml of oxygen per kg of body weight per minute.
            From Ellestad MH: Stress testing principles and practice, ed 4, New York, 1996, Oxford University Press.


    .Example of Low-Level Exercise Testing
        ('')
            | Time (min) | Speed (mph) | Grade (%) | MET |
            |------------|-------------|-----------|-----|
            | 0          | 2           | 3.5       | 2   |
            | 3          | 2           | 7         | 3   |
            | 6          | 2           | 10.5      | 4   |
            | 9          | 2           | 14        | 5   |
            | 12         | 2           | 17.5      | 6   |
            | 15         | 3           | 12.5      | 7   |
            | 18         | 3           | 15        | 8   |
            | 21         | 3           | 17.5      | 9   |

            MET, resting metabolic rate.


    .Example of Sub-Maximal Testing Protocol 
    • Six-Minute Walk Test 
    • Self-paced test of walking capacity
    • Standardized instructions and encouragement are commonly 
    given during the test
    • Distance walked is strongly related to measures of peak 
    exercise performance and moderately related to physical 
    activity in daily life
    • Reference equations available for the 6MWD, allowing 6MWD 
    to be reported as a percentage of the predicted walking 
    distance


    .Criteria for Terminating Submaximal/ Low-Level Testing ('')
        | Box 8-4 Criteria for Termination of Maximal and Low-Level/Submaximal Testing | |
        | --- | --- |
        | Criteria for Termination of Maximal Testing | Criteria for Termination of Low-Level/Submaximal Testing |
        | Increasing frequency or pairing of premature ventricular complexes | An oxygen consumption level of 17.5 ml of oxygen per kg (6 METs) achieved |
        | Development of ventricular tachycardia | 70% to 75% of age-predicted maximal heart rate achieved |
        | Rapid atrial arrhythmias, including atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter, with uncontrolled ventricular response rates | Fatigue or dyspnea |
        | Development of second- or third-degree heart block | Maximal heart rate of 120 to 130 beats per minute |
        | Increased angina pain (Level 2 on a scale of 4) | Frequent (nine or more per minute) unifocal or multifocal premature ventricular contractions, paired premature ventricular contractions, or ventricular tachycardia |
        | Hypotensive blood pressure response (20 mm Hg or greater decrease) | ST-segment depression of 1.0 to 2.0 mm |
        | Extreme shortness of breath | Claudication pain |
        | Dizziness, mental confusion, or lack of coordination | Dizziness |
        | Severe ST-segment depression. The American College of Sports Medicine recommends termination when the ST segment is depressed 2.0 mm or more, although some testing personnel may proceed when changes of greater magnitude are demonstrated as long as there is no evidence of other abnormal responses. | Decrease in systolic blood pressure of 10 to 15 mm Hg below peak value |
        | Observation of the patient reveals pale and clammy skin (pallor and diaphoresis) | Hypertensive blood pressure (systolic >200 mm Hg, diastolic >110 mm Hg) |
        | Extremely elevated systolic or diastolic blood pressure, or both, which may or may not be associated with symptoms. | Level 1 (out of 4) angina |
        | On achievement of predicted maximal heart rate; it is usually safe to proceed with the test beyond the predicted maximal heart rate if the patient is able and willing to continue and if other indications to terminate the test are absent. | |
        | Presence of leg fatigue or leg cramps or claudication pain | |
        | Patient request for termination of test | |


    .Other Types of Exercise Testing
    Exercise Testing with 
    Ventilatory Gas 
    Analysis
    • Provides additional 
    information 
    regarding O2
    exchange, 
    breathlessness

    Exercise Testing with 
    Imaging Modalities
    • Radioactive Nuclide 
    Perfusion Imaging-
    may use imaging 
    immediately after 
    exercise test
    • Thallium Stress 
    Test

    Pharmalogical Stress 
    Test
    • Used when a patient 
    is unable to perform 
    upright exercise on 
    a treadmill or cycle
    • Injection of a 
    pharmacological 
    agent to induce 
    physiological stress


    .Interpretation of Exercise Testing
    • Maximal heart rate for exercise intensity recommendation
    • Onset of anginal symptoms and detection of CAD
    • Heart rate recovery
    • Attenuated heart rate recovery associated with increased risk of CV 
    events and mortality


    Exercise Prescription for Aerobic Conditioning

    • Exercise Testing is GOLD standard to determine max HR, but not always realistic or able to be 
    formally completed in a clinical setting (graded treadmill, 6 MWT, submaximal testing)
    • 208 – 0.7 (Age) if exercise testing not possible

    Determining HR max

    • HR max – HR rest = HRR
    • (HRR  desired HR percentages) + HR rest 

    Training Heart Rate Range

    • IE: return to running s/p surgery and no CV history - choose a maximal HR training range to 
    make physiological changes 

    HR percentages determined by patient tolerance and level of function

    > > > 

    Cardiovascular Diagnostic Tests & 
    Procedures 

    .Cardiac Catheterization 1
    • Procedure for cardiac catheterization
    • Insertion of a catheter into the CV system 
    to measure pressures or perform 
    angiography
    • Performed in a special room in radiology
    • Catheter is inserted into brachial artery or 
    femoral artery
    • Interpreting the test results
    • Assess the ventricular function and 
    severity of coronary artery stenosis
    • Some believe catheterization is overused 
    and less invasive procedures should be 
    used
    • Has greater predictive accuracy in 
    assessment of CAD than exercise testing


    .Cardiac Catheterization 2
    • Indications for cardiac catheterization
    • Cardiac arrest or ventricular fibrillation
    • Pulmonary edema
    • Intolerance of or noncompliance with medical therapy for angina
    • Job description mandate
    • Significant decrease in exercise duration
    • Progressive decline in systolic BP to <100 mm Hg during exercise
    • Evidence of symptomatic hypoperfusion during exercise
    • Left ventricular ejection fraction (<35%)
    • Ventricular tachycardia with exercise


    .Example of Results of Cardiac Catherization 
    Findings
    • Left anterior descending (LAD) artery shows 90% stenosis proximally
    • First diagonal (off of LAD) shows 97% stenosis just after the origin
    • Circumflex appears to be small with a 60% lesion midvessel and 50% distally
    • Right coronary artery shows 70% stenosis
    • LV: normal in size, anteroapical hypokinesis
    • Ejection fraction (EF): 40%
    • End-diastolic pressure (EDP): 14
    • End-diastolic volume (EDV): 100

    Interpretation
    • Evidence of severe disease with anterior infarction from first diagonal with spontaneous 
    reperfusion. These results indicate patient should undergo surgical revascularization to ensure 
    adequate cardiac perfusion. In addition, EF is decreased and borderline for cardiac muscle 
    dysfunction, and EDP and EDV are elevated. Anteroapical hypokinesis means the anteroapical
    region is moving sluggishly—indicating that the area is severely ischemic or possible injury.

     
    .Diagnostic Testing for Women
    • Diagnosis and assessment of CAD is difficult in women
    • Need to consider more accurate tests
    • MRI and PET


    .Endocardial Biopsy
    • Samples of right or left 
    ventricular endomyocardium
    may be obtained at time of 
    catheterization
    • Determines myocardial 
    rejection in patients with a 
    cardiac transplant
    • May be used to diagnose 
    hypertrophic and congenital 
    cardiomyopathy


    .Peripheral Arterial Disease and Dysfunction and Diagnosis 1
    • Presence of peripheral artery 
    disease increases with age
    • Ankle Brachial Index
    • Noninvasive test that 
    compares BP obtained with 
    Doppler probe in dorsalis 
    pedis to BP in higher of two 
    brachial pressures
    • Marker of diffuse 
    atherosclerosis, CV risk, and 
    overall survival

    .Peripheral Arterial Disease and Dysfunction and Diagnosis 3
        .Segmental limb  pressures
            Aid in localizing 
            stenoses or occlusions 
            with placement of cuffs 
            on thigh, calf, ankle, 
            transmetatarsal region 
            of foot

            Pressure sequentially 
            inflated in each cuff 20 
            to 30 mm Hg above 
            systolic

            Pressure is measured 
            at each segment as 
            the pressure of the 
            cuff is gradually 
            released 

        .Pulse volume recordings
            Changes in volume of 
            blood flowing through a 
            limb can be detected 
            by plethysmographic
            tracings

        .Arterial duplex ultrasonography
            More precise 
            diagnostic test for 
            defining arterial 
            stenoses and 
            occlusions


    .Peripheral Arterial Disease and Dysfunction and Diagnosis, continued 4
        .Graft surveillance
            Used in patients after 
            surgical bypass graft 
            revascularization

        .Exercise studies
            Provide objective 
            documentation of 
            functional limitations 
            from PAD

            Determine 
            physiological 
            improvement 
            following arterial 
            stenosis intervention

            Cycle ergometer may 
            be the choice of 
            mode for exercise 
            testing

        .Other clinical tests
            Rubor dependency 
            test →skin color 
            changes with 
            positional changes

            Peripheral venous 
            disease and 
            diagnosis →
            venogram or 
            venography


    .Carotid Artery Disease and Diagnosis
    • Internal carotid artery disease increases 
    risk for transient and permanent 
    ischemic attacks to the neurological 
    system
    • Increased risk for coronary 
    atherosclerosis and infarction
    • Carotid Doppler evaluation most 
    commonly used
    • 3-D digital angiography and MR 
    angiography have increased sensitivity 
    and specificity to neurovascular 
    diagnosis

4.6. Cardiovascular Diagnostic Testing Self-Assessment
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////// (!!Q)

Question 1
    When a patient is diagnosed with Thrombocytopenia, which of the following symptoms may they experience? 
      High bleeding risk 
      High clotting risk 
      High fever 
      Shortness of breath 

      High bleeding risk 
        Thrombocytopenia is defined as platelets that are trending downward below 150,000 mcL. Platelets are primary clotting blood cells; therefore, low levels would lead to an increased risk of blooding with reduced clotting capability. High clot risk would be associated with thrombocytosis or polycythemia, high fever would be associated with leukocytosis or high white blood cells signifying infection, and shortness of breath would be associated with anemia or low RBC & Hgb.   

Question 2
    True or False: A patient has a Hgb lab value of 9.0 g/dL. This value would be an absolute contraindication to participate in exercise or a physical therapy treatment session. 
      True 
      False 

      False 
        While a Hgb of 9.0 is low it is not considered an absolute contraindication to exercise or physical therapy. Hgb does carry oxygen to the tissues, so the patient will require symptom monitoring to ensure they are able to participate without too much difficulty or increase in associated symptoms. Diagnosis and medical status will also need considered, as some may be transfused or require very careful monitoring at anything 8.0 and below, so it is important to check with the medical team if you have any concerns regarding Hgb lab values and mobility.
 
Question 3
    Which of the following represents an abnormal lab value? 
      HCT 60% (male) 
      Hgb 15 g/dl (female) 
      WBC 8,000 mcL 
      Platelets 150,000 mcL 

      HCT 60% (male) 
        The answer is HCT of 60% for a male patient. This value is higher than the reference range of 42-52%. All the other values are within the normal ranges. 

Question 4
    Which lab value is considered gold standard for diagnosing a cardiac injury? 
      BNP 
      Troponin 
      Triglycerides 
      Creatinine 

      Troponin 
        Troponin is considered the gold standard measure for diagnosing cardiac injury, specifically myocardial infarction. Troponin a preferred biomarker with high cardiac tissue specificity, and should be monitored as they trend upward. BNP is specific to staging of heart failure, triglycerides are specific to lipid profile, and creatinine is a kidney lab value.  
 
Question 5 
    Which of the following lab values is associated with hepatic or liver tissue can trend upward when a patient has increased fluid volume due to congestive heart failure? 
      Albumen 
      Troponin 
      Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN) 
      Creatine Phosphokinase (CPK) 

      Albumen
        Albumen is a lab value that is associated with the liver, and can be elevated in instances of high fluid volume with cardiac insufficiency. Troponin and CPK are both cardiac specific lab values, and BUN is a kidney specific.

Question 6
    Which of the following BNP lab values would indicate the presence of heart failure with a marked limitation in activity and the patient will report that they only feel comfortable at rest? 
      240 pg/mL 
      680 pg/mL 
      1000 pg/mL 
      350 pg/mL 

      680 pg/mL 
        BNP > 600 is considered NYHA class III CHF, and patients will demonstrate marked limitation in activity due to severe heart failure symptoms, even during less-than ordinary activity (walking short distances 20-100m), and comfortable only at rest. BNP 100-300 pg/mL is Class I with the presence of cardiac disease, but no symptoms/no limitations, BNP >900 pg/mL is Class IV with severe limitations and experience of symptoms even while at rest, and BNP >300 pg/mL is Class II with presence of mild symptoms (mild SOB and/or angina) and slight limitation during ordinary activity. It is important to consider these values when assessing a patient with CHF, and to know what activity level or if they are even appropriate to safely engage in during a PT session.  

Question 7
    Which of the following serum viscosity lab values would be considered an absolute contraindication to a patient participating in an out of bed mobility session with physical therapy?
      INR 6.2 
      Prothrombin Time 13s 
      aPTT 21s 
      LMWH 0.5 IU/mL 

      INR 6.2 
        An INR of 6.2 is extremely high and would be considered an absolute contraindication to a physical therapy mobility treatment session.  This patient would be at severe risk of bleeding, and a possible fall or jumping into something during mobility presents a further risk to bleeding with inability to appropriately clot that bleed. It would be best to wait until the medical team can get that lab value within or near therapeutic ranges. The other values are all within normal ranges. 

Question 8
    Which of the following lab values need to be considered prior to mobilizing a patient with a known DVT and on heparin? 
      INR 
      aPTT 
      PT 
      D-dimer 

      aPTT 
        With a known DVT a patient will be treated with IV heparin. Patients with a known DVT could be treated with heparin to reduce the clot, and risk of clot traveling to lead to PE. The aPTT lab value is important to assess prior to mobility, as the medical team will likely as that the patient be therapeutic ranges prior to out of bed mobility

                1. 24-year-old male s/p ankle fracture with hemoglobin of 8 and hematocrit of 25%

2. A hematocrit value of 59% in a male patient may indicate the following: (Multiple Choice)

   - Chronic hypoxia

3. A hospitalized patient with low hemoglobin who did not have a recent surgery will MOST likely receive a blood transfusion at what blood level value of HgB? (Single Choice)
   - 8 g/dl
   - 10 g/dl
   - 7 g/dl
   - 6 g/dl

   7 g/dl
    RUPERTA
        The patient will MOST likely receive a blood transfusion at a hemoglobin level of:

        7 g/dL

        Generally, a hemoglobin level below 7 g/dL is often considered a threshold for blood transfusion in most hospitalized patients who are not actively bleeding and have not had recent surgery. This "7/7 rule" is a common guideline used in many hospitals, though the decision to transfuse is ultimately based on multiple factors, not just the hemoglobin level alone.

        For patients without active bleeding or recent surgery, transfusion at higher hemoglobin levels (like 8 or 10 g/dL) is usually not recommended unless there are specific clinical indications. The 6 g/dL level would typically be considered too low to wait for transfusion in most cases.

        It's important to note that while 7 g/dL is a common threshold, the decision to transfuse always depends on the individual patient's clinical condition, comorbidities, and overall health status.
