9.11. Activity: Exercise Prescription Practice
    (See 'Q&A doc')
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////// (!!E)

(See similar case at: 'PE Q&A doc::14.13. Activity: Exercise Prescription Practice')

In this activity you will practice applying the principles of exercise prescription to someone who has a chronic condition. At this stage, do not worry if you do not know about all of the physiologic aspects of this specific condition – the important part is to practice designing an exercise program.  

Review the Case:
    You are evaluating a 62 y.o. female who would like to lose weight, feel better, not always be out of breath, and enjoy watching her grandson. She has been overweight for her entire adulthood and has been sedentary. She does not report any symptoms of cardiovascular distress when she has to walk quickly, but does have hypertension and her blood pressure is controlled with medication.   

    Data from Graded Exercise Test
        Treadmill Ramp Test – Achieved 3.0 mph @ 0% grade  
        BMI: 50.1 kg/m2 
        Resting Heart rate: 85 bpm 
        Resting BP: 140/88 
        Peak Heart Rate: Estimate from Gellish Equation  
        Peak BP: 170/90 

Please answer all questions.
    Question 1
        Determine a starting intensity of 30% since client has been sedentary and not exercised for a long time.
            Calculate and provide the answer for the following:  
                The target heart rate is: ___ bpm
                The target MET level is: ___

            KEY FROM CLASS ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                Heart Rate Reserve 
                    A.Estimated HR max = 208 – 0.67 (62 years) = 166 bpm 
                        I.Target HR = resting HR + 30% HR reserve → 85 + 0.3  (166 – 85) = 109 bpm 
                    B.% MET reserve to prescribe the intensity. 
                        I.Resting MET = 1 
                        II.Achieved 3.0 METs, therefore, 100% MET reserve = 3.0 – 1 = 2.0 METs. 
                        III.30% MET reserve = 0.6 METs 
                        IV.Target MET = resting MET + % MET reserve = 1 + 0.6 = 1.6 METs 

    Question 2
        Select 1 type of exercise in the compendium besides walking that is appropriate for the intensity level

            KEY FROM CLASS ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                -A.Difficult to find many activities at this low of a MET level, but a couple are: tai chi (1.5 MET, good for balance also), water walking (2.5 MET, good for joint protection), video exercise workouts (2.3 MET) 
                -B.You present options to client and they choose tai chi to begin with 

    Question 3
        Describe appropriate duration and frequency according to the guidelines and explain why you chose them.
            
            KEY FROM CLASS ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                -Guidelines recommend 30 to 60 min per day of moderate exercise, so we will start at 30 in order to achieve some success, in three 10 min bouts
                -Guidelines recommend 5-7 days per week, and we will start with 5 days to develop good habits and allow room for rest and growth during progression 

    Question 4
        Appropriately explain how you would progress this aerobic exercise program.

        KEY FROM CLASS ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
            -A.At beginning, progress duration of exercise by 3 min each week for first 4 weeks. May also go from 3 bouts of exercise to 2 bouts 
            -B.After 4 weeks, re-assess fitness by doing another submax graded exercise test. Increase intensity to 40%. Adjust target HR and MET levels and activities that client enjoys to match targets.  
            -C.After 4 weeks, increase to 6 days per week. 
            -D.Subsequently, adjust duration or intensity, but not both, to achieve greater volume of exercise.

    Question 5
        The client returns 3 years later with a new diagnosis of Coronary Artery Disease and reports chest pain with exertion. During a graded exercise test on the treadmill, she reported chest pain at a heart rate of 150 and blood pressure was 180/94. Calculate the rate-pressure product (RPP).

            KEY FROM CLASS ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                -A.RPP = HR  Systolic BP = 150 180 = 27,000
                -B.This RPP values indicates a high-intermediate hemodynamic response, which reflects a higher myocardial workload associated with angina. This is also referred to as ischemic threshold.

Module 10: Pulmonary Conditions

////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
10.0. Module Introduction
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

In this module learn about the pathophysiology, presenting signs and symptoms and exercise recommendations for several pulmonary conditions, more specifically those that fall under the categories of restrictive vs obstructive pulmonary dysfunction. You will learn the many hallmark features of each condition, and how that leads to dysfunction in interworking of the pulmonary system.

Learning Objectives
By the end of this week, you will be able to: 

Describe the pathophysiology and process of obstructive and restrictive pulmonary conditions. 
Discuss hallmark signs and symptoms related to the covered pulmonary diagnoses.
Identify risk factors associated with pulmonary disease. 
Explain medical management for each pulmonary disease and related prognostic factors. 
Assess PT findings related to each pulmonary condition that would impact exercise prescription, explain how the condition should be monitored, and recommend interventions to optimize outcomes.

10.1. Background Readings and Materials
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

Before participating in the activities for this module, please carefully read the following materials: 

Required 
Hillegass, E. (2016). Essentials of Cardiopulmonary Physical Therapy (4th ed.). Elsevier Saunders: St. Louis, MO. ISBN-10: 0323430546
Chapter 5 and 6

Recommended
Barreiero and Perillo (2004). An Approach to Interpreting Spirometry.Links to an external site. American Academy of Family Physicians, 69 (5), 1107-1114. 
This source will give you insight into spirometry testing and results. It will allow you to better understand how PFT testing is utilized for diagnosing lung disease, and how to define and interpret findings.

10.2. Review Lectures: Introduction to the Pulmonary System and Disease
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

The following lectures will serve as a review the structure and function of the respiratory system, and will then relate those pieces of information to compare and contrast in obstructive vs. restrictive lung dysfunction. These lectures will remind you of some things learned earlier this semester in order to better understand the pulmonary disease and dysfunction this module will cover.

    Introduction to the Pulmonary System

    .Pulmonary System
    • Refers to lungs and their

    network

    .Mechanics of Breathing 1
    ('') 
        A INSPIRATION
            External intercostal muscles slope obliquely between ribs, forward and downward. Because the attachment to the lower rib is farther forward from the axis of rotation, contraction raises the lower rib more than it depresses the upper rib.
                Scalene muscles
                Sternocleidomastoid muscle
                Diaphragm

        B
            BUCKET-HANDLE
            AND WATER-PUMP-
            HANDLE EFFECTS
                Vertebra
                Sternum

        C
            Internal intercostal muscles slope obliquely between ribs, backward and downward, depressing the upper rib more than raising the lower rib.
                Vertebra
                Ribs
                Sternum
                Rectus abdominis muscle
                External oblique muscle


    .Mechanics of Breathing 2
        • Air moves from areas of high to areas of low 
        pressure
        • Lungs require less pressure (-) vs 
        atmosphere (+) to pull air in and visa versa 
        to expel air out
        • Inspiration is active
        • At rest, expiration is passive with an elastic 
        recoil of lung
        • Pleurae and pleural space
        • visceral 
        • parietal
        • Muscles of ventilation
        • Move thoracic cage and abdomen to 
        create changes in volume
        • Cause reduction in intrathoracic pressure
        • Muscles of inspiration and expiration
        ('')


    .Function
        Functions
            Exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide between environment, blood, and tissue
            Oxygen is necessary for energy production
        ↓
        Physiology includes three components
            Ventilation
            Gas exchange or respiration
            Transport of gases to peripheral tissue


    .Gas Exchange 1
        • Gas exchange across the 
        alveolar-capillary and capillary-
        tissue interfaces
        • Occurs when gas reaches 
        alveolar spaces and dependent 
        on:
        1. Diffusion gradient 
        2. Surface area


    .Gas Exchange 2
        • Ventilation (V) – Perfusion (Q)
        • Refers to ratio of air (V) to blood 
        flow (Q)
        • Ventilation is optimized when this 
        approaches a 1:1 relationship
        • Normally V:Q around 0.8 
        • Gravity, body position, and 
        cardiopulmonary dysfunction can 
        influence this ratio
        • Perfusion is greatest in gravity 
        dependent areas
        ('')


    .Gas Transport
        O2 is transported 
        from the lungs to 
        tissues:
            • Dissolved in plasma 
            (PaO2)
            • Chemically bound to 
            hemoglobin 
            (oxyhemoglobin)
        ↓
        CO2 is 
        transported away 
        from the tissue:
            • Dissolved in plasma 
            (PaCO2)
            • Chemically bound to 
            hemoglobin 
            (carboxyhemoglobin)
            • Bicarbonate 
        ↓
        Dissolved PaO2 
        and PaCO2 affect 
        arterial blood pH
            • Arterial blood gases


    .Neural Control of Breathing
        Respiratory center
            Medulla oblongata
            Pons


    .Chemical Control of Breathing
        Central Chemoreceptors in 
        medulla
            • Sensitive to PCO2 and the pH of 
            blood 
            • Provide stimulatory inputs to the 
            inspiratory center to this increases 
            ventilation to reduce H+ and CO2 in 
            the blood

        Peripheral Chemoreceptors in 
        carotid and aortic arch
            • Sensitive to reduction in PO2
            • Decrease in PO2 chemoreceptors 
            become activated to send impulses 
            to inspiratory center to increases 
            rate and force of respiration and 
            rectifies the lack of O2

    Introduction to Pulmonary Disease 

    .Obstructive Lung Disease (!!E)
        • Difficulty getting air out of lungs
        • Increased air trapping
        • Common Obstructive Disorders:
            • COPD
            • Asthma
            • Chronic bronchitis
            • Emphysema 
            • Cystic fibrosis
                ¦Un policia, que te asma, 

    .Restrictive Lung Disease (!!E)
        • Difficultly getting air into lungs
        • Common Restrictive Disorders:
            • Atelectasis
            • Pneumonia
            • Pulmonary edema
            • ARDS
            • Pulmonary embolism


    .Comparison of Obstructive and Restrictive Types of Pulmonary Diseases  (!!E)
        | Characteristic              | Obstructive Disease         | Restrictive Disease                   |
        |-----------------------------|-----------------------------|---------------------------------------|
        | Breathing phase difficulty  | Expiration                  | Inspiration                           |
        | Pathophysiology             | Increased airway resistance | Decreased lung or thoracic compliance |
        | Useful measurements         | Flow rates                  | Volumes or capacities                 |


    .Pulmonary Testing
    O2 saturation
    Chest X-rays
    Blood testing – pH and dissolved O2/CO2 levels
    Ventilation – perfusion scan 
    PFTs


    .Oxygen Saturation
    • Percent of oxygen bound to Hgb
    • Assess O2 being transported by Hgb to peripheral tissues
    • Affected by:
    • Reduced oxygen uptake into lungs to be transported to HgB
    • Inability to exchange gases at alveolar-capillary interface 
    • This does not measure amount of dissolved O2


    .Dissolved CO2 and O2
    • Arterial Blood Gases
    • Assessment of acid base balance
    • High PaCO2 = acidic
    • Low PaCo2 = basic
    • Assess chemical control of breathing 


    .Imaging
        Chest X Ray
        • Areas of 
        consolidation or lung 
        size assessment

        Ventilation 
        Perfusion Scan
        • How well air moves 
        and blood flows 
        through the lungs


    .Pulmonary Function Testing
        Respiratory volumes are the amount of air inhaled, exhaled and stored within the lungs at any given time
        ↓
        Spirometry is a method for recording the volumes and flow rates of gas (air) entering and leaving the lungs
            -spirometer is a device used to measure the various volumes and flow rates observable in pulmonary function
            -information derived from a spirogram (the tracing from a spirometer) is clinically useful in evaluating pulmonary function and in diagnosing obstructive and restrictive pulmonary diseases.


    .PFT Lung Volumes and Subdivisions 
        ERV: Expiratory reserve volume; maximal volume that can be expired from a resting expiration.
        FRC: Functional residual capacity; volume of gas in lungs at resting expiratory level.
        IC: Inspiratory capacity; maximal volume that can be inspired from resting expiratory level.
        IRV: Inspiratory reserve volume; maximal volume that can be inspired from end-tidal inspiratory level.
        TLC: Total lung capacity; volume of gas in lungs at end of maximal inspiration
        VC: Vital capacity; maximal volume that can be expired after maximal inspiration
        MVV: Maximal voluntary ventilation; the amount of air that can be moved in and out of the lungs during a given time period.
        RV: Residual volume; the volume of air contained in the lungs after a maximal expiration.
        TV: Tidal Volume; amount of air that moves in or out of the lungs with each respiratory cycle.


    .PFT Single Breath Tests 
        FVC: Forced expiratory vital capacity; following maximal inspiration, entire vital capacity volume is expelled as rapidly as possible over 6 seconds.

        FEVT: Forced expiratory volume, timed; volume that has been expired at any time T during forced expiratory capacity.

        FEVT%: Percent of vital capacity volume (or FVC) that has been expired 
        at any time T during forced expiratory vital capacity.


    .FEV1/FVC
    • FEV1/FVC
    • Indicates whether there is airway obstruction
    • Normal value for this ratio is above 0.75-85 (!!E)
    • values less than 0.70 are suggestive of airflow 
    limitation and obstructive lung disease
    • Restrictive lung diseases, both the FEV1 and FVC 
    measurements decrease proportionally then 
    increase later stages


    .PFT Changes with Disease (!!E)
        ('PFT Changes with Disease.png')


    .Cardiac Complications with Lung Disease
    • Pulmonary hypertension 
    • Right heart failure symptoms
    • Edema
    • Venous congestion
    • Hypoxemia
    ('')
        Cor pulmonale, or
        right-sided heart
        failure, is an
        enlargement of
        the right ventricle
        due to high blood
        pressure in the
        arteries of the lungs
        usually caused by
        chronic lung disease

The following lectures will delve into one of the most commonly encountered pulmonary diseases, that being COPD. This lecture will review the pathophysiology, features, treatment, and physical therapy interventions in those suffering from COPD. 

('01 PT 2026_Mod 6.1_Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD).pdf')
    > > > 

    Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary 
    Disease (COPD)

    .Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD)
    • Disease characterized by the presence of airflow obstruction 
    that is attributable to either chronic bronchitis or 
    emphysema (American Thoracic Society)
    • Caused by:
    1. inhalation factors
    • Smoking, chemicals, toxins 
    2. Genetics
    • α1-antitrypsin deficiency


    .Pathophysiological Aspects of Obstructive Lung Dysfunction
    • Diseases of airways, which produce obstruction of expiratory flow
    • Airflow obstruction can be related to:
    • Retained secretions
    • Inflammation of mucosal lining of airway walls
    • Bronchial constriction
    • Weakening of support structure 
    • Conditions that lead to decreased size of bronchial lumen and 
    increased resistance to expiratory airflow


    .Chronic Bronchitis
        ('')


    .Emphysema
        ('')


    .Resultant COPD
        ('') 


    .The Combination Disease
    • Emphysema vs Chronic Bronchitis Dominant
        A
            CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS
            • Use of accessory
            muscles to breathe
            • Pursed-lip breathing
            • Minimal or absent
            cough
            • Leaning forward to
            breathe
            • Dyspnea on exertion
            (late sign)
        B
            CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS
            • Excess body fluids
            • Chronic cough
            • Shortness of breath
            on exertion
            • Increased sputum
            • Cyanosis (late sign)


    .General Clinical Signs of Chronic Obstructive Lung Diseases
    • Lung hyperinflation
    • Elevation of shoulder girdle
    • Horizontal ribs
    • Barrel-shaped thorax
    • Low, flattened diaphragms


    .General Clinical Signs of Obstructive Lung Disease
    • Delayed and incomplete 
    emptying of the lung during 
    exhalation
    • larger total lung 
    capacities 
    • Two forced expiratory 
    volumes monitored:
    • FEV1 and FVC 


    .Classification of COPD Severity (GOLD Criteria)
        ('')
            Table 6-1 Classification of COPD Severity

            | Stage             | FEV₁ (% Predicted)   | FEV₁/FVC          | General Pattern of Symptoms                                                  |
            |-------------------|----------------------|-------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
            | I (mild)          | >80                  | <0.7              | Chronic cough, ± sputum production                                           |
            | II (moderate)     | 50 to 80             | <0.7              | Chronic cough, ± sputum, and dyspnea                                         |
            | III (severe)      | 30 to 50             | <0.7              | Chronic cough, ± sputum, and dyspnea                                         |
            | IV (very severe)  | <30ᵇ                 | <0.7              | Chronic cough, ± sputum, and dyspnea                                         |
            |                   |                      |                   | Respiratory or right heart failure, weight loss                              |

            ### Footnotes:
            - a Based on postbronchodilator function
            - b A postbronchodilator FEV₁ <30% predicted or FEV₁ <50% with respiratory failure

            Adapted from Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease (GOLD Report 2008). COPD, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.


    .General Clinical Signs of Obstructive Lung Disease 1
    • Abnormal Arterial blood gas (ABG) values
    • Decreased PaO2 and Increased PaCO2
    • respiratory acidosis 
    • Dyspnea on exertion, especially during functional 
    activities
    • Secretion production and cough
    • May have increased anxiety level


    .General Clinical Signs of Obstructive Lung Disease 2
    • Breath Sounds
    • Wheezing with retained secretions
    • Rhonchi or low-pitched rattling large airway obstruction with 
    secretions along airways
    • Crackles or bubbling with presence of secretions 
    • Prolonged expiration
    • Poor Exercise Tolerance with reduction in exercise capacity 
    on testing


    .General Clinical Signs of Obstructive Lung Disease 3
    • Postural changes
    • Forward leaning with hands 
    supported
    • Permanent changes to the
    Thorax


    .Medical Management  
    • Smoking cessation
    • Pharmacotherapy for COPD
    • Pulmonary rehabilitation and exercise training
    • Surgical excision of bullae or lung volume reduction surgery
    • Oxygen Therapy


    .BODE Index
        BODE Index Table
        | Variable                            | Points on BODE Index                    |
        |-------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------|
        | Scores                              | 0       | 1        | 2       | 3        |
        |-------------------------------------|---------|----------|---------|----------|
        | FEV₁ (% of predicted)†              | ≥65     | 50–64    | 36–49   | ≤35      |
        | Distance walked in 6 min (m)        | ≥350    | 250–349  | 150–249 | ≤149     |
        | MMRC dyspnea scale‡                 | 0–1     | 2        | 3       | 4        |
        | Body-mass index§§                   | >21     | ≤21      |         |          |

        Footnotes:
        - † FEV₁: Forced Expiratory Volume in the first second (percent of predicted value).
        - ‡ MMRC: Modified Medical Research Council dyspnea scale.
        - §§ Body-mass index (BMI): Measurement in kg/m².

    .Prognosis
    • Progressive disease with expected worsening over time
    • BODE index score of 7 to 10 is associated with high mortality 
    rate of 80% in 52 months
    • End-stage COPD results in cor pulmonale (right heart failure 
    due to increased pulmonary artery pressure)
    • Prevention of COPD
    • Smoking cessation—most effective intervention

    > > > 

    Physical Therapy Management of Chronic 
    Obstructive Pulmonary Disease


    .Physical Therapy Management 1
        Secretion clearance
        Controlled breathing at rest and with activity
        Ambulation with rolling walker
        Education in use of recovery from SOB positions


    .Physical Therapy Management 2
        Endurance exercise training
        Strength training
        Thoracic stretching & Postural reeducation
        Instruction in self-management of the disease, including monitoring of weight, secretion color, and dyspnea with activity


    .Pursed Lip Breathing 
        • Great for COPD patients
        • Inhale slowly with the mouth closed 
        over several seconds
        • Increase direct line of O2 to the 
        lungs
        • Exhale through the mouth (with 
        pursed lips) 4-6 seconds
        • Increase time in exhalation for 
        air removal
        • Increased ratio from 1:2 to 1:6 (but 
        should not be  forced)


    .Positioning for Dyspnea Relief
        ('')


    .Oxygen Therapy
        • Begins with nighttime use
        • Long term > 15 hrs per day in those with resting PaO2 
        55mmHg OR SpO2 88%
        • Can be used to increase exercise tolerance BUT . . .
        • Need to remember the hypoxic drive before cranking up that O2
        • COPD patient's respiration is driven by low O2 levels, and not high 
        CO2 levels (!!E)


    .Benefits of Exercise in Patients with Pulmonary Disease
        • Focused on symptom 
        improvement, functional 
        improvements, health 
        related quality of life 
        outcomes instead of 
        pulmonary parameters.


    .Exercise Prescription 
        • Submaximal testing for intensity prescription parameters
        • Dyspnea scale to gauge intensity & maintain dynspea < 3/10
        • Strengthening program for major or large muscle groups
        • Home exercise program with specific recommendations

        Modified Borg Dyspnoea Scale ('Modified Borg Dyspnoea Scale.png')


    .Exercise Prescription (points to consider)
        1. HR is not a reliable indicator of exercise intensity in COPD patients (!!E)
        2. Unsupported arm exercise results in greater levels of dyspnea compared with lower extremity exercise in patients with COPD.
        3. Four areas to focus on:
        • lower extremity aerobic exercise
        • ventilatory muscle training
        • upper extremity resistance training
        • whole-body resistance training


    .Progressing Exercise 
        • Activity described by intensity, workloads, duration, frequency
        • Advance functional training by increasing repetitions using lower 
        weights, encouraging higher level of work within a given time, 
        encouraging fewer rest periods, decreasing dependence on 
        adaptive equipment
        • Progress can be documented using a variety of measures
        • Exercise capacity
        • Dyspnea and fatigue
        • Health related quality of life
        • Psychosocial status (anxiety/depression)


    .Interdisciplinary Management 
        Medical Team / Respiratory Therapist
            • Proper use of medicines
            Inhaler device training
            • Oxygen therapy
            • Smoking cessation 
            attempt
            • Prevention of attacks and 
            early treatment
            Indications for referral to 
            health facilities
        Physical Therapist
            • Maintaining the benefits of 
            exercise and physical activity
            • Breathing exercises
            • Relaxation Techniques
            • Bronchial hygiene techniques
            • Energy saving and daily work 
            simplification techniques
            • Strengthening and endurance 
            exercises to increase exercise 
            capacity
        Psychologist
            • Psychological 
            assessment
            to cope with 
            chronic illness
            • Evaluation of 
            leisure time
        Dietician
            • Nutritional education

    .Pulmonary Rehabilitation (PR)

////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
10.4. Lecture: Other Obstructive Pulmonary Diseases
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

The following lecture will cover two other obstructive pathologies that you may encounter in the clinical setting: bronchiectasis and cystic fibrosis. The lecture will provide some further insight on pathophysiology, diagnostic criteria, and management of each condition.  

('PT 2026_Mod 6.1_Other Obstructive Pulmonary Diseases.pdf')
    > > > 

    Other Obstructive Pulmonary Diseases

    .Bronchiectasis 
    • Dilation of the bronchia
    • Distortion of conducting airways, thickening, herniation, or 
    dilation


    .Symptoms
    • Cough with sputum production (small to large) quantities of 
    mucopurulent secretions
    • Secretion layers—white frothy, mucoid inner, purulent 
    bottom, composed of thick yellow-green plugs
    • Sputum greatest in morning
    • Recurrent, chronic, or recurring lung infections
    • Hemoptysis


    .Examination 
    • Auscultation
    • Crackles or rhonchi
    • CT Scanning
    • Dilated bronchioles 
    • ABGs
    • Hypoxemia
    • Sputum Culture 
    • Accessory muscle atrophy and postural changes


    .Medical Management 
    Goal—reduce the 
    number of 
    exacerbations and 
    improve quality of 
    life
    ↓
    Management 
    underlying condition
    ↓
    Management of 
    acute exacerbations
    ↓
    Long-term management
    ↓
    Surgery


    .Prognosis 
    • Depends on underlying disease or condition
    • Cystic Fibrosis with bronchiectasis have poorest prognosis


    .Physical Therapy Management
    • Secretion clearance techniques
    • Controlled breathing techniques coordinated with activity
    • Inspiratory muscle training to improve strength and 
    endurance of accessory muscles
    • Strength training, especially quadriceps muscle strength and 
    endurance
    • Endurance exercise


    .Cystic Fibrosis (CF)
    • Multisystem disorder 
    • Affects organs with epithelial surfaces,
    • Mucus stasis in conducting airways of lung, nasal sinuses, 
    sweat glands, small intestine, pancreas, and biliary system
    • Abnormal salt and water transport
    • Failure of airways to clear mucus normally


    .Pathophysiology
    • Genetic mutation on 
    chromosome 7
    • Abnormal CFTR leads to 
    abnormal sodium, 
    chloride, and water 
    movement across the cell 
    membrane
    • Mucus becomes 
    abnormally thick and dry


    .Pulmonary Complications Associated with CF
    • Thick mucous in the lungs results 
    in:
    • Bronchial airway obstruction
    • Bacterial infection
    • Inflammation 
    • Clinical Manifestations:
    • Cough
    • Respiratory infections
    • sinusitis and nasal polyps


    .Gastrointestinal Complications Associated 
    with CF
    • Pancreas, Gallbladder, and 
    Intestinal Tract Disease
    • Pancreatic exocrine 
    malfunction 
    • Malabsorption of important 
    nutrients including fat and 
    protein 
    • Biliary tract obstruction 


    .Other Systems Impacted by CF
    • Reproductive System
    • Musculoskeletal System


    .Early Diagnostic Testing 
    • Newborn screen—CFTR mutation screen
    • Sweat test—elevated chloride levels (≥60 mEq/L)


    .Examination
    • Radiographic Imaging
    • Xray
    • CT scanning
    • Pulmonary function tests 
    • Arterial blood gases


    .Other Examination Considerations
        Musculoskeletal
            • Kyphosis
            • Tight hamstrings 
        CF-related diabetes 
            • Glucose monitoring 
            for Hyper- or 
            hypoglycemia with 
            sxs of: 
            • Excessive fatigue
            • Confusion
            • Dizziness
        Cardiovascular 
        &Pulmonary 
            • Auscultation 
            • Reduced exercise 
            testing
            • Reduced SPO2


    .Guidelines for CF care
    • Clinic visits: four or more per year
    • PFTs: two or more per year
    • Respiratory cultures: at least one per year
    • Glucose monitoring: every year if age 14 or older
    • Liver enzymes monitoring: every year
    • Influenza vaccine: every year if 6 months of age or more, up 
    to 6 years


    .Management
    • Medical management
    • Goals include controlling lung infection, promoting mucus clearance, 
    improving nutritional status
    • Pulmonary infection
    • Pancreatic status 
    • nutritional supplementation
    • Lung transplantation
    • Prognosis
    • Dramatic increase in median age of survival
    • Prevention
    • Genetic counseling
    • Screening for CF carrier status


    .Physical Therapy Interventions
    • Secretion clearance techniques
    • Controlled breathing techniques
    • Exercise and strength training
    • Inspiratory muscle training
    • Thoracic stretching exercises
    • Postural reeducation


    .Secretion Clearance 
    • Postural drainage
    • Coughing
    ('')


    .Exercise
    • Exercise testing can help identify potential risk factors for 
    this specific population. 
    • Pulse oximetry must be monitored. 
    • Assess desaturation levels & supplemental oxygen needs
    • Exercise prescription special considerations:
    • CF-related diabetes
    • Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction

////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
10.5. Lecture: Restrictive Lung Dysfunction
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

The following lecture will cover commonly encountered pulmonary diseases that lead to Restrictive Lung Dysfunction. This lecture will review the pathophysiology, features, treatment, and physical therapy interventions in those suffering from restrictive lung dysfunction.  

('PT 2026_Mod 6.1_Restrictive Lung Dysfunction.pdf')
    > > > 

    Restrictive Lung Disease

    .Restrictive Lung Dysfunction
    • Poor Lung Compliance with Increased Work of breathing
    • PFTs
    • Volumes — IRV, VT, ERV, RV are decreased Γ('PFT Changes with Disease.png')
    • Capacities — TLC, VC, FRC are decreased
    • Increased Work of breathing


    .General Clinical Signs of Restrictive Lung Disease
    • Examination
    • Breath sounds
    • Absent ,Wheeze or Crackles 
    • Reduced chest expansion
    • Observation
    • Tachypneic with increased work of resp mm
    • Dyspnea
    • Irritating, dry, and nonproductive cough
    • Cyanotic appearance 
    • ABG changes
    • Hypoxemia (↓ PaO2) and hypocapnia (↓ PaCO2), pH ↑


    .Pneumonia
    • Inflammatory reaction of the 
    distal airways from inhalation of 
    bacteria, viruses, 
    microorganisms, foreign 
    substances, gastric contents, or 
    complication of radiation therapy
    • community or hospital acquired
    • Viral vs Bacterial
    • Sputum culture
    • Guides treatment


    .Bacterial Pneumonia 
    • Abrupt onset 
    • Lobar consolidation in one or 
    more lobes
    • High fever & chills
    • Productive cough, pleuritic pain
    • Dyspnea, tachypnea
    • High white blood cell count


    .Viral Pneumonia 
    • Bilateral diffuse scattered 
    fluffy shadows indicating 
    patchy alveolar infiltrates
    • Moderate fever
    • Myalgia or muscle pain
    • Non-productive cough
    • Normal white blood cell 
    count


    .Clinical Manifestation of Pneumonia
    • ↓ lung volumes, ↓ lung compliance, ↓ gas exchange, ↑ RR, ↑
    work of breathing
    • ↓ PaO2, may have ↓ PaCO2 as a result of breathing pattern 
    blowing off CO2
    • absent breath sounds over area of pneumonia 
    • Usually have ↑HR, especially in presence of fever


    .Pneumonia 2
    • Physical Therapy Implications:
    • Prevention is key
    • Coughing techniques
    • Positioning for improved ventilation or postural drainage 
    when appropriate
    • Supplemental O2 needs
    • Progressive exercise training when appropriate 


    .Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS)
    • Inflammation of the lung associated with aspiration, drug 
    toxicity, inhalation injury, pulmonary trauma, shock, systemic 
    infection, organ failures
    • CRITICALLY ILL with high mortality rates
    • will require mechanical ventilation with hemodynamic 
    monitoring
    • 2 phases:
    1. Exudative 
    2. Proliferative 


    .ARDS Clinical Manifestations  
    • Tachypnea
    • Decreased B chest wall expansion
    • Diminished breath sounds, crackles, wheezes
    • Hypotension, high heart rate
    • Altered mental status
    • Symmetric bilateral diffuse fluffy infiltrates on imaging
    • ↓ PaO2 (<60 mm Hg),↓ PaCO2
    • 50 mmHg – mechanical ventilation required


    .PT Management of ARDS
    • Patient Proning
    • Improve v/q ratio by allowing 
    alveoli improved available 
    surface area and inflation
    • Require ATLEAST 16 hours out of 24 in prone 
    • high need for PT resources to perform this 
    within a team approach
    • Nurse, anesthesiologist, PT, OT


    .Atelectasis
    • Partial or total collapse of 
    aveoli, lung segments, lobes


    .Mechanisms of Atelectasis
        ('')


    .Factors Associated with Atelectasis 
    • Hypoventilation 
    • Ineffective pulmonary secretion clearance
    • Inactivity
    • Upper abdominal or thoracic incisional pain
    • Compression of lung parenchyma
    • Diaphragmatic weakness or restriction
    • Post obstruction pneumonia
    • Foreign body presence


    .Atelectasis
    • Results in:
    • Hypoxemia from a V/Q mismatch
    • Transpulmonary shunting
    • Pulmonary vasoconstriction
    • Incomplete expansion of lung or loss of volume
    • Chest radiograph shows opacification
    • Compensatory hyperinflation in rest of lung tissue
    • Tracheal shift:
    • Depends! 


    .Clinical Manifestations of Atelectasis
    • Tachypnea, shallow respiration 
    • Tachycardia 
    • Crackles at involved site, diminished breath sounds, 
    • Dry or wet cough


    .PT Management of Atelectasis
    • Prevention with airway clearance and mobility/exercise
    • Deep breathing, breathing into lung segment or incentive 
    spirometry, coughing


    .Pleural Diseases
    • Pleuritis is usually associated 
    with pleural effusion. 
    • Fibrothorax is an encasement of 
    the lungs with fibrous tissue 
    that obliterates the pleural 
    cavity. 
    • Pneumothorax denotes the 
    entry of air into the pleural 
    cavity. 
    • Empyema involves pockets of 
    pus enclosed in fibrous 
    adhesions.


    .Pneumothorax 
    • Presence of air in the pleural space due to 
    Visceral pleura proliferation with movement of 
    air from within the lung 
    • Trauma/rib fracture
    • COPD
    • Tall people 
    • Associated with rib factures
    • Flail chest as a medical emergency!


    .Pleural Effusion
    • Accumulation of fluid within the 
    pleural space
    • Treated by thoracentesis 


    .Pulmonary Edema
    • Cardiogenic vs non-cardiogenic
    • Clinical manifestations: 
    • basilar infiltrates on imaging
    • ↓ PaO2, ↓ PaCO2, ↑ pH Respiratory alkalosis
    • Wet rales with ↓ breath sounds
    • Short of breath, cyanotic, ↑ RR, labored breathing
    • CHF associated
    • Large cardiac silhouette 
    • High Brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) 
    • volume overload/edema 


    .Pulmonary Embolism (PE)
    • Partial or full occlusion of the 
    pulmonary vasculature
    • Clinical Manifestations:
    • Rapid onset tachypnea, chest pain, 
    lightheaded
    • Hypotension, tachycardia, dec chest 
    Diminished breath sounds distal to 
    PE
    • Crackles or wheeze may be present
    • No sputum
    • EMERGENCY IF SUSPECTED 


    .Bronchogenic Carcinoma
    • Malignant growth of abnormal epithelial 
    cells in the bronchus
    • Clinical manifestations:
    • Cough, chest pain, unexplained 
    weigh loss, metastases to other 
    organs, dyspnea 
    • Hypoxemia (↓ PaO2) and hypocapnia 
    (↓ PaCO2), pH ↑
    • PT Considerations:
    • Absent breath sounds in area of 
    carcinoma
    • Red Flag Cancer signs and 
    symptoms 


    .Regardless of Lung Condition MUST CHECK
    • SPO2
    • ABGs
    • ALL ASSOC LAB VALUES
    • ASSOCIATED SX and SXS
    • OXYGEN THERAPY NEEDS
    • TITRATION OF O2 
    • Appropriate Exercise Testing

////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
10.6. Lecture: Other Causes of Restrictive Pulmonary Dysfunction
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

('PT 2026_Mod 6.1_Other Causes of Restrictive Lung Dysfunction.pdf')
    > > > 

    Other Causes of Restrictive Lung Dysfunction

    .Maturational Causes of Restrictive Lung Dysfunction


    .Normal Aging
        ('')
        

    .Pediatric Respiratory Distress Syndrome
    • Pediatric Respiratory Distress Syndrome
    • Hyaline membrane disease
    • disorder of prematurity or lack of complete lung maturation
    • Linked to gestational age
    • Caused by abnormalities in surfactant system and inadequate 
    surfactant production
    • Mechanical ventilation is disruptive to fragile structures
    • Treatment:
    • surfactant replacement therapy or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation 
    (ECMO); administration of corticosteroids to mother before birth


    .Interstitial Causes of Restrictive Lung Dysfunction


    .Sarcoidosis
    • Sarcoidosis
    • Enigmatic multisystem 
    disease characterized by the 
    presence of noncaseating 
    epithelioid granulomas in 
    many organs
    • Lungs and lymph affected by 
    masses or nodules or space 
    occupying lesions


    .Bronchiolitis obliterans
    • characterized by necrosis of the respiratory epithelium in the 
    affected bronchioles
    • necrosis allows fluid and debris to enter the bronchioles and 
    alveoli, causing alveolar pulmonary edema and partial or 
    complete obstruction of these small airways
    • Can impact pediatrics or older adults


    .Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis
    • Inflammatory process of alveolar wall
    • Etiology
    • Interplay between genetic and environmental causes
    • Patchy focal lesions scattered, inflammatory changes then scar and 
    become fibrotic
    • Treatment
    • corticosteroids, cytotoxic drugs, smoking cessation, maintaining 
    adequate oxygenation/ventilation, good nutrition, treatment of 
    infection, lung transplantation

    .Neuromuscular Causes of Restrictive Lung Dysfunction

    .Spinal Cord Injury (SCI) (!!E)
        | Muscles              | Level                                 |
        |--------------------------|-------------------------------------------|
        | Inspiratory          |                                           |
        | Diaphragm                | C3, C4, C5 (phrenic nerve)                |
        | External intercostals    | T1 to T12                                 |
        | Sternocleidomastoid      | Cranial nerve XI (spinal accessory nerve) |
        | Scalenes                 | C1, C2                                    |
        | Expiratory           |                                           |
        | Internal intercostals    | T1 to T12                                 |
        | Abdominals               | T7 to L1                                  |

    .Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS)
    • Progressive degenerative disease of the nervous system that 
    involves both upper and lower motor neurons
    • Involves mostly anterior horn cells of cervical, lower thoracic, 
    and lumbosacral spinal segments
    • Treatment
    • supportive therapy; physical exertion is not recommended
    • diaphragm motor pacing

    .Musculoskeletal Causes of Restrictive Lung Dysfunction

    .Diaphragmatic Paralysis or Paresis
    • Loss or impairment of motor function of diaphragm due to a 
    lesion in the neurological or muscular system


    .Kyphoscoliosis
    • Combination of excessive anteroposterior and lateral 
    curvature of the thoracic spine
    • Significant spinal curvature must be present before 
    pulmonary symptoms develop
    • Angles:
    • <70 degrees no pulmonary dysfunction
    • 70 to 120 degrees some pulmonary dysfunction
    • angles >120 degrees severe RLD and respiratory 
    failure
    • Treatment
    • Conservative with orthotic devices and exercise
    • Surgical placement of Harrington distraction strut 
    bars
    • Preventive and supportive measures for pulmonary 
    compromise


    .Ankylosing Spondylitis
    • Chronic inflammatory disease of the spine characterized by 
    immobility of sacroiliac and vertebral joints and ossification 
    of paravertebral ligaments
    • Inherited arthritic condition
    • Markedly decreased compliance of chest wall
    • Treatment
    • no cure; maintain good body alignment and thoracic mobility


    .Chest Shape
    • Pectus excavatum
    • Funnel chest; congenital abnormality
    • Sternal depression and decreased anteroposterior diameter
    • If deformity is severe, may have decreased TLC, VC, and maximum 
    voluntary ventilation
    • Pectus carinatum
    • Pigeon breast
    • Sternum protruding anteriorly
    • Associated with prolonged childhood asthma

10.7. Pulmonary Conditions Self-Assessment
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////// (!!Q)

Question 1
Which of the following muscles help to achieve the active process of inspiration at rest in a normal, nonsmoking individual? 
Group of answer choices

Sternocleidomastoid
Diaphragm
Abdominals
Trapezius

Diaphragm
    The diaphragm and internal intercostals (intercartilaginous portion) are the essential muscles to achieve the active process of inspiration at rest. Abdominal muscles assist with expiration. The sternocleidomastoid and trapezius are accessory muscles and assist with a more forceful inspiration.

Question 2
True or False: A person who is sitting upright in a chair has the greatest amount of perfusion in the apex or upper lobe of their lungs: 
Group of answer choices

True
False

False
    Feedback: Perfusion or blood flow is greatest in gravity dependent areas, which in the case of a person sitting upright in a chair the lower lobe or base of the lungs would have the greatest amount of perfusion. 

Question 3
Gas is transported away from the tissues and back into the lungs in the following ways EXCEPT: 
Group of answer choices

Dissolved in plasma
Carbaminohemoglobin
Bicarbonate
Oxyhemoglobin

Oxyhemoglobin
    Gas that is transported away from the tissues would be in the form of carbon dioxide, which is transported in 3 ways: back to the lungs dissolved in plasma as pCO2 or chemically bound to carbaminohemoglobin, and to the kidneys as bicarbonate. Only oxygen can bind to hemoglobin in the lungs and be transported to peripheral tissues.

Question 4
Which of the following statements BEST explains why increasing administered oxygen should be done cautiously in a patient with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) AT REST? 
Group of answer choices

-The body may rely on hypoxic drive to breathe (oxygen receptors) and increasing administered oxygen at rest leads to hyperoxemia suppressing the hypoxic drive.
-The body needs additional time to allow the peripheral chemoreceptors to cause an increase of ventilatory rate to improve oxygenation.
-The body is relying on carbon dioxide to regulate the respiratory cycle, and increasing administered oxygen at rest leads to inhibition of the carbon dioxide receptors.
-Increasing administered oxygen to the body oversaturates the system leading to toxicity.

-The body may rely on hypoxic drive to breathe (oxygen receptors) and increasing administered oxygen at rest leads to hyperoxemia suppressing the hypoxic drive.
    A patient with severe COPD who develops high CO2 blood levels subsequently leads to the body relying more on oxygen receptors instead of carbon dioxide receptors. This is termed hypoxic drive to breathe. If administered oxygen is too high and causes hyperoxemia (increased oxygen in the blood), the oxygen receptors may be suppressed, which reduces the drive to breathe. 

Question 5
Which of the following is the MOST common risk factor for development of COPD: 
Group of answer choices

Increased BMI
Cigarette smoking
Air pollution
Genetics

Cigarette smoking
    Cigarette smoking is the most common risk factor for development of chronic bronchitis and emphysema, thus leading to COPD. Air pollution and α1 antitrypsin deficiency (genetics) are both risk factors, but not as common as cigarette smoking. 

Question 6
True or False: Pursed lip breathing is an intervention used to improve lung capacity in a patient with COPD. 
Group of answer choices

True
False
    
False
    Pursed lip breathing is used with COPD patients with a 1:2 or 1:6 inhalation to exhalation time to improve time spent in exhalation. Those with COPD have hyperinflated lungs or increased lung capacity that can lead to air trapping, and this intervention allows for release of some of that increased air. 

Question 7
Clinical features of CF include which of the following? 
Group of answer choices

Persistent cough and recurrent lung infiltrates
Pancreatic Insufficiency
Failure to thrive with steatorrhea (excessive fat in feces)
All of the above

All of the above
    The usual clinical presentations in CF include respiratory tract symptoms (persistent cough, recurrent lung infiltrates); GI presentations include Pancreatic exocrine malfunction and failure to thrive with excessive fat in feces. 

Question 8
An irreversible dilation of one or more bronchi with chronic inflammation and infection is characterized by which of the following lung diseases? 
Group of answer choices

Cystic fibrosis
COPD
Bronchiectasis
Chronic bronchitis

Bronchiectasis
    Bronchiectasis is characterized by irreversible dilation of one or more bronchi with chronic inflammation and infection. Bronchiectasis describes an anatomic abnormality rather than a single disease. 

Question 9
Which of the following signs are associated with lung hyperinflation noted in obstructive lung diseases? 
Group of answer choices

Elevation of shoulder girdle
Horizontal ribs
Low, flattened diaphragm
All of the above

All of the above
     Common signs of lung hyperinflation associated with obstructive lung diseases included elevation of shoulder girdle, horizontal ribs, barrel-shaped thorax (increased anterior–posterior diameter), and low, flattened diaphragm. 

Question 10
Hallmark symptoms of restrictive lung disease include dyspnea, an emaciated appearance, and which of the following? 
Group of answer choices

Chest wall pain
Wet, productive cough
Dry, nonproductive cough
Fatigue

Dry, nonproductive cough
    Three hallmark symptoms typically experienced with RLD include dyspnea, a wasted and emaciated appearance, and an irritating, dry, and nonproductive cough. 

Question 11
A key medical treatment of pneumonia is which of the following? 
Group of answer choices

Determining if it is community acquired or nosocomial
Identifying the microbe (virus versus bacteria)
Identifying specific risk factors
Determining the area of lung affected

Identifying the microbe (virus versus bacteria)
    The key to treatment of pneumonia is to first identify the microbe (virus versus gram-positive or gram-negative bacteria). Specific medical treatment (specific antibiotic) is based on the identification of the microbe. The other answers are important also, but the key for survival and appropriate treatment is identification of the causative factor in order to now allow progression of the disease.

Question 12
A free-floating segment of ribs that can be identified by its paradoxical movement and is considered a medical emergency is termed: 
Group of answer choices

Lung contusion
Rib fractures
Flail chest
Empyema

Flail chest
    Flail chest refers to a free-floating segment of ribs due to multiple rib fractures both anteriorly and posteriorly that leave this part of the thoracic wall disconnected to the rest of the thoracic cage. This segment can usually be identified by its paradoxical movement during the respiratory cycle. 

Question 13
Which of the following spinal cord levels if injured would result in diaphragmatic dysfunction? 
Group of answer choices

C4-5
T1-2
T4-5
T7-8

C4-5
    C3, C4, and C5 (phrenic nerve) if injured would result in diaphragmatic dysfunction. 

Question 14
On a chest radiograph, the classic finding of an elevated hemidiaphragm indicates which of the following musculoskeletal causes of restrictive lung dysfunction? 
Group of answer choices

Kyphoscoliosis
Ankylosing spondylitis
Diaphragmatic paresis
Pectus excavatum

Diaphragmatic paresis
    Diaphragmatic paralysis or paresis is the loss or impairment of motor function of the diaphragm because of a lesion in the neurological or muscular system. In this condition, the negative pleural space pressure moves the diaphragm in a cephalad direction so that the diaphragm’s resting position is elevated. Elevated hemidiaphragm is a classic finding on chest radiograph 

Question 15
Which of the following causes of restrictive lung disease is characterized by necrosis of the respiratory epithelium in the affected bronchioles? 
Group of answer choices

Bronchiolitis obliterans
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
Sarcoidosis
Kyphoscoliosis

Bronchiolitis obliterans
    Bronchiolitis obliterans is characterized by necrosis of the respiratory epithelium in the affected bronchioles. This necrosis allows fluid and debris to enter the bronchioles and alveoli, causing alveolar pulmonary edema and partial or complete obstruction of these small airways.

            Answer Key COPD Case Study Part 1  
            INSTRUCTIONS 
            The following case will be presented in 3 progressions/sections, and each section will have associated 
            questions. You will break out into your respective groups and answer the questions. 
            Section 1 
            The patient is a 65-year-old woman with a history of COPD, formally diagnosed as stage 1-2 last year,  
            who presents to his primary care provider’s (PCP) office complaining of a productive cough off and on 
            for 2 years and shortness of breath for the last 3 days.  
            She reports that she has had several chest colds in the last few years, but this time it won’t go away.   
            She has been feverish for a few days but does not have a specific temperature to report. She reports 
            that she has had several chest colds in the last few years, but this time it won’t go away.   
            She has been feverish for a few days but does not have a specific temperature to report.  
            PMH:  reports smoking a pack of cigarettes a day for 25 years plus, chronic productive cough yearly > 4 
            years,   
            The patient tells the MD that her main complaint is dyspnea with mobility resulting in low activity 
            tolerance 
            • She has a cough throughout the day 
            • Reports increased productive cough with infections 
            • Signs and symptoms with walking: 
            o Wheezing 
            o Tripoding 
            Briefly review productive cough, wheezing and tripoding prior to moving into next sections 

            

            QUESTIONS 
            1. Would you predict this patient to have Emphysema or Chronic Bronchitis Dominant COPD, and 
            what may you observe about the patient based on your prediction? 
            Chronic bronchitis & chronic bronchitis dominant COPD have an excess in body fluids and 
            chronic cough related to hypersecretions. Both demonstrate increased SOB, especially with 
            exertion  
            2. What are some pulmonary diagnoses to consider? 
            Pneumonia, COPD exacerbation, pulmonary edema, etc 
            3. What vitals would be important to consider? 
            SpO2 & respiratory rate as primary, but also will need to consider all others such as BP, HR and  
            4. How is COPD staged? What would constitute a stage 1-2 dx? 
            PFT testing is completed an FEV1/FVC ratio will determine the presence of an obstructive 
            condition or COPD, and that is a test that reveals a ratio of <0.7. Stage 1 FEV1 (% predicated) >80 
            and stage 2 50 to 80. Both will have chronic cough with or without sputum and dyspnea. 


            Part 2 
            Upon further assessment, the patient has crackles throughout the lower lobes of her lungs, with 
            occasional expiratory wheezes throughout the lung fields.  
            Her vital signs are as follows: 
            • BP 142/86 mmHg HR 102 bpm 
            • RR 32 bpm Temp 38.8°C (101.8F) 
            • SpO2 86% on room air 
            Based on these findings, the PCP decides to call an ambulance to send her to the Emergency 
            Department (ED).  

            

            QUESTIONS 
            1. Are the vitals normal? Are they concerning? What is your interpretation of the patient’s vital 
            sign measures? 
            The vitals are not normal. Blood pressure and RR are both elevated, and oxygen saturation is 
            low. These vitals demonstrate poor oxygenation status, along with high BP leading to the heart 
            having to work harder to maintain CO. 
            2. Why did the MD send this patient to the ED? 
            The patient presents with concerning vitals along with a high temperature, they are at risk based 
            on their patient history for pulmonary infection. They likely appear to be in respiratory distress 
            and will require further workup and possible external oxygen needs.  
            3. Why would a chest x-ray be taken? And what may it reveal? 
            Hyperinflated lungs, possibly enlarged ventricle if late stage COPD with HF as a response to pulm 
            HTN, consolidation d/t mucus  
            4. Describe what one might observe in this patient. For example, how may this patient appear in 
            terms of her breathing pattern, chest wall motion, muscles of respiration, and work of breathing 
            The patient would likely demonstrate increased work of breathing and based on her history of 
            COPD and current productive cough she may have an increase in accessory muscle use and 
            reduced lower chest wall expansion and/or diaphragmatic involvement in inhalation. 
            5. What may be the line of action for the 86% SpO2? Describe potential medical treatments for the 
            oxygen saturation reading. 
            Oxygen therapy likely will be required with this patient. While they have COPD, and we are 
            aware of the careful considerations required with giving supplemental O2 to those with COPD, 
            this patient is in respiratory distress and an SpO2 <88% could be dangerously low as related to 
            partial pressure of oxygen that is associated with that reading. Supplemental oxygen of some 
            sort could be the first line of action for medical treatment in this patient. 


            Part 3 


            In the ED they performed ECG monitoring, continuous vital sign monitoring, and imaging. Findings 
            included:  
            • ECG Sinus tachycardia with occasional premature atrial contractions 
            • Resting Vitals: HR 112, BP 140/72, SpO2 91% on 2L O2, RR 21 
            • Lungs: end expiratory wheeze, decreased breath sounds bilateral lung bases, SOB/DOE, RR 21, 
            SpO2 91% on 2L O2  
            • Extremities: clubbing, generalized weakness 
            • PFT: FEV1: 1.5 L (40% of predicted), FVC: 2.74 L (60% of predicted), FEV1/FVC ratio: 0.55 (45% of 
            predicted) 
            • Chest x-ray: 

   
            QUESTIONS  
            1. Why would this patient have end expiratory wheezing? 
            Airflow obstruction as related to diseases of airways can produce obstruction of expiratory flow. 
            This patient could have airflow obstruction related to retained secretions, inflammation of 
            mucosal lining of airway walls, bronchial constriction related to bronchitis and weakening of 
            support structure related to emphysema – both present in COPD. 
            2. What is digital clubbing and why would this be present? 
            Digital clubbing is the appearance of clubbing in the distal fingers and is a measure of poor 
            oxygenation status to the peripheral tissue. When it is present it is indicative of a chronic oxygen 
            deprivation.  
            3. If this patient has a lung condition, why would there be a presence of arrhythmias on ECG? 
            Explain how the cardiac system would be impacted by pulmonary disease? 
            End-stage COPD or even other pulmonary disease can result in cor pulmonale or right heart 
            failure due to increased pulmonary artery pressure which can increase right ventricular 
            workload as it attempts to pump blood against the constricted pulmonary artery into the lungs. 
            4. Are the PFTs consistent with an obstructive or restrictive condition? Explain your answer, and 
            how would you stage it if appropriate? 
            Obstructive lung disease, especially based on the FEV1/FVC ratio: 0.55 (45% of predicted), which 
            is below 70%. Stage 3 based on the GOLD criteria. 

 
            5. If there is concern for bacterial pneumonia due to cough and fever, what diagnostic testing 
            would be ordered, what clinical signs and symptoms would be present, and what may an x-ray 
            reveal in lungs that are infected with pneumonia on top of having COPD? 
            A sputum culture would be ordered to determine if there is an infection present. The patient 
            would report an abrupt onset of symptoms with high fever & chills, productive cough, pleuritic 
            pain, dyspnea, and tachypnea.  The Xray would reveal hyperinflated lungs from the COPD, there 
            would be apparent areas of consolidation. 
            6. Challenge: Describe the chest x-ray. 
            Right lower lobe consolidation in a patient with known chronic obstructive pulmonary disease

                                Vitals are WNL, except for SpO2 
                           
                            2.Would supplemental oxygen be required? What about this patient would require careful monitoring of supplemental oxygen use? 
                                Yes, 85% is low and below an appropriate and safe threshold of SpO2, careful titration is required as not to dampen respiratory drive.
                          
                            3. Would you communicate anything to the medical team? 
                                Yes, with the drop in SpO2 we may need to approach the medical team for oxygen titration orders  
               
                .Section 3 
                    The patient is seen 1 to 2 times a day for PT and demonstrates improvements in physical function. You have been working on progressive aerobic training to improve gait distance. On the treatment today the patient is preparing for discharge and the PT is asked to perform gait training/ambulation with the patient on ‘room air’ to determine need for oxygen. The patient ambulates 250 feet with supervision and a wheeled walker, SpO2 is 90% before ambulation, 96% during and immediately after ambulation. The patient is cued to take deep breaths and recovers to 90% in 2 minutes.

                    QUESTIONS 
                        1.Would you use heart rate to predict the exercise intensity for this patient while performing gait? 
                            HR is not a reliable indicator of exercise intensity in COPD patients, and intensity is monitored by dyspnea or ratings of perceived exertion. COPD patients may reach SOB prior to reaching a heart rate that would be considered intense exercise based on aerobic exercise prescription equations or maximal testing.  
                        2.Will this patient likely need supplemental O2 based on these findings? 
                            This is a difficulty one, as the patient does appear to need it with exertion, so this is not for us to determine, but rather report the SpO2 walking test findings.  
                        3.Name an intervention that would assist with inhalation/exhalation timing for this patient and explain why it is appropriate for a COPD stage 3 patient. 
                            Pursed lip breathing is a fantastic breathing technique for patients with COPD. The technique consists of breathing into the nose with a closed mouth, then exhaling out through the mouth with pursed lips over an extended time. The inhalation phase with the mouth closed ensures there is a direct line of oxygen reaching the lungs with no escape through the mouth. Then the extended exhalation through pursed lips promotes a slow prolonged exhalation to work on reduced air volume and a relaxed approach to breathing 
                        4.What are some key aspects of patient education with this patient in preparation for discharge? 
                            Activity pacing, especially positions for dyspnea relief and possibly need for AD to allow for improved activity pacing (rolling walker or rollator with seat),  
                        5.Is this patient appropriate for pulmonary rehabilitation? 
                            Yes, this can improve QoL, self-efficacy, and overall functional capacity.

        Answer Key: Restrictive Lung Dysfunction Case  
            You will need to refer to the lectures and the Hillegass text to complete this activity.

        INSTRUCTIONS - Opening Questions: (See RUPERTA's on Q&A doc if something is not answered here)
            1.Is restrictive lung dysfunction a disease? 
                Restrictive lung dysfunction is not a disease: It is an abnormal reduction in pulmonary ventilation. 
            
            2.Name 3 specific causes of restrictive lung dysfunction and how it leads to a reduced or abnormal pulmonary ventilation. 
                They can mention a variety of disease processes occurring in different body systems, trauma, or therapeutic measures.     

            3.What are the classic signs and hallmark symptoms of restrictive lung dysfunction? 
                -The classic signs of RLD include tachypnea, hypoxemia, decreased breath sounds, dry inspiratory rales, decreased lung volumes, decreased diffusing capacity, and cor pulmonale. 
                -The hallmark symptoms of RLD include shortness of breath; cough; and a wasted, emaciated appearance. 

            4. Describe the main differences between bacterial and viral pneumonia:      
                Bacterial 
                    • Abrupt onset 
                    • Lobar consolidation in one or more lobes 
                    • High fever & chills 
                    • Productive cough, pleuritic pain 
                    • Dyspnea, tachypnea 
                    • High white blood cell count 
                Viral
                    • Bilateral diffuse scattered fluffy shadows indicating patchy alveolar infiltrates 
                    • Moderate fever 
                    • Myalgia or muscle pain 
                    • Non-productive cough 
                    • Normal white blood cell count   

            5. Describe the mechanisms that lead to atelectasis, how the trachea may shift based on each of those. Describe in detail the term pneumothorax as a mechanism of atelectasis using the words “simple” vs “tension” pneumothorax. 
                -Clarification on atelectasis regarding pneumothorax and other conditions.  Atelectasis is a blanket term and represents disorders that lead to an area of the lung that cannot expand. 
                -Generally speaking those mechanisms can be a collapse, compression, or obstruction (Hillegass pg 150). Considering the related tracheal shift (which does not happen in every case) - think whether there is an increase in pressure or volume increase (away from) or reduced pressure or volume loss (toward). Pneumothorax is a term used for air entering the pleural cavity as a mechanism of atelectasis,  and it can be simple (no shift) vs tension where you will have a tracheal shift away from the insult. This is a form of passive atelectasis, which can occur with general shallow breathing at low TV, extended bed rest, trauma, as a few examples (can be a result of a severe infection like pneumonia).  A tracheal shift toward the side of the lung collapse can occur when there is a single segment of lung collapse.  In these cases, the tracheal shift is seen typically when the upper lobe is affected, a pneumectomy (surgical removal of lung tissue), and fibrosis of the an area of the lung as a few examples.  

            6. Case Part 1: A 55-year-old male presented to the ED after a car accident. During the crash he suffered a blow to his his right lower side (thorax). He was rushed to the ED, was told he sustained rib fracture, and sent home. After 3 days of complete immobility due to pain he

.Which of the following spinal cord levels if injured would result in diaphragmatic dysfunction?
    T1-2
    C4-5
    T4-5
    T7-8

    C4-5
    C3, C4, and C5 (phrenic nerve) if injured would result in diaphragmatic dysfunction.

.On a chest radiograph, the classic finding of an elevated hemidiaphragm indicates which of the following musculoskeletal causes of restrictive lung dysfunction?
    Kyphoscoliosis
    Ankylosing spondylitis
    Pectus excavatum
    Diaphragmatic paresis

    Diaphragmatic paresis
    Diaphragmatic paralysis is loss/impairment of motor function of diaphragm because of a lesion in the neurological or muscular system. Negative pleural space pressure moves the diaphragm in a cephalad direction, elevated hemidiaphragm classic on radiograph

.Which of the following causes of restrictive lung disease is characterized by necrosis of the respiratory epithelium in the affected bronchioles?
    Bronchiolitis obliterans
    Kyphoscoliosis
    Sarcoidosis
    Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis

    Bronchiolitis obliterans
    Characterized by necrosis of the respiratory epithelium in the affected bronchioles. This necrosis allows fluid and debris to enter the bronchioles and alveoli, causing alveolar pulmonary edema and partial/complete obstruction of small airways.

6.10. Module 6 Quiz ------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Question 1 REPE
    Chronic obstructive pulmonary diseases (COPD) are diseases of the airways that produce obstruction to expiratory airflow. Which of the following problems relates to COPD? 

    All of the above
    Inflammation of mucosal lining of airways
    Retained secretions
    Bronchial constriction related to spasm of the smooth muscle

    All of the above
    COPDs are diseases of the airways that produce expiratory airflow obstruction. Causes of this obstruction include retained secretions, inflammation of the mucosal lining of airway walls, bronchial constriction related to increased tone or spasms of bronchial smooth muscle, and weakening of the support structure of airways walls.
    
Question 2
    Generally, COPD is BEST diagnosed using which of the following tests? 

    Exercise testing
    Pulmonary function testing
    Chest x-ray
    Arterial blood gases

    Chest x-ray
    CXR findings are evident only in severe CODP cases. It is of limited value in diagnosing obstructive lung disease. Results of spirometry testing (PFTs) are more important in identifying the presence of most obstructive lung diseases.
    
Question 3
    Which of the pulmonary function test findings BEST indicates COPD? 

    High FEV1, no change in FEV1/FVC, low residual volume
    High FEV1, high FEV1/FVC, low residual volume
    Low FEV1, low FEV1/FVC, high residual volume
    Low FEV1, no change in FEV1/FVC, no change in residual volume
    
    Low FEV1, low FEV1/FVC, high residual volume
    Pulmonary function test findings indicative of CODP include low FEV1, low FVC resulting in a decrease in the FEV1/FVC ratio as lung disease worsens. Individuals with COPD require increased time to expel air from their lungs. Additionally, less air can be exhaled in 1 second. Lung volumes (TLC, RV) increase due to the inability to exhale air.

Question 4 REPE
    Clinical features of CF include which of the following? 

    Persistent cough and recurrent lung infiltrates
    All of the above
    hypertrophy of respiratory accessory muscles
    Failure to thrive with steatorrhea (excessive fat in feces)
    
    All of the above
    The usual clinical presentations in CF include respiratory tract symptoms (persistent cough, recurrent lung infiltrates) along with increase in accessory muscle use; GI presentations include meconium ileus and failure to thrive with excessive fat in feces.

Question 5
    Destruction of alveolar walls and enlargement of the airspaces distal to terminal bronchioles describe which of the following lung conditions? 

    Emphysema
    Chronic bronchitis
    Cystic fibrosis
    Bronchiectasis

    Emphysema
    Emphysema is defined as a condition of the lung characterized by destruction of alveolar walls and enlargement of the airspaces distal to the terminal bronchioles.

Question 6 REPE
    Hallmark symptoms of restrictive lung disease, such as in viral pneumonia, include dyspnea, an emaciated appearance, and which of the following? 

    Wet, productive cough
    Dry, nonproductive cough
    Redness in distal extremities
    Chest wall pain
    
    Dry, nonproductive cough
    Three hallmark symptoms typically experienced with RLD include dyspnea, a wasted and emaciated appearance, and an irritating, dry, and nonproductive cough.

Question 7 REPE
    Which of the following causes of restrictive lung disease is characterized by necrosis of the respiratory epithelium in the affected bronchioles? 

    Bronchiolitis obliterans
    Asbestosis
    Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
    Bronchopulmonary dysplasia
    
    Bronchiolitis obliterans
    Bronchiolitis obliterans is characterized by necrosis of the respiratory epithelium in the affected bronchioles. This necrosis allows fluid and debris to enter the bronchioles and alveoli, causing alveolar pulmonary edema and partial or complete obstruction of these small airways.

Question 8 REPE
    The key to medical treatment of pneumonia is which of the following? 

    Determining the area of lung affected
    Identifying the microbe (virus versus bacteria)
    Determining if it is community acquired or nosocomial
    Identifying specific risk factors

    Identifying the microbe (virus versus bacteria)
    The key to treatment of pneumonia is to first identify the microbe (virus versus gram-positive or gram-negative bacteria). Specific medical treatment (specific antibiotic) is based on the identification of the microbe.

Question 9
    Hypoxemia (↓ PaO2) and hypocapnia (↓ PaCO2), pH ↑ is MOST associated with which of the following conditions? 

    Atelectasis
    Chronic Bronchitis
    Cystic Fibrosis
    COPD
    
    Atelectasis
    Hypoxemia (↓ PaO2) and hypocapnia (↓ PaCO2), pH ↑ is respiratory alkalosis, and based on the lecture “Restrictive Lung Dysfunction,” patients may appear tachypneic defined as a high respiratory rate that will demonstrate an increased work of resp mms. Tachypnea may appear as a hyperventilation, which is due to the reduced O2 levels, and when the O2 levels decrease to a certain degree that hyperventilatory status may lead to a reduced CO2. This occurs as the patient is working to take in O2 at a high rate all the while blowing off CO2 at a high rate as well. This will lead to an arterial blood gas change with a PaCO2 that is lower than normal, leading to what is called respiratory alkalosis, or an alkalotic blood pH. Atelectasis is the only restrictive lung condition on the list above. 

Question 10
    On a chest radiograph, the classic finding of an elevated hemidiaphragm indicates which of the following musculoskeletal causes of restrictive lung dysfunction? 

    Diaphragmatic paresis
    Pectus excavatum
    Ankylosing spondylitis
    Kyphoscoliosis

    Diaphragmatic paresis
    Diaphragmatic paralysis or paresis is the loss or impairment of motor function of the diaphragm because of a lesion in the neurological or muscular system. In this condition, the negative pleural space pressure moves the diaphragm in a cephalad direction so that the diaphragm’s resting position is elevated. Elevated hemidiaphragm is a classic finding on chest radiograph.
