Module 11: Arterial Blood Gases (ABG) & Oxygen Status
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////


////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
11.0. Module Introduction
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

In this module you will explore clinical laboratory studies of arterial blood gases (ABGs) and oxygen status within a patient. You will discover how arterial blood gases relate to patient status and how testing can impact a PT treatment and plan of care, and how to utilize those results to modify intervention based on these findings. We will also discuss the relationship between a patient’s oxygen saturation, as found on pulse oximetry devices, and how that relates to a patient’s ABGs and other symptom presentation.  

Learning Objectives
By the end of this week, you will be able to: 

Interpret the results of pulmonary diagnostic tests including objective information derived from laboratory, diagnostic, and procedure data.
Create a physical therapy treatment plan based on degree of abnormality of laboratory values and provide rationale for postponing physical therapy intervention when a patient has critical pulmonary findings.
Determine modifications and appropriateness for exercise based on pulmonary lab values and diagnostic testing.
Analyze lab values that may change based on the inter-relationship of the pulmonary system with other bodily systems.

        MRS. GLENN, a 72-year-old fe-
        male on a medical-surgical
        floor, was hospitalized 3
        days ago for pneumonia.
        Since her admission, she
        has been on continuous
        pulse oximetry and is re-
        ceiving oxygen (2 L /minute
        by nasal cannula) and an-
        tibiotics. A chest X-ray taken earli-
        er today showed little change in
        her pneumonia. She has a history
        of chronic lung disease.
        At the beginning of the shift, the
        nurse hears the low alarm of Mrs.
        Glenn’s pulse oximeter sound, indi-
        cating a reading of 89% to 90%.
        On assessment, the nurse finds the
        patient alert, oriented, and in no
        apparent distress. Mrs. Glenn’s
        heart rate is 96 beats/minute; respi-
        ratory rate, 24 breaths/minute with
        diminished breath sounds; blood
        pressure, 124/80 mm Hg; and tem-
        perature, 38.1° C (100.6° F). 
        Because the nurse is unfamiliar
        with Mrs. Glenn, she consults the
        respiratory therapist (RT), who’s
        preparing to administer a breath-
        ing treatment. The RT assures her
        that Mrs. Glenn’s pulse oximetry
        values are always low, close to her
        baseline of 92%. 
        The nurse wonders how to inter-
        pret the patient’s pulse oximetry
        values in this context. She vaguely
        remembers something about the
        oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve
        and wonders if a better under-
        standing of the curve would aid
        her assessment.

        The oxyhemoglobin dissociation
        curve (OHDC) indicates the rela-
        tionship between the oxygen satu-
        ration of hemoglobin (SaO2) and
        the partial pressure of arterial oxy-
        gen (PaO2). Neither linear nor static,
        the curve can change or shift de-
        pending on various factors. Yet un-
        derstanding the curve and its impli-
        cations for patient care can be
        challenging. 
        Pulse oximetry has become an
        essential tool in various settings for
        monitoring a patient’s oxygenation
        status. It indirectly indicates arterial
        hemoglobin saturation, measured as
        oxygen saturation by pulse oxime-
        try (SpO2). However, this technique
        is limited because oximetry meas-
        ures just one component of oxy-
        genation. For a more accurate pic-

        ture of the pa-
        tient’s overall oxy-
        genation status, you need to assess
        pulse oximetry values in the con-
        text of the OHDC. This article de-
        codes the curve to make it more
        understandable and discusses the
        benefits and limitations of pulse
        oximetry.   

        The curve: Just the basics
        No doubt you remember learning
        about the OHDC as a nursing stu-
        dent. It’s discussed in nearly every
        nursing textbook. Nonetheless, it
        can be a somewhat puzzling con-
        cept to grasp and apply in clinical
        practice. To understand it, think
        about the oxygenation process oc-
        curring in the body. Staying alive
        hinges on adequate oxygen mov-
        ing from the lungs to body tissues
        and cells. For this to occur, the
        lungs, blood, and environment
        within the body must be function-
        ing properly: 
        • The lungs must receive enough
        oxygen to be perfused and ven-
        tilated optimally.
        • Oxygen must be transported via
        the blood to the tissues. 
        Only 2% to 3% of the oxygen
        going to the tissues dissolves in
        plasma; the remainder travels in
        the plasma by attaching to hemo-
        globin molecules. The most impor-
        tant factor in the amount of oxygen
        that binds (attaches) to hemoglobin
        molecules is the partial pressure of
        arterial oxygen (PaO2); the higher
        the pressure, the more readily oxy-

        Decoding the
        oxyhemoglobin dissociation
        curve
        Understanding the curve helps you 
        put pulse oximetry in context.
        By Julia Hooley, MSN, RN


        www.AmericanNurseToday.com January 2015 American Nurse Today 19

        gen combines with hemoglobin in
        red blood cells. This hemoglobin-
        oxygen linkage is called oxyhemo-
        globin. 
        Hemoglobin is made up of four
        strands of amino acids. If oxygen is
        linked fully to all four strands, he-
        moglobin is 100% saturated with
        oxygen. Transport of sufficient oxy-
        gen to the tissues depends on an
        adequate number of hemoglobin
        molecules, as well as sufficient
        blood volume and circulation (car-
        diac output and blood pressure).
        Once hemoglobin transports oxy-
        gen to the tissues, the body’s envi-
        ronment determines how much (or
        how little) of the oxygen dissoci-
        ates (unloads) from hemoglobin for
        use. Oxygen dissociation from he-
        moglobin is determined by tissue
        demand for oxygen. That’s where
        the OHDC comes in. 

        Relationship between PaO2
        and SaO2
        The OHDC represents the relation-
        ship between PaO2 and SaO2. Nor-
        mal PaO2 ranges from 80 to 100
        mm Hg. Normal SaO2 measures

        about 97% but may range from
        93% to 97%. (See The curve: Relat-
        ing SaO2 to PaO2.) 
        The OHDC isn’t a straight line.
        Instead, it’s S-shaped. The flat up-
        per portion where the curve is
        more horizontal depicts oxygen
        loading onto hemoglobin in the
        lungs. The pressure of oxygen en-
        tering the lungs exceeds the oxy-
        gen concentration in blood
        returning to the lungs.
        This enables oxygen
        to bind more easily
        to hemoglobin. 
        A significant
        PaO2 change in
        this relatively flat
        part of the curve
        produces only a
        small change in SaO2.
        Thus, a patient’s oxy-
        genation status is better
        protected at this flat portion. For
        example, if PaO2 drops from 96 to
        70 mm Hg, hemoglobin saturation
        decreases from 97% to approxi-
        mately 92%. Clinically, this means
        that if the patient receives supple-
        mental oxygen, PaO2 will increase—

        but with little effect on SaO2.
        Hemoglobin can’t be saturated
        more than 100%, but PaO2 can rise
        significantly above 100 mm Hg if
        the patient receives high oxygen
        concentrations (as occurs with a
        hyperbaric oxygen chamber). 
        At the steep lower part of the
        curve (under the “knee”), where
        PaO2 measures between 40 and 60
        mm Hg, oxygen is released from
        hemoglobin to the capillaries at the
        tissue level due to increased oxy-
        gen demand. At this part of the
        curve, an increase or decrease in
        PaO2 leads to a large SaO2 change.
        This means giving supplemental
        oxygen will significantly increase
        the patient’s SaO2. 
        A shift to the left or right 
        Now comes the more complicated
        part. The OHDC isn’t static or con-
        stant, because certain factors can
        alter hemoglobin’s affinity for oxy-
        gen. Depending on oxygen de-
        mand at the tissue level, oxygen
        will bind to hemoglobin more or
        less readily than normal. Various
        factors cause the curve to shift to
        the left or right of its normal posi-
        tion. (See Why the curve shifts and
        How 2,3-DPG affects the curve.) 

        Connecting the curve with pulse
        oximetry readings
        PaO2 and SaO2 values can
        be obtained only from
        an arterial blood gas
        (ABG) sample. But al-
        though ABG studies
        are the gold standard
        for obtaining PaO2
        and SaO2 values, fre-
        quent ABG sampling
        isn’t always feasible or
        cost effective. For ongoing
        monitoring, pulse oximetry
        provides a convenient, continuous,
        and noninvasive way to measure
        SaO2 indirectly and monitor trends
        in the patient’s oxygenation status. 
        Be sure to check for subtle or
        sudden changes in oximetry values.
        Changes in oxygenation status can

        precede clinical signs and symp-
        toms. By detecting these changes
        early, clinicians can make timely
        modifications to the plan of care. 
        Generally speaking, a pulse
        oximetry value of 95% or higher is
        clinically acceptable, whereas a val-
        ue of 90% or lower is a red flag.
        On the OHDC, a SaO2 value of
        90% correlates to a PaO2 level of 60
        mm Hg. PaO2 pushes or loads the
        oxygen onto hemoglobin. So if this
        level isn’t adequate, suspect the pa-
        tient’s overall oxygenation is abnor-
        mally low. 

        What pulse oximetry values can’t
        tell you 
        Pulse oximetry can’t tell you the
        patient’s hemoglobin level or iden-
        tify nonfunctional hemoglobin. In
        an anemic patient, hemoglobin
        may be fully saturated and SpO2
        may be normal—yet the patient
        may be hypoxic due to lack of
        available hemoglobin to carry oxy-
        gen to the tissues. 
        Likewise, hemoglobin may be
        fully saturated but with dysfunction-
        al strands, such as carboxyhemo-
        globin or methemoglobin strands.
        Hemoglobin binds much more
        readily to carbon monoxide than to
        oxygen. Hemoglobin may be fully
        saturated and the pulse oximetry
        value may be 98%, yet hemoglobin
        may be saturated with carbon
        monoxide instead of oxygen. Car-
        boxyhemoglobin levels are elevated
        in heavy smokers. Methemoglo-
        binemia may occur in patients re-
        ceiving nitrate or lidocaine therapy.
        Pulse oximetry also reveals
        nothing about the patient’s partial
        pressure of arterial carbon dioxide
        (PaCO2) or ventilation status. Say,
        for example, a patient’s receiving a
        high percentage of supplemental
        oxygen by face mask for several
        hours after surgery. If the patient is
        too sedated to breathe effectively,
        PaCO2 may rise to a dangerous lev-
        el even though SaO2 may be near
        normal from the supplemental
        oxygen. So be sure to obtain base-

        line ABG values and recheck them
        periodically. 

        Factors that can reduce pulse
        oximetry accuracy
        Certain technical and patient vari-
        ables can reduce the accuracy of
        pulse oximetry. 
        • Technical variables: Motion arti-
        fact, ambient light, dark nail pol-

        ish, improperly placed sensors,
        and patient movement can cause
        inaccurate readings. Clinicians
        should try to control these vari-
        ables to the extent possible. 
        • Patient variables: Pulse oximetry
        is less accurate when SpO2 val-
        ues are below 70%, limiting its
        effectiveness in severely hypoxic
        patients. Values also may vary in

        Why the curve shifts
        The normal oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve (OHDC), shown here by the solid blue
        line, indicates that when the partial pressure of arterial oxygen (PaO2) is 40 mm Hg, oxy-
        gen saturation of hemoglobin (SaO2) is 75%. At the tissue or capillary level, a PaO2 of 40
        mm Hg is normal. At this point, about 25% of the oxygen carried on hemoglobin from
        the tissues to the lungs has been unloaded and used at the tissue level. Much of the
        oxygen still remains on the hemoglobin molecule, indicating an oxygen reserve isn’t
        normally used at the tissue level. However, this reserve is available when extra oxygen
        is needed, as during strenuous exercise or high metabolic demand. 
        Conditions that alter hemoglobin’s affinity for oxygen can shift the OHDC to the
        right or left. 
        • A shift to the right (dotted purple line) decreases hemoglobin’s affinity for oxygen for
        a given PaO2 value, and the SaO2 value decreases below normal. Hemoglobin releas-
        es oxygen to the tissues more readily in an effort to keep tissues well-oxygenated
        (because oxygen demand is higher than normal). Causes of a shift to the right in-
        clude increased body temperature, acidosis, exercise, and elevated 2,3-diphospho-
        glycerate (2,3-DPG) or partial pressure of arterial carbon dioxide ( PaCO2) levels. 
        • A shift to the left (dotted green line) increases hemoglobin’s affinity for oxygen. It 
        can result from increased blood pH, decreased body temperature, or reduced 2,3-
        DPG or PaCO2 levels. In a leftward shift, less oxygen is released to the tissues but
        more oxygen is bound to hemoglobin in the lungs; the SaO2 value is higher than
        normal for a given PaO2 value.

        Pulse oximetry values in the context
        of the curve 
        Understanding how to use pulse
        oximetry in the context of your pa-
        tient’s OHDC can improve out-
        comes. Used correctly, pulse ox- 
        imetry gives an overall indication
        of a patient’s oxygenation status
        and promotes early intervention for
        high-risk patients. It also allows
        early recognition of conditions that
        increase tissue demand for oxygen,
        helping to ensure that the patient’s
        oxygen supply (hemoglobin satura-
        tion) meets demands. 
        Keep the following key princi-
        ples in mind when caring for pa-
        tients like Mrs. Glenn—those with
        underlying lung disease who’ve
        suffered an acute respiratory insult
        that puts them at risk for impaired
        gas exchange.
        • After assessing the patient’s res-
        piratory status and determining
        that the pulse oximeter is func-
        tioning properly, visualize the
        spot on the OHDC where the
        SpO2 value
        would line
        up with
        the

        PaO2 value. Is this spot at the
        flat part or the steep part of the
        curve? 
        • When the pulse oximeter’s low
        alarm goes off, don’t assume
        you need to start giving oxygen
        or increase the oxygen flow. As-
        sess the patient, not the ma-
        chine: Is the patient in respirato-
        ry distress? Check the oxygen
        supply: Is the oxygen tubing
        kinked? Is the oximeter applied
        properly? Does the patient have
        a disease or condition that in-
        creases oxygen demand, such as
        fever, acidosis, or infection? If
        so, decreasing SpO2 values may
        indicate the need to contact the
        physician for further orders, in
        addition to increasing the oxy-
        gen flow.
        • If the pulse oximetry value is
        within a normal range, don’t as-
        sume the patient is adequately
        oxygenated. Instead, assess res-

        piratory status,
        especially if the
        patient’s receiv-
        ing supplemental
        oxygen. Is the pa-
        tient breathing ade-
        quately? Because of compensa-
        tory mechanisms, good SpO2
        values may give false reassur-
        ance despite deterioration in the
        patient’ respiratory status. For
        example, patients in near respi-
        ratory failure may be hyperventi-
        lating, resulting in respiratory al-
        kalosis. This causes the OHDC
        to shift to the left, with more he-
        moglobin hanging on to oxygen
        instead of releasing it at the tis-
        sue level where it’s needed. 
        • Patients with similar SpO2 values
        don’t necessarily have the same
        total oxygen content in their
        blood. Suppose, for instance, Mr.
        M and Mr. R both have SpO2 val-
        ues of 97%, but Mr. M’s hemo-
        globin value is 15 g/dL, whereas
        Mr. R’s hemoglobin value is 8
        g/dL. In this case, oxygen-carry-
        ing capacity is greater in Mr M
        than in Mr. R, who may be
        showing signs of hypoxia. 
        • Interpret values in light of the
        patient’s overall condition. Pa-
        tients with chronic disease, such
        as chronic obstructive pulmo-
        nary disease (COPD), may func-
        tion adequately despite lower
        SpO2 values. Be sure to check
        the patient’s baseline ABG and
        pulse oximetry values, watching
        for trends. Also remember that
        PaO2 values normally decrease
        with age. Elderly patients typi-
        cally try to compensate for a
        low PaO2 value with a right-
        ward shift of the curve. But 
        this shift doesn’t completely
        compensate for the hypoxic
        changes and hypercapnia that
        come with aging. As a result,
        many older adults have de-
        creased activity tolerance. 
        • Collaborate with other profes-
        sionals involved in the patient’s
        care. Review the physician’s or-

        How 2,3-DPG affects
        the curve
        A phosphate found in the blood, 2,3-
        diphosphoglycerate (2,3-DPG) forms
        when red blood cells break down
        glucose to make adenosine triphos-
        phate. It decreases hemoglobin’s
        affinity for oxygen, promoting oxy-
        gen release in the tissues. 
        Some hormones, such as thyrox-
        ine, human growth hormone, epi-
        nephrine, and testosterone, increase
        2,3-DPG production and cause the
        oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve
        (OHDC) to shift to the right. Also, 2,3-
        DPG levels are higher in people liv-
        ing in high altitudes. As blood cells
        age, 2,3-DPG levels decrease, causing
        oxygen to bind tightly to hemoglo-
        bin and the OHDC to shift to the left.

        monitoring needed and specific
        protocols to follow. Consult with
        the respiratory therapist about
        proper pulse oximetry alarm set-

        with evidence-based practice
        guidelines for using pulse

        Clinical scenario revisited
        Mrs. Glenn’s pulse oximetry values
        continue to remain low, in the up-
        per 80% range. Her vital signs are
        unchanged. The physician calls
        with orders to obtain a urine cul-
        ture and start another I.V. antibi-
        otic. The nurse clamps the catheter
        to obtain the culture, but when she
        returns to collect the culture, she
        sees that only scant urine has been
        collected. 
        Mrs. Glenn remains alert but
        seems a bit restless. The nurse helps
        her to the chair to eat dinner.
        Twenty minutes later, she walks by
        and sees Mrs. Glenn slumped over
        in her chair and unresponsive. She
        calls for help to get her back to bed.
        Although the nurse
        attempts oral
        suctioning, the
        patient re-
        mains unre-
        sponsive. 
        Because
        Mrs. Glenn
        has “do not re-
        suscitate” orders,
        no further interven-
        tions are taken. The nurse
        calls the patient’s husband. When
        he arrives 30 minutes later, he tells
        the nurse, “I know you gave her
        good care and probably didn’t
        know she was going to die, but I
        would have liked to have been here
        when it happened.” 
        Later, the nurse reflects on her
        experience with Mrs. Glenn. She re-
        alizes she missed or ignored clues

        of quickly developing hypoxia. Al-
        though Mrs. Glenn was a COPD
        patient and thus her pulse oxime-
        try values were lower than normal,
        the nurse didn’t carefully review
        her ABG values and previous pulse
        oximetry values. If she had re-
        viewed these in light of the OHDC,
        she might have realized the SpO2
        decrease from 91% to 88% placed
        Mrs. Glenn at the steep part of the
        curve. Her estimated PaO2 would
        have been lower than 60 mm Hg.
        As her PaO2 continued to drop, her
        SpO2 value would have fallen rap-
        idly. Getting her up to eat in-
        creased her oxygen demands and
        contributed to further SpO2 lower-
        ing. Her increased pulse and res-
        piratory rates and decreased blood
        pressure and urinary output also
        indicated worsening hypoxia. 

        Pulse oximetry is used in a wide
        range of care settings to assess
        oxygenation status. But it must be
        correlated with the OHDC to get a
        full picture of the patient’s condi-

        tion. Correlat-
        ing SpO2 with
        PaO2 values
        provides valu-
        able clues
        about the bal-
        ance between
        oxygen supply
        and demand. When
        combined with astute assessment,
        understanding this relationship 
        can lead to earlier detection of
        oxygenation problems and allow
        prompt intervention. Ignoring or
        misinterpreting the relationship
        between SpO2 and PaO2 can lead
        to disastrous consequences for
        vulnerable patients, such as Mrs.
        Glenn. O

11.2. Lecture: Arterial Blood Gas Analysis
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////// 

The following lecture will teach you how to thoughtfully analyze arterial blood gases, and how that analysis can impact your PT decision making when treating a patient with pulmonary disease.

.('PT 2026_Mod 7_Arterial Blood Gases.pdf')

Cardiopulmonary PT 1 

Arterial Blood Gas (ABG) Analysis

Department of Physical Therapy 




.Arterial Blood Gases (ABGs)
• Tool to determine the effectiveness of alveolar ventilation 
• Examines acid –base balance (pH), ventilation (CO2), and 
oxygenation levels (O2)
• Acid-base balance must be maintained for normal cellular functions 
to occur
• Disturbances in this system can occur due to respiratory or 
metabolic dysfunction


.Terminology 1
    PaO2 (Po2)
    • partial pressure of dissolved 
    o2 in plasma (80-100 mmHg)

    PaCo2 (PO2)
    • partial pressure of dissolved 
    co2 in plasma (35-45 mmHg)

    Arterial pH 
    • measure of acidity or alkalinity 
    of the blood (7.35-7.45)
    • Inversely proportional to 
    number of H+ ions in the 
    blood

    HCO3
    • level bicarbonate in the blood 
    (22-28 mEq/liter)

    Reported as
    • pH/PaCO2/PaO2/HCO3


.Terminology 2
    Hypoxemia
    • PaO2<normal

    Hyperoxemia
    • PaO2>normal

    Hypocarbic
    • PaCO2<normal

    Hypercarbic
    • PaCO2>normal

    Hypoxia
    • SpO2<95%

    Acidemia
    • pH < 7.35
    • Acidosis – process 
    that causes acidemia

    Alkalemia
    • pH>7.45
    • Alkalosis – process 
    that causes alkalemia

.('')
    | Table 10-5 Normal ranges (±2 SD) for arterial blood gas values
    |--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    |                  | pH           | Pco₂ (mm Hg)   | Po₂ (mm Hg) | HCO₃⁻    | BE    | % SAT |
    | Normal value     | 7.40         | 40             | 97          | 24       | 0     | 97%   |
    | Normal range     | 7.35 to 7.45 | 35 to 45       | >80-100     | 22 to 28 | ±2    | >95%  |
                                                         HR = 60-100  RR = 12-20

.Regulation of pH
    Kidneys
    Excrete excess hydrogen (H+) ions in the 
    proximal tubule to reduce acidity of body
    Excrete Excess HCO3 ions if body too 
    alkaline or retain HCO3 if too acidic
    Could perform these measures to counter 
    respiratory acidosis or alkalosis

    Lungs
    Increase in PaCO2 increases acidity of 
    blood, as sensed by the medulla, therefore 
    increasing ventilation to blow off CO2 to 
    bring blood back to normal Ph
    Could also increase ventilation to counter 
    metabolic acidosis (or increased H+ 
    retention)


.Acid-Base Imbalance
    • Respiratory and metabolic disorders can cause states of 
    alkalemia or acidemia
    • What is the primary process?
    • Respiratory system (respiratory acidosis or alkalosis)
    • Metabolic system (metabolic acidosis or alkalosis)


.Compensated vs Uncompensated
    • Acid – base imbalances can be compensated OR 
    uncompensated
    • Uncompensated:
    • if the nonprimary system fails to compensate for the primary 
    system, the disorder is then referred to as uncompensated 
    (indicated by a continued high or low pH)
    • Compensated: 
    • pH return to normal by the nonprimary system


.Some Examples of Causes of Acid Base Imbalances
    Respiratory Acidosis
        • COPD
        • Sedation
        • Head Trauma
        • Drug overuse
        • CNS disorders
        • Chest wall trauma

    Respiratory Alkalosis
        • Pulmonary Embolism
        • Pregnancy
        • Anxiety
        • CHF (with pulmonary edema)
        • ARDS
        • Sedation 

    Metabolic Acidosis
        • Lactic acidosis
        • Ketoacidosis associated with:
            • Diabetes
            • Starvation
            • Alcoholism 
            • Chronic Diarrhea 

    Metabolic Alkalosis
        • Excessive Vomiting
        • NG suction
        • Diuretics
        • Hypokalemia 
        • Excessive antacid ingestion 
        • Administration of HCO3


.Assessing Arterial Blood Gases 1
• How to determine if it is respiratory or metabolic of origin
• Examine the pH
• If due to respiratory issued examine the PCO2 or PO2
• If due to metabolic issues examine the HCO3
• HCO3 is a basic molecule
• PCO2 is an acidic molecule


.Assessing Arterial Blood Gases 2
• If pH change is due to primary respiratory dysfunction
• Low pH, high PaCO2 is respiratory acidosis
• High pH, low PaCO2 is respiratory alkalosis
• If pH change is due to primary metabolic dysfunction
• Low pH and low HCO3 indicates metabolic acidosis
• High pH and high HCO3 indicates metabolic alkalosis


.Determining the Primary System/Process
    |--------------------------------------------
    |                      | pH | PaCO2  | HCO3
    |----------------------|----|--------|-------
    |Respiratory Acidosis  |  ↓ | ↑      | normal
    |----------------------|----|--------|-------
    |Respiratory Alkalosis | ↑  | ↓      | normal
    |----------------------|----|--------|-------
    |Metabolic Acidosis    | ↓  | normal | ↓
    |----------------------|----|--------|-------
    |Metabolic Alkalosis   | ↑  | normal | ↑
    |--------------------------------------------


.Metabolic Compensation 
• To determine if the patient’s primary respiratory process has 
been compensated by the renal system examine HCO3
• High HCO3 in respiratory acidosis indicates compensated 
respiratory acidosis
• Low HCO3 in respiratory alkalosis indicates compensated 
respiratory alkalosis


.Respiratory Compensation
• To determine if the patient’s primary metabolic process has 
been compensated by the respiratory system examine 
PaCO2
• Low PaCO2 in metabolic acidosis indicates compensated metabolic 
acidosis
• High PaCO2 in metabolic alkalosis indicates compensated 
metabolic alkalosis


.Determining Compensatory Status
    Fully Compensated States
                          pH                         PaCO2 HCO3
    Respiratory Acidosis  Normal, but closer to 7.35 ↑     ↑
    Respiratory Alkalosis Normal, but closer to7.45  ↓     ↓
    Metabolic Acidosis    Normal, but closer to 7.35 ↓     ↓
    Metabolic Alkalosis   Normal, but closer to 7.45 ↑     ↑


.Partial Compensation
• This can occur when the compensatory system kicks in, but 
the pH has not changed yet
• You will see an abnormal pH with abnormal respiratory and 
metabolic ABG:
• pH 7.32, pCO2 68, PO2 80, HCO3 29
• Low pH, high CO2, High HCO3 = partially compensated respiratory acidosis


.Determining Partially Compensatory Status
    Partially Compensated States
                          pH PaCo2 HCO3
    Respiratory Acidosis  ↓  ↑     ↑
    Respiratory Alkalosis ↑  ↓     ↓
    Metabolic Acidosis    ↓  ↓     ↓
    Metabolic Alkalosis   ↑  ↑     ↑


.Respiratory Examples
    Uncompensated 
    Respiratory 
    Acidosis 
        pH 7.30 (low)
        PaO2 96 (normal)
        PaCO2 58 (high)
        HCO3 22 (normal)

    Compensated 
    Respiratory 
    Acidosis 
        pH 7.38 (normal)
        PaO2 96 (normal)
        PaCO2 58 (high)
        HCO3 31 (high)

    Uncompensated 
    Respiratory 
    Alkalosis 
        pH 7.50 (high)
        PaO2 90 (normal)
        PaCO2 30 (low)
        HCO3 22 (normal)

    Compensated 
    Respiratory 
    Alkalosis 
        pH 7.43 (normal)
        PaO2 90 (normal)
        PaCO2 30 (low)

11.3. Name the Primary Process Activity
    (See also: 'ANKI::7.5. Activity - Name the Primary Process')
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

In this activity you will be presented with four values: pH, PO2, PCO2, HCO3 and determine what the primary process is:
    normal
    respiratory acidosis
    respiratory alkalosis
    metabolic acidosis
    metabolic alkalosis

------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1. pH 7.3, PO2 96, PCO2 37, HCO3 12
    Metabolic acidosis
    Respiratory acidosis
    Respiratory alkalosis
    Metabolic alkalosis
    Normal

    Metabolic acidosis
    This is metabolic acidosis due to the low pH at 7.3 and low HCO3 at 12, while the respiratory numbers are WNL. This indicates a primary metabolic process, which may occur in a patient who is in diabetic ketoacidosis.


2. pH 7.56, PO2 88, PCO2 20, HCO3 22
    Metabolic acidosis
    Respiratory alkalosis
    Normal
    Respiratory acidosis
    Metabolic alkalosis

    Respiratory alkalosis
    This is respiratory alkalosis due to the high pH at 7.56 and low PaCO2 at 20, while the metabolic numbers are WNL. This indicates a primary respiratory process and may be seen in a patient with a restrictive condition like ARDS who is hyperventilating.

3. Ph 7.49, PO2 80, PCO2 40, HCO3 38
    Respiratory alkalosis
    Respiratory acidosis
    Metabolic alkalosis
    Metabolic acidosis
    Normal

    Metabolic alkalosis
    This is metabolic Alkalosis due to the high pH at 7.49 and high HCO3 at 38, while the respiratory numbers are WNL. This indicates a primary metabolic process and may occur in a patient who has had excessive antacid ingestion.

4. Ph 7.22, PO2 96, PCO2 37, HCO3 10
    Respiratory alkalosis
    Normal
    Metabolic acidosis
    Metabolic alkalosis
    Respiratory acidosis

    Metabolic acidosis
    This is metabolic acidosis due to the low pH at 7.22 and low HCO3 at 10, while the respiratory numbers are WNL. This indicates a primary metabolic process.

    Why metabolic?
    Ph 7.22, PO2 96, PCO2 37, HCO3 10 - uncompensated metabolic acidosis - low pH, low HCO3
    to change this to compensated metabolic acidosis you would see the following number  Ph 7.35, PO2 96, PCO2 25, HCO3 10 - normal pH, low CO2, low HCO3 (lower CO2 as the respiratory system works to blow off an acidic molecule to compensate for the lower basic HCO3)

5. Ph 7.29, PO2 88, PCO2 56, HCO3 22
    Metabolic alkalosis
    Metabolic acidosis
    Normal
    Respiratory alkalosis
    Respiratory acidosis

    Respiratory acidosis
    Respiratory acidosis due to low pH (7.29) and high PaCO2 (56), metabolic numbers are WNL. A primary respiratory process, which may occur during a COPD exacerbation where a patient retains high levels of PaCO2 and the PaO2 may also decline.

6. Ph 7.5, PO2 120, PCO2 45, HCO3 22
    Metabolic acidosis
    Normal
    Respiratory acidosis
    Respiratory alkalosis
    Metabolic alkalosis

    Respiratory alkalosis
    This is respiratory alkalosis due to the high pH at 7.5 and high at PaO2 at 120, while the metabolic numbers are WNL. This indicates a primary respiratory process and may be seen in a patient who is being over oxygenated with supplemental O2.

7. Ph 7.4, PO2 90, PCO2 40, HCO3 22
    Metabolic acidosis
    Respiratory acidosis
    Normal
    Respiratory alkalosis
    Metabolic alkalosis

    Normal
    All numbers are in the normal ranges.

11.5. Lecture: Relationship Between Oxygen Saturation and Partial Pressure of Oxygen
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

In the following lecture you will learn the relationship between oxygen saturation, or SpO2, and partial pressure of oxygen, or PaO2. This relationship will be described by the oxyhemoglobin disassociation curve and how that relationship can impact patient care. 

('PT 2026_Mod 7_Relationship Between Oxygen Saturation and Partial Pressure of Oxygen.pdf')
    Cardiopulmonary PT 1 

    Relationship Between Oxygen Saturation and Partial Pressure of Oxygen 

    Department of Physical Therapy 


    .Relationship Between SpO2 and PaO2
    • Oxyhemoglobin Dissociation 
    Curve (OHDC)
    • How readily O2 will bind and 
    unload from hemoglobin
    • Affected by PaCO2, body 
    temperature & blood pH
    • PaO2 is the “pushing” force for 
    loading O2 onto HgB


    .Oxyhemoglobin Dissociation Curve (OHDC) 1
    • The Horizontal Portion


    .Oxyhemoglobin Dissociation Curve (OHDC) 2
    • The Steep Lower Portion


    .Connecting Pulse Ox and PaO2 Readings 
    • ABG is GOLD standard to 
    obtaining  PaO2
    • Small changes in SpO2 can 
    indicate larger shifts in PaO2 
    status
    • SpO2<90%
    • May be red flag as it associates 
    with a PaO2 of 50-60mmHg based 
    on the curve
    • May not be loading O2 onto HgB 
    at a level able to oxygenate the 
    tissues and unload oxygen 
    adequately 


    .SpO2 and PaO2 
        Oxygen Saturation (SpO2 %)  Oxygen Partial Pressure (PaO2 mmHg)
        97-99                       99-100

    .Shifting the Curve
        ('')


    .Limitations of Pulse Oximetry 1
    • CANNOT tell you a patient’s:
    • actual HgB level 
    • non-functional HgB
    • PaCO2 levels


    .Limitations of Pulse Oximetry 2
    • Poor Accuracy:
    • Technical variables (nail polish, ambient light, improper sensor 
    placement)
    • SpO2 < 70% less effective in true readings
    • Poor perfusion status
    • Hypotension, arrythmias, heart failure 
    • Vasoconstrictive conditions
    • Sickle cell anemia, hypothermia, smoking, medications


    .Clinical Relevance 1
    • Assess Respiratory Status
    • Determine SpO2
    • Find the spot on the curve that meets that SpO2 reading
    • Is this spot on the steep part of the curve?


    .Clinical Relevance 2
    • If the reading is LOW DO NOT ASSUME O2 is needed, assess 
    the patient
    • Are they in respiratory distress?
    • Is their current tubing kinked?
    • Was the SpO2 device applied adequately?
    • Does the patient have a disease or condition that may require 
    increase in O2 demand? (infection, fever, acidosis)


    .Should I Use Supplemental O2?
        Are they hyperventilating 
        and still on supplemental 
        O2?
            • Example: patient in 
            respiratory failure may he 
            hyperventilating to blow of 
            CO2 and bring in more O2 
            leading to rise in PaO2 
            and reduced PCO2 = 
            respiratory alkalosis
            • O2 binds to HgB with 
            increased affinity and not 
            unloading at the tissue 
            level

        .Patients with similar SpO2 
        levels may not have same 
        total O2 content
            • Example: Patient 1 and 2 
            have SpO2 of 97% But 
            patient 2 is hypoxic, why?
            • Patient #1 HgB of 15 
            dg/dL
            • Patient #2 HgB 8 dg/dL

        .Patient Condition
            • COPD patients function at 
            low levels of SpO2 
            • Elderly patients & hypoxia 
            and hypercapnia that 
            come with aging


    .Clinical Example
    • Before beginning an intervention with a patient, a therapist 
    reviews the chart by obtaining ABG values and looking over 
    their previously completed evaluation.  
    • During therapy session, the patient becomes short of breath, 
    the clinician remembers nothing from their evaluation that 
    would indicate a pulmonary pathology, and takes a pulse ox. 
    The pulse ox is at 98%, but the patient appears in respiratory 
    distress.
    • Why could this patient short of breath?

11.6. ABGs & Oxygen Status Self-Assessment
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////// (!!Q)

.
    Which of the following conditions BEST describes metabolic acidosis?

    Low bicarbonate level (HCO3–)
    Alveolar hypoventilation
    High bicarbonate level (HCO3–)
    High partial pressure CO2 (PaCO2)

    Low bicarbonate level (HCO3–)
    A low HCO3- produces metabolic acidosis. A high PaCO2 is respiratory acidosis. Alveolar hypoventilation is respiratory acidosis. High HCO3– is metabolic alkalosis.

.
    Which of the following organs is responsible for the regulation of the major blood base, bicarbonate (HCO3–)?

    Lungs
    Liver
    Kidneys
    Heart

    Kidneys
    The kidneys are also primarily responsible for regulation of the major blood base––bicarbonate (HCO3-). Bicarbonate is responsible for 60% to 90% of the extracellular buffering of nonvolatile acids.

.
    Which of the following conditions BEST describes respiratory alkalosis?

    Low bicarbonate level (HCO3–)
    Hypocapnia
    Low partial pressure CO2 (PaCO2)
    High bicarbonate level (HCO3–)

    Low partial pressure CO2 (PaCO2)
    Low partial pressure CO2 would result in respiratory alkalosis due to the loss of CO2 or acid elevating the pH value. High HCO3– leads to metabolic alkalosis. Hypocapnia is metabolic alkalosis. Low HCO3- is metabolic acidosis.

.
    Which of the following conditions would contribute to reduced reliability of a pulse oximetry reading?

    Poor peripheral circulation
    Nail polish
    Decrease in Hgb levels
    All of the options

    All of the options
    The pulse oximetry readings should not always be taken at face value by the therapist. Readings can be distorted from a variety of sources from poor circulation and artifact to hemoglobin levels.

.
    Which statement regarding pulse oximetry is correct?

    SpO2 of 70% is indicative of a PAO2 level of 60mmHg.
    An acceptable pulse ox reading is 85%.
    Pulse ox is useful for determining a patient’s ventilatory status.
    Pulse oximetry reveals nothing about the patient’s PaCO2 status.

    Pulse oximetry reveals nothing about the patient’s PaCO2 status.
    A pulse ox reading indicates how much O2 is loaded onto HgB and has no relationship to PaCO2. A patient may have high PCO2 levels that are getting to dangerous levels, but SpO2 may appear near normal without revealing the patient is in a hypercapnic state

.
    The steep or lower part of the OHDC ↓ (under the “knee”) represents: (!!E)
    ('') ← See ANKI

    Oxygen loading onto HgB in the lungs
    Oxygen exiting HgB in the lungs
    Oxygen released from HgB to the capillaries at the tissue level
    Oxygen unloading onto HgB from the capillaries at the tissue level

    Oxygen released from HgB to the capillaries at the tissue level
    Levels of 40-60 mmHg the oxygen saturation (SpO2) will be <80%, a patient will demonstrate signs and symptoms of hypoxia ↓ (Hypoxia SpO2 < 95%). Adding supplemental O2 at this level will create larger/significant increase in SpO2, as even a small increase in PaO (Pressure of Oxygen (PaO2) (80-100 mmHg)) will increase SpO2.

.
    A patient has been admitted to the hospital due to complaints of difficulty breathing. His ABGs report pH = 7.20↓, PaCO2 = 63.4↑, PaO2 = 51↓, HCO3– = 30↑; PFTs report TLC = 120% predicted, VC = 115% predicted, RV = 130% predicted, FEV1 = 48% predicted. A chest x-ray indicates infiltrates in the right lower lobe. Which of the following diagnostic conclusions BEST summarizes this patient’s condition?

    a. The patient has a lung infection, acute respiratory alkalosis, and mild restrictive pulmonary disease.
    b. The patient has a lung infection, acute metabolic acidosis, and mild chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
    c. The patient has pneumonia, acute metabolic alkalosis, and severe restrictive pulmonary disease.
    d. The patient has pneumonia, acute respiratory acidosis, and severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

    d. The patient has pneumonia, acute respiratory acidosis, and severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
    This patient has pneumonia (infiltrates on chest x-ray), acute respiratory acidosis with partial compensation causing him to develop respiratory failure, and severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (noted by the elevated lung volumes from PFTs).

Oxygen titration: Physical Therapy Role in Oxygen Titration when Treating Patients
INSTRUCTIONS
Please carefully read the following stance regarding the role of the Physical Therapist and titrating of supplemental oxygen. After you read this, please consider the questions for class discussion. 
PHYSICAL THERAPIST AND TITRATING OF SUPPLEMENTAL OXYGEN
In APTA's Guide to Physical Therapist Practice, supplemental oxygen is listed as a procedural intervention within the scope of physical therapist practice under “Prescription, Application, and, as Appropriate, Fabrication of Devices and Equipment (supportive device) to improve ventilation and respiration/gas exchange.”

However, confusion exists as to the physical therapist's role in the administration of oxygen when prescribed by a physician. Specifically, APTA members have reported that their authority has been questioned by managers or other providers when performing tasks such as disconnecting the oxygen from the wall unit and re-attaching it to a cylinder or adjusting the oxygen level within the parameters set by the physician. This resource is intended to assist in answering questions and provide resources for information on issues related to oxygen administration during physical therapy interventions.
APTA is unaware of any regulations that prohibit the use of oxygen for patient/client management if it is prescribed and if parameters set by the physician are maintained. Physicians often specify the oxygen flow rate in their orders. Any deviations from prescribed dosages require an updated order from the physician under these circumstances. Alternatively, physicians may prescribe maintenance of a specific oxygen saturation (SpO2) level during rest and activity (eg, "maintain SpO2 > ____%"). In these situations, physical therapists may titrate the oxygen flow to maintain patients/clients at or above this threshold saturation value. Physical therapists discussing the oxygen needs of their patients/clients with physicians should request orders using an SpO2 threshold to ensure safety and effectiveness during physical activity and exercise.

1.	When considering a patient’s O2 status is SpO2 the most VALID measure of oxygenation?
2.	Consider a patient with COPD who is on 2L of supplemental oxygen and about to initiate performing a 6 MWT. At rest they are at 90% O2 saturation. As they begin to perform the test their O2 remains at 90%, but they report breathlessness. You increase the oxygen and they increase SpO2 to 96%, again remain breathless. Why could this be happening?
3.	Consider a patient with viral pneumonia who is on mechanical ventilation. They are receiving a large amount of oxygen, but their PaO2 and SpO2 remains unchanged, and they are still becoming more hypoxemic. Why is this happening? 
4.	With the knowledge PTs have on oxygen saturations, pressures and respiratory conditions should they be able to work freely in administering oxygen as needed during exercise interventions?

Question 1
A patient has the following arterial blood gas values: pH = 7.35, PaCO2 = 68, PaO2 = 80, and HCO3– = 30. Which of the following statements is the MOST accurate interpretation? 
Group of answer choices

Uncompensated metabolic acidosis
Uncompensated respiratory acidosis
Compensated metabolic acidosis
Compensated respiratory acidosis

Compensated respiratory acidosis
    The pH is on the low end of normal and a high PaCO2 is persevered concluding that the state is respiratory acidosis, but it is compensated because HCO3 is high and working to buffer the system.

  Compensated metabolic acidosis

    El hcO3 està alt perque acaba de compensar a la acidesa respiratoria.

  Uncompensated respiratory alkalosis

Question 9
Which of the following statements regarding pulse oximetry or SpO2 is true:

  It cannot tell you the total HgB levels
  The most accurate reading is that below 70%
  Nail polish allows for improved readings
  It can assist in knowing PaCO2 levels

It cannot tell you the total HgB levels
    SpO2 readings detect the amount of HgB attached to RBC, therefore they are unable to give you true reading of total HgB available for attachment.

Question 10
A patient with COVID-19 is on a ventilator due to associated ARDS, and this patient is having continuous blood draws to ensure ABGs are obtained to better understand ventilatory status and need for ventilator setting adjustment. You are called into to start PT, and work on proning the patient. You initiate your session with a thorough chart review. You are just alerted that a new ABG reading has been reported, and which of the following partial pressure of  values would indicate holding your PT session due to ventilator failure and warrant you to contact the medical team immediately? 

  Partial pressure CO2 = 50
  Partial pressure CO2 = 35
  Partial pressure CO2 = 40
  Partial pressure CO2 = 45

Partial pressure CO2 = 50
    A patient who is found to have a partial pressure CO2 of 50 mm Hg or greater indicates the condition of ventilator failure

Question 5
When considering the oxyhemoglobin disassociation curve, a shift to the right can indicate all of the following except: 
Group of answer choices

HgB will release more oxygen to the tissues
An increase in body temperature due to exercise
An SpO2 that will decrease below normal
HgB holding on tightly to oxygen

HgB holding on tightly to oxygen
    The curve will shift as certain factors can alter HgB’s affinity of O2. These conditions will shift the curve right or left. A shift to the right, indicated by the purple dotted line in the figure, represents a decrease in HgB’s affinity for O2 at a given PaO2 value, and SpO2 decreases below normal. HgB releases O2 more readily to keep tissues well-oxygenated as the demand for oxygen is much higher then normal. Causes for a rightward shift would include an inc body temp, acidosis, exercise, and an inc PaCO2. A shift to the Left, indicated by the green dotted line in the figure, represents an increase in HgB’s affinity for O2 at a given PaO2 with less O2 being released to tissue, but more O2 bound to HgB leading to a SpO2 reading that is higher for a given PaO2 Causes of a leftward shift are a dec in body temp or states of alkalosis. 

Question 6
Patient 1 has a SpO2 of 97% and a HgB of 8.0, while patient 2 has a SpO2 92% and a HgB of 15. Which patient would have the reduced exercise tolerance in terms of possible shortness of breath or muscle fatigue.  
Group of answer choices

Patient 2
Patient 1

Patient 1
    Patient 1 may be at 97%, but with only 8.0 HgB they have less ability to carry oxygen to tissues vs patient 2 who has a normal HgB but maybe a little bit lower of SpO2.

compensated metabolic alkalosis
uncompensated respiratory alkalosis
uncompensated metabolic alkalosis
uncompensated metabolic acidosis

uncompensated respiratory acidosis
    pH 7.30 (low), PaO2 96 (normal), PaCO2 58 (high), HCO3 22 (normal) leading to an uncompensated respiratory acidosis.

Question 9

    The first step is to examine the pH and determine if it is high meaning alkalotic or low meaning acidic. Unit 1: Pulmonary Diagnostic Testing
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////


////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
12.0. Module Introduction
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

In this module you will explore pulmonary diagnostic testing. This module will cover clinical laboratory studies as they relate to the pulmonary system, other critical pulmonary lab values along with diagnostic testing and imaging modalities that can give the medical team, including the PT, a clear objective information about a patient’s current pulmonary status. You will discover how pulmonary function testing, imaging results and other various testing can impact a PT treatment and plan of care, and how to utilize those results to modify exercise for an individual with a pulmonary condition.  In Unit 2 of this lab you will review your cardiopulmonary examination techniques in order to prepare for the upcoming lab and comp check in 1B. 

Learning Objectives
By the end of this week, you will be able to: 

Interpret the results of pulmonary diagnostic tests including objective information derived from laboratory, diagnostic, and procedure data.
Create a physical therapy treatment plan based on degree of abnormality of laboratory values and provide rationale for postponing physical therapy intervention when a patient has critical pulmonary findings.
Determine modifications and appropriateness for exercise based on pulmonary lab values and diagnostic testing.
Analyze lab values that may change based on the inter-relationship of the pulmonary system with other bodily systems.

    Cardiopulmonary PT 1 

    Pulmonary Diagnostic Imaging 

    .Pulmonary Diagnostic Testing 
        Imaging, tests and procedures provide the physical therapists with valuable information
        Physical therapists must have a fundamental understanding of pulmonary testing to aide in clinical decision making 


    .Chest Imaging
        • Predominant diagnostic test to determine anatomic abnormalities and pathological processes within the chest


    .Chest Radiograph 1
        • Static view of chest anatomy
        • Air, fat, water, bone
            • Air is dark to bone, which is white on radiograph
        • Standard chest radiograph taken in two views
            • posteroanterior (PA) and left lateral 
            • Other views: decubitus, lordotic, oblique, AP at bedside
        • What is being assessed?
            • Thorax, lungs, heart, hila, lung fields


    .Chest Radiograph 2
        Radiograph produced is referred to as a roentgenogram


    .What is being assessed? 1
        Bones and Soft Tissues - Thorax, ribs, diaphragm

        ('')

        • “Bat Wing” infiltrate
        ('')

        • Acute vs chronic changes in chest radiographic imaging and treatment planning 


    .Patient Case Example
        Two chest radiographs of a 77-year-old woman demonstrating rapid clearance of congestive heart failure.
            The initial chest radiograph ('')
            One day later and after diuresis, the chest radiograph ('')


    .A systematic approach for interpreting the chest radiograph
        • Assess the technical quality of the study.
        • Evaluate the location of all catheters, tubes, and hemodynamic support devices.
        • Assess the cardiovascular status of the patient.
        • Check for abnormal parenchymal opacities.
        • Look for pleural effusions.
        • Compare with the prior studies; does the patient look the same, better, or worse?


    .Computed Tomography (CT) Scan 
        • Digital chest radiography, involves narrow beam of x-rays moving across field of examination
        • Primarily used for diagnosis of tumors versus calcifications or nodules
        • Single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) 
        • tumors and in staging of malignancy
        • Helical CT 
        • pulmonary embolism (PE)
        ('')


    .Advantages and Disadvantages of CT
        Advantages
            • Much more sensitive
            • Evaluates: lungs, heart, mediastinum, pleura, chest wall, upper abdomen
            • Localizes disease 
            • Guidance of interventional procedures
            • Can detect occult pneumothorax or effusions
            • Evaluates chest tube placement
            • Can contribute new information
            • May detect unsuspected abnormalities
        Disadvantages
            • Risk of transporting patient out of the intensive care unit environment
            • Significant increased radiation
            • Risks of intravenous contrast (if given)


    .Pulmonary Arteriography
        • Emboli read as complete obstruction, intraluminal filling defects, or decrease in flow rate
        • Advantages
            • gold standard
        • Disadvantages
            • invasive, increased morbidity/mortality, associated with complications, time consuming, expensive
            • Due to disadvantages, imaging with CT has become more widely used
        ('')


    .Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)
        • Involves the interaction of 
        stimulated hydrogen nuclei 
        and strong magnetic field
        • Primarily indicated for 
        evaluation of chest wall 
        processes 
        • May be indicated in individuals 
        with an abnormal chest 
        radiograph that shows a 
        nodule or mass
        ('')


    .Ventilation and Perfusion (V/Q) Scans 1
        • Xenon gas is used to measure regional distribution of 
        ventilation in the lungs
        • Patient inhales the gas and holds breath while ventilation 
        scans are made over the lung field
        • To measure regional distribution of pulmonary blood flow in 
        the lungs, patient is injected intravenously with radioactive 
        iodine, then serial perfusion scans are made
        • V/Q scans are indicated to rule out pulmonary emboli

    .Ventilation and Perfusion (V/Q) Scans 2
        Multiple perfusion defects in left upper lobe and right midzone on perfusion 
            ('')
        scan. Normal ventilation scan.
            ('')
    

    .Bronchography
        • evaluation and management of some 
        congenital pulmonary anomalies as 
        well as some acquired diseasesof the 
        tracheobronchial tree
        • Bronchogram
        • Contrast bronchography 
        ('')

    .Bronchogram
        • X-Ray with Bronchiectasis 
        appearing as prominent, 
        thick bronchial markings in 
        the right paracardial region 
        of the lung (arrows).
        • Further testing with a 
        Bronchogram 
        demonstrating ectasia and 
        irregularity of the bronchi. 
        ('')

////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
12.3. Lecture: Other Pulmonary Testing
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

The following lecture will present cardiovascular diagnostic tests and procedures frequently used by medical professionals to stage and diagnose cardiac and vascular diseases. This lecture will review imaging, clinical testing, and other various procedures that the physical therapist must recognize and/or utilize when treating patients with cardiovascular conditions.

('PT 2026_Mod 7_Other Pulmonary Testing.pdf')
    Cardiopulmonary PT 1 

    Other Pulmonary Testing

    .Tests of Lung Volume and Capacity
        Simple spirometer testing
        Graphic tracing called a spirogram

    .Comparing Spirograms
        ('')


    .Review of PFT Interpretation (!!E)Fer una mnemo mirant el grafic més avall
        | Measurement                          | Obstructive     | Restrictive    |
        |--------------------------------------|-----------------|----------------|
        | Tidal volume (TV)                    | N or ↑          | N or ↓         |
        | Inspiratory capacity (IC)            | N or ↓          | N or ↓         |
        | Expiratory reserve volume (ERV)      | N or ↓          | N or ↓         |
        | Vital capacity (VC)                  | N or ↓          | ↓              |
        | Forced vital capacity (FVC)          | N or ↓          | ↓              |
        | Residual volume (RV)                 | N or ↑          | N or ↓         |
        | Functional residual capacity (FRC)   | N or ↑          | ↓              |
        | Forced expiratory volume in 1 (FEV₁) | ↓               | N              |

        Γ Use this image as a reference: 'Pulmonary Function Test General Clinical Signs of Obstructive Lung Disease.png


    .Blood Gas Analysis
        Crucial to assessment of problems related to:
            • acid–base balance
            • ventilation
            • oxygenation
        Typical report contains:
            • arterial pH
            • partial pressures of CO2, O2 (PCO2, PO2 )
            • oxygen saturation (SpO2)
            • bicarbonate concentration (HCO3)
            • base excess

   
    .ABG Ranges
        | Table 10-5 Normal ranges (±2 SD) for arterial blood gas values
        |--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
        |                  | pH           | Pco₂ (mm Hg)   | Po₂ (mm Hg) | HCO₃⁻    | BE    | % SAT |
        | Normal value     | 7.40         | 40             | 97          | 24       | 0     | 97%   |
        | Normal range     | 7.35 to 7.45 | 35 to 45       | >80         | 22 to 28 | ±2    | >95%  |


    .Blood Gas Analysis & PaCO2
        • PaCO2 directly reflects adequacy of alveolar ventilation 
            • Hyperventilation—PaCO2 <40 mm Hg ¿?< How can be this possible?
            • Hypoventilation—PaCO2 >40 mm Hg
            • Ventilatory failure—PaCO2 >50 mm Hg
        • To determine the nature and severity of the illness with accuracy, the relationship of arterial pH and arterial CO2 tension is assessed


    .Blood Gas Analysis & PaO2
        • Assessing oxygenation and hypoxemic status
            • Oxygenation status of a patient is assessed by determining the extent to which the observed PaO2 is above or below normal range
                • PaO2 = 60 to 80 mm Hg—mildly hypoxemic
                • PaO2 = 40 to 60 mm Hg—moderately hypoxemic
                • PaO2 = 40 mm Hg—severely hypoxemic


    .Blood Gas Analysis 1
        Kidneys
        • Excrete excess hydrogen (H+) 
        ions in the proximal tubule to 
        reduce acidity of body
        • Excrete Excess HCO3 ions if 
        body too alkaline 
        • Could perform these measures 
        to counter respiratory acidosis 
        (or increased co2 retention)

        Lungs
        • Increase in PaCo2 increases 
        acidity of blood, as sensed by 
        the medulla, therefore 
        increasing ventilation to blow off 
        co2 to bring blood back to 
        normal Ph
        • Could also increase ventilation 
        to counter metabolic acidosis 
        (or increased H+ retention)


    .Blood Gas Analysis 2
        • Clinical notes
            • ABGs are time dependent
            • In acute care, used to assess current situations
            • ABGs are repeated if ventilator modes or support change
            • Venous blood gases can provide status of pH and PaCO2


    .Pulse Oximetry 1
        • Measurement of oxyhemoglobin 
        saturation
        • Pulse oximeter
        • quick and accurate 
        measurement
        • Results O2 Hb%


    .Pulse Oximetry 2
        • How does it work?
            • Light emitting diode & detector 
        • For an accurate measure:
            • Check for a uniform pulse wave on the 
            plethysmograph when available


    .Organigrama ('SPO2 Organigrama.png')
        (!!E.Alg)Recoda que tot lo que siguen organigrames, hi ha que repasar-ho per al exàmen final


    .Hematological Tests
        • Hematological tests aid in the assessment of cardiopulmonary disease
            • Typical tests include ABGs, electrolyte analysis, complete blood cell counts, coagulation studies
        • Explore patient examples as related to pulmonary dysfunction: (!!)Preguntar a RUPERTA per a examples
            • Anemia
            • Polycythemia 
            • Leukocytosis 


    .Cytological Testing
        • Cytological tests are used to identify specific microorganisms that may cause disease
            • Sputum culture 
            • Blood culture

12.4. Pulmonary Dx Testing Self Assessment
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

1. On a chest radiograph, which of the following objects results in a dark image due to its low density?
    Air
    Bone
    Fat
    Water

    Air
    The principal objects shown on a chest radiograph are air, fat, water, tissue, and bone; Γ(no muscles). Air in the lungs has a very low density and thus allows greater x-ray penetration, resulting in a dark image on the radiograph––radiolucency.

2. Which of the following pathological conditions would MOST likely result in tracheal deviations on a chest radiograph?
    Pulmonary embolism
    Pneumothorax
    Pulmonary edema
    Patient is upright

    Pneumothorax
    Pathological conditions can result in tracheal deviations. For example, a large pneumothorax can push the trachea toward the contralateral side of the chest, or a massive atelectasis can pull the trachea toward the ipsilateral side of the chest.

3. From the list provided which of the following chest imaging techniques is considered the BEST diagnostic tool for determining the presence of a pulmonary embolus (PE)?
    Magnetic Resonance Imaging
    Ventilation Perfusion Scan
    Chest radiograph
    Computed Tomography

    Computed Tomography
        -CT scans are considered to have greater reliability than V/Q scans for diagnosis of PE. Angiography with CT is now considered the gold standard for diagnosis of PE.
            V/Q scans
                Why is it called a VQ scan?
                    -A VQ scan is short for Lung or Pulmonary Ventilation (V) and Perfusion (Q) Scans. It's an imaging test that measures air and blood flow in your lungs.

            Pulmonary Embolus (PE)
                -A pulmonary embolism (PE) occurs when a blood clot gets stuck in an artery in the lung, blocking blood flow to part of the lung. Blood clots most often start in the legs and travel up through the right side of the heart and into the lungs. This is called deep vein thrombosis (DVT).

.Which of the following spirometric or air volume measurements would serve to assist the clinicians in determining whether the patient presented with obstructive or restrictive pulmonary disease? (read carefully)
    Total lung capacity (TLC)
    Forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1)
    Maximal voluntary ventilation (MVV)
    Forced expiratory flow rate between 25% and 75% of FVC

    Total lung capacity (TLC)
        TLC has a distinct change, whereas FEV1, FEF 25–75, and MVV, would have similar changes for both obstructive and restrictive diseases or no change at all. Also, read carefully, as it asks for a volumetric measurement (TLC), and not a flow rate.

        Total lung capacity would be either normal or increased in obstructive disease and decreased in restrictive disease. TLC would have a distinct change, whereas the other answers, FEV1, FEF25–75, and MVV, would be noted to have similar changes for both obstructive and restrictive diseases or no change at all. Also, it is important to read the question carefully, as it asks for a volumetric measurement (TLC), and not a flow rate measurement (FEV1, FEF25–75, and MVV).

.A pulmonary diagnostic test was completed for a patient with pneumonia, and it was found that Staphylococcus aureus was the primary microorganism that needed to be treated with IV antibiotics. Which of the following tests made this discovery?
    Chest Xray
    Arterial blood draw
    Pulmonary Function Test
    Sputum Culture

    Sputum Culture
    A Sputum culture is a type of Cytological tests are used to identify specific microorganisms that may cause disease.

.A patient has been admitted to the hospital due to complaints of difficulty breathing. His ABGs report pH = 7.20, PaCO2 = 63.4, PaO2 = 51, HCO3– = 30; PFTs report TLC = 120% predicted, VC = 115% predicted, RV = 130% predicted, FEV1 = 48% predicted. A chest x-ray indicates infiltrates in the right lower lobe. Which of the following diagnostic conclusions BEST summarizes this patient’s condition?
    a. The patient has a lung infection, acute respiratory alkalosis, and mild restrictive pulmonary disease.
    b. The patient has a lung infection, acute metabolic acidosis, and mild chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
    c. The patient has pneumonia, acute metabolic alkalosis, and severe restrictive pulmonary disease.
    d. The patient has pneumonia, acute respiratory acidosis, and severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

    d. The patient has pneumonia, acute respiratory acidosis, and severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
    This patient has pneumonia (infiltrates on chest x-ray), acute respiratory acidosis with partial compensation causing him to develop respiratory failure, and severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (noted by the elevated lung volumes from PFTs).

12.7. Module 12 Quiz
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

Question 1
Which of the following abnormal findings would be MOST likely in a chest radiograph of a patient with moderate to severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?

  Tracheal deviation toward the contralateral side
  Opacification of the costophrenic angles
  Flattened hemidiaphragms
  Increased vascular markings

Flattened hemidiaphragms
The radiograph of a patient with moderate to severe COPD will show widened intercostal spaces, flattened hemidiaphragms, squared off costophrenic angles, and rib angles that approach 90 degrees.

Question 2
Which of the following abnormal findings would be MOST likely in a chest radiograph of a patient with pneumothorax?

  Tracheal deviation toward the opposite side
  Opacification of the costophrenic angles
  Flattened hemidiaphragms
  Tracheal deviation toward the same side

Tracheal deviation toward the opposite side
A massive pneumothorax can pull the trachea toward the opposite side of the chest due to the buildup of air in the pleural space. A massive collapse can cause for deviation to the same side.

Question 3
Which of the following changes in a chest radiograph would BEST indicate an acute change?
  
  Flattened diaphragms
  Interstitial thickening
  Abnormal lung volumes
  Fluffy infiltrates or effusions

Fluffy infiltrates or effusions
Acute changes in a chest radiograph would include fluffy infiltrates or increased opacity. Chronic changes include flattened diaphragms, changes in rib angle and intercostal spaces, abnormal lung volumes, and interstitial thickening. 

Question 6
A patient just underwent a pulmonary function test with a final report of increased total lung capacity. The physician orders a lung diagnostic testing procedure to see of the lungs are hyperinflated as related to the increased in total lung volume. Which of the following tests would he order?

  Ventilation perfusion scan
  Chest x-ray
  Bronchoscopy
  Cardiac catherization

    Chest x-ray
    Predominant diagnostic test to determine anatomic abnormalities and pathological processes within the chest, such as lung hyperinflation in COPD. 

Question 7
Which of the following chest radiograph views is the MOST common or standard routinely taken?

  Anteroposterior view taken at patient’s bedside
  Posteroanterior view and lateral view
  Oblique view in standing
  Decubitus view in supine, prone, or side lying

Posteroanterior view and lateral view
The standard chest radiograph is routinely taken in two views at near total lung capacity: (1) a posteroanterior view with the patient in the standing position and (2) a left lateral view.

Question 8
The hila comprising pulmonary blood vessels, bronchi, and group of lymph nodes are important areas to recognize when assessing a chest image, and this area is anatomically located at which of the following spinal levels?


  C7 to T1
  T2 to T3
  T4 to T5
  T8 to T9

T4 to T5
The hila, formed by the root of the lungs (comprising the pulmonary blood vessels, the bronchi, and a group of lymph nodes), is located at about the T4 to T5 level and appears as poorly defined areas of variable density in the medial part of the central portion of the lung. Knowledge of this area is important when assessing chest imaging.

Question 8
If a patient is exercising and you want to obtain a blood pressure, which of the following techniques would be appropriate to gauge exercise BP response? 
Group of answer choices

Obtaining systolic BP using the cuff and palpating the radial artery
Obtaining diastolic BP using the cuff and palpating radial artery
Obtaining radial heart rate and multiplying it by total peripheral resistance
Obtaining brachial heart rate, then radial heart rate and multiplying

Obtaining systolic BP using the cuff and palpating the radial artery

    This technique is appropriate for measuring exercise blood pressure for several reasons:

    1. Systolic blood pressure: During exercise, systolic blood pressure increases linearly with increasing workload. It's a key indicator of cardiovascular response to exercise.

    2. Use of cuff: The blood pressure cuff is still the standard tool for measuring blood pressure, even during exercise.

    3. Palpation method: Using palpation of the radial artery is a reliable method when auscultation (listening with a stethoscope) might be difficult due to movement and environmental noise during exercise.

    4. Practicality: This method is relatively quick and easy to perform during exercise, causing minimal interruption to the patient's activity.

    5. Focus on systolic pressure: During exercise, systolic pressure is more informative and easier to measure accurately than diastolic pressure. Diastolic pressure often remains stable or may even decrease slightly during aerobic exercise.

    6. Reliability: The radial artery is easily accessible and provides a clear pulse for palpation, making it a reliable site for this measurement.

    This method allows for monitoring of the systolic blood pressure response to exercise, which is crucial for assessing cardiovascular function and safety during physical activity. It's a practical compromise between accuracy and feasibility in an exercise setting.

Question 9
When placing a BP cuff on a patient’s arm the practitioner will know the cuff size is accurate by: 
Group of answer choices

observing the cuff index falls between the range lines
being able to place 4 fingers underneath the cuff
asking the patient to deeply inhale and observe the cuff movement
placing the stethoscope underneath to make sure it fits

    The practitioner will know the cuff size is accurate by observing the cuff index falls between the range lines.
        Here's why this is the correct answer:

        1. Proper cuff sizing is crucial for accurate blood pressure measurement.

        2. Most modern blood pressure cuffs have an index marker and range lines printed on them.

        3. When the cuff is wrapped around the patient's arm, the index marker should fall within the range lines indicated on the cuff.

        4. If the index marker falls within this range, it indicates that the cuff size is appropriate for the patient's arm circumference.

        5. This method ensures that the bladder inside the cuff covers about 80% of the arm circumference, which is necessary for accurate readings.

        The other options are incorrect:

        - Being able to place 4 fingers underneath the cuff is not a standard method for determining proper cuff fit.
        - Asking the patient to deeply inhale and observe cuff movement is not related to cuff sizing.
        - Placing the stethoscope underneath to make sure it fits is not a method for determining proper cuff size.

        Proper cuff sizing is essential because using a cuff that's too small can lead to falsely high readings, while a cuff that's too large can lead to falsely low readings. The index marker method is a quick and reliable way to ensure the correct cuff size is being used.

Question 10
When assessing radial heart rate, the practitioner should place their thumb over the radial artery in the wrist and count beats over 60 total seconds.  
Group of answer choices

True
False

False

From ANKI --------------------------------------------------------------------
    Quiz M05
        .Which of the following reasons are considered an indication for a Holter Monitor?
            Identifying symptoms caused by arrhythmias
            Describing the arrhythmias noted with activity
            Evaluating antiarrhythmic therapy or pacemaker functioning
            All of the options

            All of the options
            Identifying symptoms possibly caused by arrhythmias, describing the arrhythmias noted with activity, and evaluating antiarrhythmic therapy or pacemaker functioning are all indications for Holter monitor use.

        .Which of the following is the best imaging modality that detects calcium in the coronary arteries and is a noninvasive method to detect and quantify coronary atherosclerosis?
            Computer tomography
            Single-photon emission computed tomography
            Electron beam computed tomography
            Magnetic resonance imaging

            Electron beam computed tomography
            The electron beam computed tomography is used to detect calcium in the coronary arteries and is a noninvasive method to detect and quantify coronary atherosclerosis. Calcium in the coronary arteries may be an early sign of coronary artery disease.

        .Which of the following factors enhance the safety of exercise testing?
            Knowledge of when to exclude a patient.
            Knowledge of when to terminate an exercise test.
            Knowledge and skills to react to an abnormal response.
            All of the factors

            All of the factors
            All of the factors listed enhance the safety of exercise testing. Additionally, having the necessary equipment available for emergencies and having the patient sign an informed consent are important factors.
